div.head: Poem?.
div.p: Poem?.

THE RIGHT KIND OF F:LLOW. The right kind of a7fellow is modest and mellow, And geneious and brsive and benign; - His nature's apparent and clear and transparent, Like yours, gentle reader and mine. He has no verbosity, no tongue tortuosity, And never is boastful and loud; ' He is gentle and quiet and plain in his diet, And never gets mad in a crowd.: He is grand and majestic, yet meek and domestic, And spends his spare evenings at ,home ; He's a tireless searcher for all kinds of virtue, Like the perpetrator of this " pome." He don't play the fiddle, part his hair in the middle, Nor dress like an angelic dude; When he goes to a party with Meigs or Mc.Carty, He never is noisy and rude.; He lives with frugality and sweet hospitality, And wants pie but two times a day; He never eats onions, nor treads on your bunions, or growls when you get in his way. He is wise and he's witty, preserving and gritty, And has a magnificent head; He's all light and sweetness, he's thorough com- pleteness; He's perfection, in short—but he's dead!
Uariettes,

Modesty is woman's courage. The ripest fruit will not fall into your mouth. The Chinese never boil their eggs; they invariably roast them. The pleasure of doing good is the only one that does not wear out. "Grape juice kills more than grape shot," says Mr. Spurgeon. If a woman's face is her fortune, a man's cheek is .frequently his. "They sap it takes a WiSe an to make a fool." "You're Very vain to say so." Enough is always something more than a Wan pOtiataSes —to obtain one leads to wishing for two. A woman is never so badly in love that she does not try to find out the cost of her engagement ring. Men are so simple, and yield so much to necessity, that be who will deceive will always find him who will lend :himself to be deceived. The study and delight of a celestial spirit is to observe infinite wisdom carrying into effect the designs of in- finite benevolence. The largest fee Sir Astlev Cooper ever received (says the Hospital) was literally thrown at his head, He operated very successfully on a millionaire, by name Hyatt, and so delighted was the old man with his re- covery that he gave £3OO to each of his attending physicians. "But you, sir," cried the !patient to Sir Astley, "deserve something better. Take that, sir !" With that he flung his nightcap at the surgeon. Sir Astley replied with dignity, as he picked up the cap, "Sir. I will pocket the affront," and well for him that he did, for the cap was lined with a draft for 1,000 guineas. My mother often went to Bowood, and used to tell a I good story against our old friend Mr. Nassau Senior. -.Once when she was there with the Seniors and a large party, Tom Moore, who lived near and was a frequent ' visitor, was prevailed upon to sing. All prepared to Aisten to the charming performance, save Mr. Senior, who -eat down at a small writing-table and began to write with a quill pen upon Lord Lansdowne's very ribbed paper. He was compiling a paper on statistics, or some- thing of that sort. Moore began, but his singing was rendered impossible by the persistent scratch—scratch, and he turned round to see who caused the odious noise. Mr. Senior looked up, and said innocently, "Oh, you don't disturb me I assure you; pray go on. I rather like it." This caused an outburst of laughter absolutely puzzling to the unconscious statistician.—M's. Ross in Murray's Magazine. The town of having sent deputies to Pope 'Urban V., found the Pope very ill in bed. Never- theless, -without any mercy to the sick man, the • orator made a very long and a very impertinent harangue. '"Have you anything more to say?" asked his Holiness, harassed and indignant at the man's barbarity. "I have to add," re -ned the orator, "that if you do not grant my request, that I am commissioned to go through my speech a second time." His Holiness immediately ordered that all his demands should be fully and, in. stantaneously complied with. Such was the power of eloquence! "The path of duty," said a much-tried traYeller, "is tuidOilltedly through the Custom House." :1 Yes, sir," said a man with a grudge against the orator of the day; "his speech was funny enough to make a donkey laugh. I laughed till I cried." "If Britannia rules the sea," said Marlow, "there's one thing she ought to be made to do right off." "What's that ?" "Put muzzles on the sharks." A FEW TOUCHES OF SARCASM.—Like ridicule, irony is often more effective than argument, and may convey suggestions and ideas in a terse and pithy manner, as when one says, "You can't always judge by appear- ances: the man who wears a diamond pin may be • really wealthy." A gentleman, it was once said, never • inflicts pain. On which a wit remarks, "This is hard •on the dentists." Not a bad story is told of an aged -clergyman who met a man loudly declaiming against • foreign missions. "Why," asked the objector, ' doesn't 'the Church look after the heathea at home ?"' "We do," said the clergyman, quietly, and gave the man a tract. "So far as you saw," said a counsel to a witness, • "she vrae doing her ordinary household duty?" "I should say so—she was talking," was the ironical reply. "He never had but one genuine case in his life," said a lawyer of a rival, "and that was when heiprosecuted his studies." Some lawyers have had curious experiences of ironical wills. There is the not unfamiliar case of the French merchant who left a handsome legacy to a lady who had refused to marry him twenty years before, in gratitude for her kindness in not taking him at his word. There is a good deal of pointed satire in such ironical facetise as the following i—" We are reminded that the mania for adulteration is so great that you can't buy a quart of sand and be sure that it is not half sugar." A resident in a suburban house was asked how his house had fared during a snowstorm. "Oh, badly," was the reply; "my cistern is the only dry place in it." " Wot'll I do with this burglar alarm, Bill—take it along ?" asks burglar number one. Second burglar. "Yes ; slip it in the bag; we can get something tor it." "Turin's MANY A Stse."—The cattle and sheep got skeared and restive, and Tim and Tim's wife and the pal was at no end of a business to keep the lot together, capering round 'em most of the blessed time; and as soon as the faintest glimmer of light showed over the mountains and the herd quieted a bit, they all three lay down fairly fagged, and leaving the dogs to watch, slept till sun-up. Presently the youngster awoke, they heard him begin singing out something about when had they crossed the Grip, but they didn't pay much attention, till Tim pulled himself together and stood up; the sight that met him, he says, he ain't likely to disremember to the end of his born days. "I thought I'd gone crazy," says he. "for the Devil's Grip, instead of flowing to the south of us where it had been at sundown, was flowing north." He called his wife and pal to ask if his eyes told true, and all three stared speechless at the strangeness of the look-out. On the right ran the "Grip" sure enough, carrying along with it in angry fashion rubbish and trees, dead and living by the score; on the left was a wet wilderness of shingle and sand—the bed where a river had been. They got over the river without cross- ing, for the river had crossed them. How? Well, it was an uncommon puzzling thing at first sight, but there was no geping over the fact that somewhere higher :up amongst the hills a landslip had come down and filled up the usual track the river took, so it had to make another for itself right away. Tim said it must have forked off like a pair of braces, and he never saw a pair of 'em afterwards but it made him soreer feel thankful, know- ing the near shave they'd had for their lives. Yes, we never do things by halves in this country, and it's a good - story BO far, but that's hot the finish by a long way. As they were driving the things over, the men walking and the nags following behind, tney suddenly became aware • that they was footing it over a very gold-mine, for here and there among the stones and muck they found the colour almost without looking; in small flakes it was, same as is found in plenty hereabouts if you'll work hard, , but there Tim said it looked as if it might have been I scattered broadcast. They held a consultation and talked over what they should do, and it was decided that the pal should ride forward to ',yell and put in for the claim, while the rest of 'em bided there till he returned, and picked up what they could till he brought tools and • Government papers that gave 'em full rights to it. So the pal, his licked off as fast as his nag could carry; and 'Jam, he just camped it out again on the other side, but sit took him and his wife all their time to keep the flock together. and it was only once or twice during the day - was able to take a snail, and scramble down the steep hi, •• ' here aim), a • this fort he h (sure knew was re to banks t,o . be Ina before lo; The next morning by times ha was at the bank again grid sot a staggerer, and no mistake, for the river was there before him for blessed if it hadn't gone back to its original bed during the night, and the. gold lay out of any man's reach under forty feet of shinino, water.—From The World of Aden:clime. for June. div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
All " instructions " the Speaker has firmly put down, Although some were quite famous productions : But this state of things makes poor Webster look brown, For he only can speak on instructions.

A report from Yokohama states that Sir Edwin Arnold has found his long-lost son. He was third mate on a tramp steamer. The boy was educated for the Navy, but being wild he ran away to sea. Having drifted round the world for six years, he finally meets his father in Japan.

I see it is stated that Sir Walter Scott "is believed to have made £500,000 by his novels." I do not know by whom such extravagant nonsense is " believed," but it would surprise me considerably to find that Sir Walter's novels yielded him more than £150,000. The best price he ever received (.C18,000) , was paid for the "Life of Napoleon."

The Duke of Orleans, who has just come amongst us, is sketched in a magazine article by a friend who knew him well when he w undergoing his mili- tary education at the Royal Military College, Sand- hurst. He was then a bright, lively, intelligent lad, who proved his capacity by passing well through the Sandhurst examinations, despite the disadvan. tage he was under in having to pass in a foreign language.

No wonder that the Congress of the United States refuses English authors copyright. Mr. John Wana- maker, the Postmaster-General of the great Re- public, is engaged in the pirate trade, and offers to sell the " Encyclopmdia Britannica " at six shillings a volume—underselling all other pirates. It is in his capacity of the Whiteley of Philadelphia, not as head of the United States Post Office, that Mr. Wanamaker makes his offer.

A revolution is threatened in the wine trade. Someone has discovered a method of making wine from raisins, which, it is said, gives better results than wine made from grapes. However that be, the French Government have been so much influenced by the proposal as to impose a heavy excise duty on raisins. Mr. Childers is pressing Sir James Fergus- son to lay on the table any papers that may have reached the Foreign Office on the subject.

It has been asserted by physiognomists that we come to resemble those amongst whom we live by unconscious imitation of the expression of their features. The photographic Society of Geneva, has been testing the truth of this theory. From photo- graphs of seventy-eight old couples, and of as many adult br9thers and sisters, it was found that twenty-fir:oar of the former resembled each other much more strongly tl9 an as many of the latter, who were thought most like each other.

The promoters of the Wenlock Olympian Games will welcome the announcsment that Sir William Dyke, on behalf of the Education Department, has conceded a point, which has been agitated for dur- ing forty years, in making a grant for physical edu- cation. The chief of a Liverpool gymnasium is to visit a number of foreign schools and inspect the exercises in use there, some of which are said to expand the chest by two inches in the same period that an expansion of half an inch would take place as a result of drill.

There is a great sensation in the House over Com- mander Bethell's frank characterisation of the " shadowing " process in Ireland as "damnable." Commander Bethell is an honest Tory, who was greatly shocked by a sight of some of Mr. Patrick O'Brien's instantaneous photos of priests and others being shadowed by policemen. The photos were taken in every possible attitude, and at all stages of the process, and being shown over the House, caused a number of remarks that would have made Mr. Balfour's ear tingle.

The special correspondent of the " Telegraph,' who has been talking with Bismarck, tells some- thing of the ex-Chancellor's habits. With regard to smokingßismarck makes an important confes- sion. He says :—Cigar smoking I have given up altogether. of course under advice. It is debilitat- ing, and bad for the nerves. An inveterate smoker such as I usedto be, probably gets through 100,000 cigars, in his life, if he reaches a fair average age. But he would live longer, and feel better all his time if he did without them.

The "Pall Mall Gazette" says :—Stanley's book will be published on the 24th, or a week later than was expected. This delay has been caused by the Scribners, who, not unnaturally, demand coin- cidence of publication on both sides of the Atlantic. Mr. Marston intends to keep a sharp look-out for newspapers which may help themselves too frcely to the book, which, by the way, Mr. Marston de- clares is all "plums." On the 26th the " firm " will ' celebrate the event by a dinner party, at which, of course, Mr. Stanley will be the honoured guest.

A Correspondent at Ober-Ammergau, referring to a report published in some of the English papers to the effect that the Passion Play would not by the common vote of the people be repeated after this year, says :—" There is hardly any form of punish- ment the Ober-Ammergauers would not apply to the one among them who dared suggest such a thing as stopping the plays. If the writer had said Wilt he thought the 700 players would undertake a tournee through Europe and America in• a couple of years, I should be rather disposed.to believe him."

"The Star" salutes the first lady Senior Wrangler. Miss Fawcett has probably done more to advance the "rights of woman" than any single member of her sex; and, remembering the services of her father and mother to the same cause, there is no one whom the world should be more pleased to see in such a position. We have now had a lady "Senior Classic" and a lady "Senior Wrangler." Women have measured themselves against men in the toughest intellectual contests. and proved them- selves the stronger. A lady Prime Minister and a lady Archbishop of Canterbury are only a question of time.

-- Miss Fawcett is going to stay up in Cambridge, her idea being to " tutorise" for lathes, though no- thing is definitely settled. She has still a final ex- amination to pass. in view of which she will have to d ecide wh at branch of mathematics she will specially pursue. She is most-popular at Newnham, as she was at Clapham, ;her character being frank, gener- ous, impulsive, and altogether sweet and unaf- fected.

Good news for all who go down to Euston and King's Cross in hansoms, and for all travellers be- tween the north and south of the metropolis! The Bloomsbury barriers are howled over. The County Council has burst the Duke of Bedford's bonds I asunder. On Tuesday the Bill promoted for this purpose was passed as to its preamble, and what is more, the Select Committee refuses to grant com- pensation either to the Duke or any of his. tenants. This makes an end of the barriers at Sidmouth-st , Upper Woburn-place, Torrington-place, and Gordon- at. incidentally. it is one of the most gratifying victories of public interest over private pOvilege that have been won for a long time.
Dockers

Toni Mann, the president of the . Union, Is thirty-five, having been born at Foleshill, War- wickshire, in 1856. Foleshill is in the centre of the coalfields, and Tom worked in the mines as a boy. He was next in Birmingham, and came to London in 1887. It was not until 1881 that he joined the Amalgated Society of Engineers. We learn these facts, from the dockers' little paper, the " Monthly Record," which also says of Mr. Mann :--"How much we owe to his ready pen, his eloquence born of his earnestness, and his Indefatigable spirit and love of the work his office entails upon him, can only be measured by the strength of our union, which he has done much to build up."

Mr. Andrew Carnegie, the Scottish-American millionaire, is again in this country, but he modestly' stayed away from the opening of the great free library which be has presented to the city of Edin- burgh. There were many excellent libraries in Edinburgh before, such as the Mechanic's, or that of the Philosophic Institution. There is also the great Advocates Library; but, although it receives by the copyright law a copy of every book publiShed in Great Britain, it shuts its doors to the general public, and is mainly used by the advocates. The Carnegie Library is situated on George the Fourth Bridge, close by the historic High-st. It will be a great boon to the working classes who live 'in the neighbourhood. . --

Ann Jane. Th' lark, an thrush, an th' blackbird, wi a lot mooare o' th' feathered tribe.made th' sweetest music wi'd yerd fur monny a day. Well, when wi geet whoam wi fund Ann Jane o ow a fluster, an' aw could see at snmmat wur up. Con theaw find us owt t drink, owd lass ?" aw sed "wi are welly dried up." Wot dun yo' say to a drop ov buttermilk?" hoo sed "Its wo'th its' weight i' goold at this toime o'th ye'r." Eawr John sed he cud roll in it, he wur that thirsty, an' wi drank a quart between us to th' grate setisfackshun or Ann Jane, whoa browt on th' dumplin'. " Wheay, wheer's th' beef an th" taters ?" aw sed. " Th' beef's not quoite dun yet, so yo' mun be gooin' on wi' th' puddin' fust," boo sed.

Neaw whether it wur th' walk at ud gan us a good anpytite fur dinner aw kno' not, but wi tucked in wi might an main, forgettin' aw abeawt th' beef till wi f'und wi'd no reawm fur it. Ann Jane sed boo wur glad t' yer that becos' it bein' Whit-Monday th' shops wur aw shut up an' hoo'd not been able t' get ony flesh meat, but boo thowt if wi geet a sup o' buttermilk an pleonty gooseberry puddin' wi shouldn't want varry much mooare ov onything. When wi yerd this, wi brast eawt lafin' at th' trick th' owd lass ud sarved us, but at th' same toime wi thowt it wur th' best gooseberry puddin' wi'd ever bed.
NEW BOOKS, &c.

"My Religion" is tbe title of one of the most int- portant woehe Which has been issued by that eminent Russiari Writer, Count L. N. Tolstoi. The volume is translated by Mr. HuntQton Smith, who accompanies it by an appropriate preface, dealing with the works and the character of the author. Count Tolstoi himself, in the introduction, says "I have not always been possessed with the religious i ideas set forth n this book. For thirty-five years of my life I was, in the proper acceptation of the word, a nihilist—not a revolutionary socialist, but I a man who believed in nothing. Five years ago faith came to me. I believed in the doctrine of Jesus, and my whole life underwent a sudden trans- formation." It is the object of "My Religion" to state the reasons for this transformation. Tolstoi, enthusiast,or dreamer, as he may be called, is essen- tially a reasoner and logician, looking at matters from his point of view. In this work hes brushes aside dogmas and traditions, and goes straight to the words of Jesus Himself, putting upon them throughout what he believes to be a plain, common- sense interpretation. Having got at the common- sense v i 'view of the meaning, he nsists upon the com- mandments given being literally followed. He I starts with Matthew v, 38 and 39--" Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth. But I say unto you That ye resist not evil." He proceeds to show that this teaching— " Resist not evil "—is in entire opposition to the old doctrine of violence, and there must be no more re- sistance to evil of any kind if a man would become a true Christian. In support of this, he quotes the texts which refer to *" turning the other cheek," "being used despitefully," &c., And so with the text 'Judge not that ye be not judged." Count TolstoFs contention is that this is a condemnation of Civil Courts, and tribunals of every kind. His broad argument iv that "Fire cannot extinguish fire; so evil cannot suppress evil." Coming to the passage that "Whosoever is angry with he brother without a, cause shall be m danger of the judgment," he ehovvs how the words "with- out cause"' were a stumbling block to his eccep- tance of the teaching as in harmony with, the rest of Christ's commandments, and now he satisfied himself that the phrase is not to be found he the most ancient readings, and ought therefore to lie struck out as destructive to the true meaning of the text. Count Tolstoi pursues, a similar course with other portions of Scripture and his expositions and amendments certainly tend toeiarmonise them' as a whole. He explains, far instance, that the most difficult of all injanctions "Love your enemies"—refers not to enemies in the crdinary sense, not in the ordinary sense a ipersonal enemy,- but is employed in the Gospels n, the sense, of as hostile people. His interpretation of the text, there-- fore, is -ST bu have heard that you must love-those of your own race, and hate. foreigners, but say unto you, love everyone without distinction of nationality?' "Swear no at all "is, as might be expected, accepted in its plain signification os an injunction not to enter into (paths of any kind, in any sort of court, or for any sort of purpose. Count Tolstoi is, of course, quite aware that this interpre- tation of Christianity is diametrically opposed to the received teaching, and that if the doetrineof Jesus is applied as he says it should be applied,-it' will overturn the foundations of existing society. But what of that if the people become truly Christian? His point is that they will cease to-do evil, and learn to do well, ancr that there will be no need of all the props and stays of State, which are based, from', beginnins to end, upon the theory that violence must be resisted lnoviolence. No one can read "My Religion" without' perceiving that' Count Tolstoi means what he says, and that he, is - keen critic and close reasoner. His answer to the- thousand and one sneerers who say that his teach ing won't work is that he is making it wovkin'his own case, and the question for theregt of the world is—" Are they ready to go and doelikewiser- The I work is published' by Mr. WalterSeott, of London, •as part of the series of Count Tolatoi's worka In the" Great Writers Series," issued by the same firm, we have the life of" George Elliot," fix= the pen of Mr. Oscar Browning. This biography-of the great novelist will doubtless be welcomed by a large body of readers, and particularly bYthiese who cannot afford to procure the "Life and letters of George Elliot," as published by her husband, Mr. John Cross. .Mr. Browning is not content with giv- ing a mere skeleton outline of the main facta-of the life of George. Elliot." He introduces a coneider- able amount of suggestive and discriminating criticism. He was, personally acquainted with the novelist for a considerable number of year', .and speaks, therefore, as to many points, with.. direct aurhority. It is hardly necessary to say that he regards George Elliot" as the greatest female writer of fiction that the world has yet known, " Scribner's Magazine" for Ju ine s distinguished in its frontispiece by a splendid portrait of Mr. Stanley,from a photograph taken at Cairo in. March, 1890. This is followed by an article on the-o-Emin Pu.sha Relief Expedition," from the pen of Mr. Stanley. The article quotes largely from the book which is about to,be publish ed„but it is exoeedingly interesting, and exceedingly -7aluable in so far as, it anticipates that work. It is accompanied by portraits of Emilie and Stanley's principal, officers,. and with illustrations of some of the princiPaiL scenes and event& in his men/treble journey through Darkest Africa. Other illustrated papers- in this - month's issue are "The Ciey House,"" Barbizone and "Jean Francois Millett." The first part is given of a promising story with the title of "Jerry.!" "In the Valley ''reaches chapter 32, and,there is..a third article " The Rights of a Citizen." We had occasion last week to quote fully from an article in the "Westminster Review on "Home, Rule all Round," by Ur. John Lenge. M.P. The other papers in the June number are also strong and noteworthy. The topics are as follow :—"The , Index Librolum Prohibitorum," "Fusion or Diffu- sion," "The Legitimacy of Children," " Politicall Economy and Social Reform," "Earl Grey and the Princess Lieven," "The Compleae Gentleman," "Home Affairs," &c. The "Century Magazine" leads offewith a portinit I of Mr. Walter Besant, the novelist, followed by an I illustrated article on "London Polytechnics and , People's Palaces." The "Artist Letters from. Japan," I illustrated, are continued, and there are some striking illustrations of " Track Athletics in America," Amongst other papers,. illustrated, should be named," rhe Women of the French Salons," "A Modern Colourist." and the "Biography of Joseph Jefferson." The fiction, continued and complete. maintains the high reputation of the magazine. we The "Newbery Ho Megazine," published by Messrs. Griffith, Ferree, and Co., is &comparatively new venture, which admirably maintains the lines upon which it set out as a "monthly review for clergy and laity." It is a matter of course to say that it is difficult to satisfactorily, eater for both classes, but this difficulty has been overcome in the "Newbery *House Magazine." "Our Pilgrimage Ober-Amtnergau " illustrated, will be read 'with th eipecial interest' w at the presenthamsomiuesnt been t, bwhn pentehre_ celebrated "Passion Play" formed. Two other illustrated artyes are " Reli- gious Art at the May Exhibition," and " Popular Astronomy." Other well-written articles, are on such topics as "Lux Mundi," " Gambling," "Jewels and Gems," "The' Miracles of History," " Sermon Outlines," &c. " Lippincott's Magazine " is distinguished by lead- ing off each month with an excellent complete novel. The one in the current number is by Mary E. Stickney, and its title is " Circumstantial Evi- dence." It is followed by papers on The origin of Chinese Culture and "Gorge Henry Boker,"eteleiction for the People," " A Popular Topic '-,=”Round Robin Talks,' 'A Dead Man's ' k." 1. .

spite of the exhibition of numerous photographs in the shops the person of the General is little known, so that his appearance excites no attention. His erect bearing shows no trace of the hard work he has to do. He is a tall, powerful man. whose white hair and bushy eyebrows much resemble those of the ex-Chancellor. He has an amiable expression of face, and his courteous and friendly manner to his subordinates is much praised.

Sir William Harcourt says that the greatest man of affairs he ever knew was Count Schouvaloff. He was Russian Ambassador during the Beaconsfield Ministry, when the relations of Russia and England were so severely strained. He knew what took place in the Tory Cabinet within an hour or so, and was ' able to checkmate every move with hnerring in- stinct. He had one great weakness. After be had taken his many bumpers at dinner—he was glad to have a bottle of champagne at his side after dinner. " Ah. you treat me," he used to say to the friends who were kind to his weakness "As if I were Lord --" a peer, known to most of the world for his devotion to the worship of Bacchus. Count Schou- { valoff died the other day in his sixtieth year.

The perennial character of the Irish question is I curiously illustrated in a letter written fifty-five years ago by Walter Savage Landor to the Earl of Mulgrave, then Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland. It formed the dedicatory letter of "Pericles and Asp- sia," which, though it was omitted from the first edition, is reinstated in the charming edition which forms the latest issue of the Temple Library, pub- lished by Messrs. Dent. "our Excellency," Landor writes, will correct the faults, and inasmuch as sagacity, integrity, firmness, and moderation can do it, will compensate for the iniquities and atrocities of six centuries. You will unite Great Britain and Ireland, which our Princes and Parliaments, until now, have never wisely planned nor honestly in- tended." The "until now," though at last within Imeasurable distance, remains, unfulfilled.

The official announcement about Prince " Eddie's" new title is rather an inconvenient one, "Duke of Clarence and Avondale" is a mouthful ot a name, and there seems to be no more reason for so styling His Royal Highness than for speaking of the claim- ant Eimz of Hanover as "Duke of Cumberland and Teviotdale," i)r the Duke of Connaught as "Duke of Connaught and Strathearne." There are even more tremendous accumulations of ducal honours in some families which are not royal. The Duke of Hamilton is also Duke of Brandon in the English peerage and Duke of Chatelherault in Prance. The late Duke was in the habit of signing himself by the abbreviated form of" Ham., Chat., and Bran.;' and tradition relates that having once so signed a letter to a firm of tradesmen His Grace received an answer addressed "Messrs. Ham, Chat, and Bran," and beginning "Gents."

Sir Frederick Leighton, Mr. Alcoa Tademarand Mr. Du Manner have severally received kind notes from M. Pasteur, thanking them for the little sketches with which they illustrated the album that has just been presented to the great chemist. Last year, at A time when M. Pasteur was made the subject of certain attacks, Mrs. -Priestley, wife of the well- known physician, drew up a little memorial expres- sing in a couple of sentences the high appreciation in which the signatories held the services M.Pasteur had rendered to mankind. A large number of signatures were obtained in the United States. Then the book came over here, and some hundreds of the most disquished people in London signed it. Sir Henry Roscoe brought it down to the House of Commons. and obtained a large number of signa- tures, including that of Mr. Gladstone. The artists named not only signed their names, but contributed little sketches, Du Manlier very appropriately drawing a dog. M. Fasteur has been greatly pleased by this unique international tribute.

div.head: ANN JANE AN' TIT DUMPLIN'.
div.p: ANN JANE AN' TIT DUMPLIN'.
Br WILKINS MICAWBER.

Aw'd had mi dinner and wur just havin' a quiet smoke an' readin'' th' " Examiner," when Ann Jane remoinded mi at it wur Whit-sunday t' morn, an' if aw intended t' celebrate th day i'th' usual way wi gooseberry puddin avi'd better stir mysel an coome an help her t' pick th' fruit, or else aw'd hay t' goo

beawCit. Neaw fur sum years its anus bin a custom wi us t' hay a gooseberry puddin—if wi con get it—on Whit-Sunday, just lqike sum fooak goo in fur eatin cod-fish an mackerel on good Friday, tho' fur mi own part aw'd rayther hay a bit ov beef, but then aw reckon it wouldn't do fur eNeryb(xly's taste t' be

t' same, would it? Well, aw'm varry fond ov a bit ov gooseberrypud- din mysel, providin' th' paste isn't too thick, so aw followed th' owd lass into th' garden fur t' look fur th' berries. Aw say look, becos aw man te'l yo we'd ony two trees, an' at this toime o'th year th' berries bein' rayther small, an' Ann Jane a bit near sighted, it w'd have getten dark befooare hoo'd fund enoo t' mak' a puddin wi, if aw hadn't gone an' helped her. Aw'd no sooner getten in th' garden than aw wur merch't back agen fur summat t' put em in. Neaw ther wur sev'ral basins on th' shelf at w'd hay dun varry noicely, but summat put it mi yed t' tak a milk dish at had bin Ann Jane's mother's, which stood .on th' top-mooast shelf ov o', and in order t' get at it aw had t' stand on a little table, but whether aw oer-balanst mysel, or th' table cocked oer, aw dunno, bu' aw coome to th' floor wi a bonny bang, smashin' th' mich-prized milk dish t' pieces an neorly killin' repel' th' bargain. Ann Jane wur coomin' t' see No heer aw wur and had just getten to th' door when aw tumbled, an' boo fund mi lyin' on mi back i' th' middle o' th' kitchen floor. " Theau great yorney" boo sed, " what art dociii theere ? Doesta kno theau's neorly freetent th' Joffe eawt omi ,Theau'll bi playin thi tricks. once too often." Aw thowt it best fur Viet hur see at it wur no joke this toinae, so aw groant once or twice, an' when hoo seed mi pale face an mi tire stanclin' straight up boo lookt quoite concerned an helpt mi into th' rocking cheor. "Art hurt?" hoo sed, an wur proceedin t' syrapa- ' thisewi me when boo spotted th' brokken milk-dish, an' settin up a skroike cried eawt—" Theau doesn't meon t' say theau's brokken mi mother's milk-dish; doesta Efrayhum r "Aw couldn't help it" aw replied," th' table gay way, an aw've neorly brokken mi neck besides th' milk dith." "Eh dear," boo sed," aw nevvur seed gel crazy foos as you men are i' mi boife. Whatevvur put it in thi yed t' get th' milk-dish when ther wur plenty ov basins close to thi hand? Avvd put it up them thinkin it wod bi eawt o thi road." "Well," aw sed, " th' toime 'at wants overt th' crockery line theau mun fotch it thysel." " Theau'rt a poor mon ivt cawn't fotch a dish beaut breakin it. Bu then au reckon o men are pretty mich alioke i' that respeckt ;;aw've yerd mi moather say !at mi feyther couldn't goo to: th' cub- bort beaut breakin something." Ony mooare-talk oh th' subjeckt wur interrupted bi Lb' postman bringin' us •st letter fro eawr John's wiofe sayin'atO being well tha'd cum_' an spend Whit-Mondap we us an hay' a look at th' "Ship Cut." When, Ann Jane had read th" letter hoc,' seeomed better tempert, altbo boo gan' th' postman a blowin' up fur knockitiso leawd. "Aw tell thi wot, Efrayhum, doesn't think it ud bi better if wed th puddin o' Monday istead, en t' morn Tbeau knows you lad's varry fond. o' paddin, an wi mutt get a bit ok sumtnat extra for em. The. don't cum ev'ry day." "Pleos thisel,' aw sed." Alter wot'S happen't, awm nobbut i' poor trim fur pikin' gooseberries aw con tell thi," and shortly after aw went t' bed. Th' nett mornin'ini yed ached, an aw felt stiff an sore, so aw stopt r bed aw day au' rested mysel • listning to th' sparrows chirp.in' th' spouts till aw went sleep ogen. Aw wakken tiff abeaut eix o'clock th' followin' mornin' feelin' mich better ter havin' visited th' Land o' Nod. Aw geet up then and made th' tore, an aw'd th' kettla boilin' an a bit or bacon frizzlin befooar Ann Jane londed deawnstears. At eight o'clock wi' wur i th' garden pickin' gooseberries, and bi th' toime wi'd getten enoo eswr John and his wiofe arrived. After tha'd bad a bit o' surathin' t' eat, wi trotted off to th' "Ship Cut," leovin Ann Jane awhoam t' look after th' heawse an boil th'dumplin. We'd a varry noice walk althe it ud a bin moore interestin' if th' men ud bin warkin' an' th' mas- hineery gooitf, but th' navvies nur aw gone a plea- suring. "Brownie "wi his Darkie "wi his spade, an Lanky "wi his barrow, wur not te bi seen, whoile Daresb'ry " an th' tother little en- gines at hay done sich good wark carryin' away thousands ov tons ov sand an' stone / wur moshun- less, wi not even a whistle, an th' ekskavator wi thoose terrible teeth lay powerless to move at th' bottom o th' minim' But fur aw that ther wur pleonty. to look at, an mich to marvel at. Leoviti th'" Ship Cut" atyrhelwall, we geet into th' country lanes an th‘ green-fields wheere th' buttercups and daisies grow, an little childer roam content an happy.' Th' hawthern an laburnum, too, wur at its best an wi geet a bit t' tak whoant to
Diary." &c., concluding with the customary sprightly, "Contributions from the Wits." _ _

The "English. Illustrated Magazine" has for front: ispiece a highly finished portrait Of Mr. W. G. Gragle; he cricketer, aid it is followed by an article on ' cricket by that gentleman. There is an illustrated paper on `• Laceinaking in Ireland,' and another illustrated article with the title ot "A Castle on Mount Etna." Mr. William Morris commences what is likely to prove a charactelistic story with he title of "The Glittering Plain,or the Land of Living Men." Lady Blennerhassett contribute an article on "German Girlhood," and there is a musical set- ting of Tennyson's beautiful poem "Crossing the Bar.'

_ We have received copies of two sermons by tho Rev. F. K. Freeston, of Cake-st. Chapel, Warrington, They have been printed in each case by request, and at the cost of members of the congregation. The first bears the title of "A Creedless Faith," and in it Mr.Freeston.with conspicuous clearness and method, sets forth what may be termed the Unitarian view of creeds and dogmas. There is every evidence that Mr. Freeston has read much and thought much, and that he is, a rational and earnest exponent of his views of the truth. "Fidelity the fruit of Faith "is the title of the second sermon. Mr. Freeston has no sympathy with what some people call "good- natured neutrality." "Charity," he says, "let us have charity always." " Charity always, but neu- trality never." In another passage he remarks—"A doctrine is a growing plant, with its roots in the soil and its leaves in the sun, budding into flower and bringing forth fruit as the pride and pledge of its health and vitality. Dogma, is the same plant dried and dead, perhaps within the pages of some dust be-ridden book, with no fragrance but that of the musty tome, no colour but that of its faded past, no power save that of crumbling decay. Doctrine we desire, dogma we deplore." It will be seen from these extracts that Mr. Freeston is a thinker, and that he has something better to offer than lifeless dogma. Mr. John Ileyvvood, publisher, Manchester, offers a whole library for a shilling to those who are holi- day-making, or otherwise in the humour for read- ing, fiction. This is a series of a dozen stories issued at id. each, with the title of " Seaside Library." Each story is, of course, different, the quality is fairly good, there is plenty of incident, and altogether "lots for the money.'

div.head: BALOON IN MID-ON.
div.p: A BALOON IN MID-ON.

Captain Lindh,. of the Swedish barqUe Architect, of Helsenburg, whicharrived on Tuesday at Queenstown, reports having been in close company with a: large baloon for a short Time in mid-ocean at nine o'clock at night on the 24th ult. The baloon was well inflated with gas at the time ; but how many persons occupied seats in the car Captain Lindh cannot say, as darken- mess prevented him from ascertaining. He states that , while on deck with all the crew he sew, a baloon travel- ling rapidly through the air. It was bearing down on thew, and was only 20ft. above thelevel of the sea. Captain Lindh first intended to make preparations to capture it and rescue theoccupants from their very dan- gerous position but on cOnsideration it was decided not to run the risk: The baloon was wafted speetlily with a fresh south-west breeze' until it almost touched the vessel. It had long and stent ropes hanging out from the car,. with grappling irons attached.. Captain Lindh said that, judging from the way the windebad been blowing since he had sailed from Florida, the baloon had been blown off the' coast of ,Newfoundlarrd, and it was reasonable to conclbde that when the occupants realized thii they let off an escape of gas and threvr out,their grapplings with the hops-of strik_ nig one of the•nurnerous fishing vessels off that coast.

The mathematical tripos lists were published at Cam- inridge University,- on Saturday. The first eight wrang- lers are—Bennett, (St. John's), Segar (Trinity), Brand Pembroke), Vangoat (Trinity), Crawford (King's), Reeves (St. John). Troup (Pembroke), Alexander - (St. John'). Miss Gi P. Fawcett, of Newnham College, daughter of the late Professor Fawcett, is declared to be. above the s enior wrangler. Miss Fawcntt is about 3. or 22'years of age. During the time thn- has been at Nvenhain the greatest expectations of; :lor knowledge of mathematics have been entertained,.and her position in the triples ti us year occasions no surprise. On ker narme.bng, read out there was loud cheering. MissFawc ett, it is stated, was a long way ahead of Mr. Bennett,, the Senior Wrangler, forshe obtained four hundred marks more than he. Miss Fawcett is about twenty-one y ears of age, tall, slenderand has dark hair, whilst her pale face is full of intellectnal force mingled with sweetne as. She is a student at Clough Hall, the largest and In test addition lo Newham College. This hall was opei ted by the Princess of Wales a few years ago. Notwithstanding her ad- vanced years; and somewhat delicate health, she takes a inost'nctive iriterese in the college, and no one is more .. pleased at the brilliant success of Misssrawcett, though kliss-Clough's delight is shared by Miss Helen Gladstorie the vine-prim ipal, .whose devotion teNewnham cannot praised. HOITANG OF ' THE WORICENG CLASSES.

The-Housing of the Working Classes Acts (Amend- ment > Bill, pio 3pared'and brought in by-Mr; Ritchie, Mr. VO.ttliews a,nd Mt. , Long, has been circulated. It. definenthZ duties of local authorities and officers as to the closing and demolition of dwellings, deemed unfit for 'Hunan habitation, . A building considered to be obstrun die, that is,in dosa-prenitnity to or in contact with ether ' buildings, so as to ,prevent-the carrying out of requisite improvements itu the latter, may be altered or derool- isbed. When an. order for demolition has been carried out, the space on, which the buildings formerly' stood- may be dedicated as highway or open space; or appro- priated, sold, or-let, for. the erection of working-class dwellings ;or exchanged for neighbouring land more suitable for such erection. Ldcal authorities are em- powered to borrow money for purposes of purcht3se •• or compensation. A, specially appointed officer may at twenty-four hours' notice demand admittance to pre- mises ifor the purposes of inspection or valuation under ' 'the. Act. Where removal is necessitated by operations 'under the Act; the tenant, if a weekly tenant, rsay be con3Pensated for the- cost incurred:in removing.—A .Bill /to consolidate the Housing of the .Working Clasaus Acts d's also brought, fervrard by the three above-named ' 'members.

div.head: NOT' WLSER BUM STRONGER.
div.p: NOT' WLSER BUM STRONGER.
LORD HARTINGTON'S VIEW OF WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.

Lord Haeington, speaking at the annual meeting of the Women's Liberal Unionist Association at St. Georges Hall,London,,on•Wednesday, said he had never taken an active part in what were called women's rights, nor had he ever voted for the admission of women to the Paxlia- mentary,franchise. At the same time, no one could I deny there were a very large number of women who who were morn fitted for the exercise of the franchise • than was the case of 'a greatquamber of men. If he hesi- tated to vote for the admission of women to the fran- chise, his reasons were exclusively of a practical charac- ter. Men might not be wiser, but they, were stronger than wc-)men„,and he entertained some doubt whether merlin an important crisis,wouldconsent to be governed by women. The want of the possession of the suffrage did not, however, prevent women from exercising an indirect inhaence in politics. TWO. CHILDREN BURNT TO DEATH.

On Sunday night, two children, one aged three years and the other 14 months,were burned to death by & fire which occurred in Richard-st., Glasgow, pind themother, Margaret Evans, throwing herself through the window, ,received injuries which are likely to prove fatal'. The Iroom they occupied was in the third storey. Mrs. Evans ,returned home ha the afternoon, and went to bed with her two children. Before the neighbours were aware that anything was amiss, the woman had pulled down the lower sash of the window and precipitated herself on to the pavement beloW. It was then seen that the house was on fire, and the briaades were summoned. On en- tering the room,, the firemen found the two children lying in bed dead, and charred beyond recognition. The fire was extinguished without difficulty.

Snow felt a short time at St. Louis on Thursday after- noon, followed by one of the most phenomenal hail- storms on record. One hailstone measured at the Signal Service Station proved to be nine inches in circum- ference.

• SMATOIIT TO iite KNEE 3. , TEEN manager looked at the prisoner, as if ;Wang that he had mastered his obstinacy by the product,on of thi handkerchief, and them, as it was nearly time helm to go, he said: - "Look here, Mark; you see what a little thing up- sets the best-laid plots. But there, say no mtve • only this: I'll forgive yozinn one condition. "What is that ? " said Mark, absently. "That you inaki.i restitution. Now, teR Me; where is' the money? :those notes cannot have beewchangeci, and there are all those securities." Mark gazed at him in we dreamy wayr baralY comprehending his words, for his thoughts were Wi;la his dead mother, and her horror could she hero been there to know that her idolised son was a 0011Onon thief—a burglar who stopped anottiing to, Ow hii ends, even toslieltering himself blind his own brother, while with plausible words and' paltry cajolerf h. offered him his sympathy. "Do you hear, Mark?" said the old man, eiza• patiently. "'Come, man, make 'a clean breast of it, and cast away this cursed thing which tempted you7'. Mark still gazed at him vacantly... for now he thoughts were with Ruth. What was he to do to save. her tram a life of misery with the man- she loved , How was she to be taught his true chartipter

—His true character? Here Mark stopped; for after all what neidencelad be beyond the finding of that handkerchief to show that Martin was guilty? Might it,not all prorate) be a mistake? "No," he groaned to himself; it was no misnike; but he could not say., himself at Martin's enemas —he could not denouncehim. "Mark Woolford," said the old manager, rising, "I have been deceived in you. I hoped for repentance end a desire to make amends for the sin you have- ecra- mitted. But once more I ask you—ervine you my word as a man that I will not have the inform:Von ueed against you at your trial—where is that money rr t "I cannot tell you," said Mark, desperately. "Will you give it up to its owners, whom you bents so injured by your act?" "I cannot," was the stern reply. "Then I have done with you, said the old man fix a furious whisper. "Coward !—scoundrel wretch: I was ready with forgiveness, believing in your temptation. I was ready to give you my hand-- to condone the past; but I find that you are after alb a villain—rotten to the core." He strode out of the place without another word',. leaving Mark pale as ashes, drinking more and more deeply of his bitter cup, but recalling the past and. trying to gain strength from tbe promise hehad wade. Martin was his next visitor, and he came in a eool, easy way, holding out his band, which was not taken. "Sulky, oh?" he said. " Well, being Shut up like this must make a man gruff." There was silence for a time, during which Mark eyed him curiously, almost deubtine his guilt. "When did you see Huth? " said Mark, at last. Martin returned the curious look, and then with a smile full of cunning: "That's private," he said. "Why P" " Let me ask you- another question," said Mark, which you may answer or net as you please;" and as he spoke he gazed searchinuly in his brother's face: "What have you done with the money?" "Money!" said Martin, calmly. "What mooPy ? The— Oh, I see; the Boys. I offered you to go off with." "The money you took from the strong vault," said Mark, in a whisper. Martin gazed at him, wonderingly.. " Why, Mark, old man," he said, "are you going off your head? What do you means I don't keep accusing you of that coup." Mark went to the little wicket in the door, and con- vinced himself that they were not being watched by any inquisitive warder. He then thrust his hand into his breast, and turned to his brother, who was seated upon the stool. Martin, I swore to your mother, upon her dying bed, that I would be like a guardian to you. Have I done my duty 2" "Oh, yes," said the other, lightly ; "but what have you got in your breast ?" "Your condemnation," said Mark, so sternly that Martin started up, but his brother was between him and the door. "I 'say, no violence," he exclaimed. "A word from me wilthring help. Are you mad ?" "Nearly," was the calm reply; "but listen : In spite of all my efforts you have gone on from bad to worse— gambling, dissipation, neglect ef duty—till I have felt that I must interfere and put a stop to the ietimacy between you and Ruth." "Oh, that's the sore Once, is it?" said Martin, sontemptuously. "But I would not," continued Mark, without hei ding , the interruption. "I-was hopeful that the pure love of an innocent girl alight lead you into a better

course." "Oh, come, Mask," cried'Martin. "I came here to help and comfort you, and you begin to preach. use what you are aiming at. You know that you will be taken care of for a couple o? years, and you want to put a stop to anything between Ruth and me, so that youmay cut in when you come out." "Silence, boy !" said Mark, hoarsely. "You meature DIQ, by your own paltry. spirit. Listen while I tell you —I know all." • "All what?" • "Your cowardly sin; and I tell you this, that you shall see Ruth no more." "Who's to stop the ?" • "I," said liark, in a- low, deep- whisper. "Did I not tell you,tbat I know' all?" ' "Bali! your trouble haw turned your brain, Miliek. Them-her:alto. Lome to help you, and now I find that your old jealousy of Ruth's preference for me has blandtesp. There, ',must. gO ; I shan't get in again, before your trial." "Sit down again," said Mark, so fiercely, that the young maw shrank back, looking ashy pale. "I tell you that you shall see Ruth no more, for you are too great a villain to pollute her again with your touch." Go on," said Martin, "rn bear it. I cannot turn upon you now." - 'Look here, Martin: clever, etunning,unscrupulons men make their plane—perfect, as they think, but they always leave one little thing undone. A man- -God forgive me. No! No man—a coward without a spark of feeling elected, no doubt urged theretc by BOMA of his scoundrelly associates, to rob his em- ployers.. His schemes were clever, and he was sue. 04300'0. He carriede off his plunder after narrowly escaping•being,twice a murderer—in one case of a man who had, with all his eccentricity, treated him with the indulgence of a father." "Web, I know alltthie said Martin. "Why did you do it then ?" "That creature as I my,* continued Markt, "laid hisschemes well; he escaped, but he allowed an inno- cent-man to be seized for his sin without a word. AU looked smooth for him—the world believed even his friends believed the unfortunate scapegoat guilty ; and this- wretch mocked at his sufferings and, smugly se3- satisfied, waited till his third victim wan punished before calmly sitting down to the enjoyment of his plunder. But he forgot one thing—cleveras he was he left behind him the damning token of his guilt, ready to show all men who the real offender was.' ' "What do you mem, Mark ?" cried Martin, whose face had assumed a cadaverous hue, as. he strove in vain to free his eyes from his brother's stern gaze. "This!" cried Mark, tearing the handkerchief from his breast. "See: the rohbeeleft this in the.hedroona, ready for his victim to staunch his wound, perhaps save his life. Look, Martin, it has the robber's name in the corner—the name worked there by a tender mother who—l thank heaven—is dead. Read! The villain's name is "Hush f' whispered Martin, as he snatched the handkerchief away. "Would yos betray your own brother?' Mark smiled bitterly to see how lliartin,was thrown off his guard, and the eagernesswith which-he thrust the handkerchief out of sight. "Betray you?" he said. "Why not? Why should I suffer for you, sir? Martin, we shall change places." " Mark, for God's sake !—for our mother's sake!" rasped the wretched man, throwing himself upon his knees—unnerved, beaten, helpless ma a child---" have mercy on me. I was mad." "Ask mercy of your Maker," sail Mark, sternly, as he gazed down at the abject, trembling wretch before him. all his dash and jauntiness gone, and nothing but the grovelling, unmasked coward clinging to lii4 accuser's knees, imploring him to be silent. "I was mad," he whispered again. "I hid Tronoy to pay. I was driven to it by others. I did not know what I was doing. Mark—brother !" "Stop! You are no brother of mine." "But give me another chance,Mark,and I'll amend. I'll turn over another leaf— I'll —" "Silence! there is no time to waste," sad Mark, sternly. "Listen to me. Go at once to the hout,?‘ jou have disgraced—take from my desk—you kno,s the inner drawer—you robbed it once and I forgave you —take from it the ninety pounds there are there; and after you have written anonymously to the notice,

telling the-in—where Humphreys' money is bidden —eecape--anywhere—take a new name: begin anew life." "Oh, I can't—l can't," moaned Martin. "I do not ask you where you mean to go, and you will not be pursued, for, by the vow I made our mother, I will suffer this punishment—sufftr m your place. All I insist upon is repentance, and that you never see Ruth again. Now go—' t once. Yeure hence, when we have both purged our...ive a from the clinging stains of this crime, we may, perhaps, meet again. 'But you'll betray me. You'll get yourself set iree by putting the police on my track." "Not know me yet!" said Mark, bitterly. then, and learn what a true brother really ie. Tb! thought will come perhaps with years, for again tell you that I will suffer for your sin, that you raa9 live on and repent. Once a convict, I believe that you would never rise. At Ws moment there was a rattling nobs at the door, and a warder opened it to signify that the visitor must leave. Mark stood there motionless, as his brother shrank from the cell, and then sat down to try and crush out the strong desire for liberty and love that had corae upon him with overwhelming force. He had one satisfaction, though:' Ruth' Urns saved from what must have proved to be x life of mnery• He planned that he would ask Miss llopstock to take charge of Ruth ; and then, heartsick' and, weary, be threw himself down, to try and :deep awal the thoughts of the present ; while Martirrlusetetted to the nearest tavern, where there was a parlour; ordering e: - glass of brandy, and seizing the opportunity to throir-' be blood-stained handkerchief in the fire, and watcheu it till the last piece of tinder had turned grey. , " Where is his evidence now?" he said,,raockingl° , °I don't think rater quite crushed yet."

A verdict in which the judge said he quite concurtel' and after delivering a long homily upon the heineirgle-f of the offence as committed by amen in a poson °I trust, he sentenced the prisoner to ten years' 1°,1.1* servitude--a sentenee so severe on account of aggravated assaults. a be Mark was not surprised. The old warder hesitated for a moment, 100 steadfastly steadfastly in Mark's eyes • and then his hand °l's upon that which was offered with a strong grin., ,s 1 ' "I believe you are, sir, and some day I shall." s It was a trifling act, but it made the pris°ll;l4l friend, whom he had to thank for sparing On and nights of weary suffering, besides other go"d that he did not expect. tri Back in his cell, Mark Woolford sat down and get rid of his excitement and agitation, en-aocl ivepare himself for his lot. As he grew more calm, he began, to be more t't teals about Ruth. Miss Klopstock would be sure t° irea charge of her, and old Mr. Klopstock ilways o°lo her, and had a kind word for her when he cathe%.oo mind then was pretty well at rest about Ruth, for w of evident that she had not made herself the rowel Martin's flight. r tio His brain burned, though, to know more e los brother. There could be no doubt that by thi.Sti ~ he would have left the country—but the r onSY 'as to Surely he would not have been such a villao take that now. This was a bitter thought, for he doubted '''.Bsl4gt man's repentance, and he conld•not help feeling sitl one who would leave his brother to bear the 11„ndes of his crime, would not be moved by roanY 'lit of feelings of honour. Still, to set others on the se,ed oot the money was to betray , his brother, and he con' stir. P'rt Night at last, and for the first time for weeks, tocl Woolford slept soundly. He had done his dHe ,111,7' the now had gained the victory over self. -sh4oestit worst, too, and how long he had to wait for perhaps to be set free before. sftet The consequence was that he rose morhine morning with an increased feeling of elasticitY,e'e tf down to the prison routine, and reekon'l4 hours that were passing of his shameful life. div.head: :SILVER JITBILRE
div.p: :SILVER JITBILRE

Cardinal Manning was 'on Sunday afterneon presented with a cheque 'for £3:X76, and a handsome illuminated address, from the congregation of the Pio-Cathedral, Kensington, and others, in commemoration- of his epis- copal silver jubilee. The ceremony took 'place at the Archbishop's house, ;Westminster, and amongst thope present were 'the MarOuis of Ripon, Mr. Justice Mathew, Judge Stoner, Mr. William O'Brien, M.P. the Dowager- Duchess of Newcastle, many of the Itome,n -Catholic clergy and laity. ,Lord Ripon, in making the presenta- tion, referred to the great part Cardinal Manning had taken in almaiit everyemovement of his timeitiiat had for its object the elevation or improvement of the poor, not alone of the Catholic, body, but of aii sects and religions. Cardinal Manning, in the course of his reply, stated that the money would be devoted to the reductionnf the debt on the completion cif the Pro-Cathedral at Kensington. A large company which included several of the English Catholic Bishops, the Duke of Norfolk, the Marquis of Ripen,and maw othenwell-known public men,assembled on Thursday, to present to Cardinal Manning a personal testimonial in celebration of his Eminences Silver Jubilee- The Duke of 'Norfolk made the presentation, which consisted of an iilluminated address and cheque for £7,500. Several speeches were delivered in which the eminent public services of Cardinal Manning were ' heartily'acknowledged. 'Replying, his Emineute con- trasted the position of England now with what it was twenty-five years ago from a Roman Catholic, point of view, and then gave a detailed account of the various I uses to which he intended to put the money which had been subscribed. Among the many gifts those of the I dock labourers and workers on the Thames were "itSpe- cially ace,eptable. To those he would add the gifts of his political friends, and together they should go to provide a bed in the accident ward of the London hospi- tal.

div.head: METHODIST NEW CONNEXION
div.p: THE METHODIST NEW CONNEXION
CONFERENCE.

The sittings of the Methodist New Connexion Confer- ence commenced on Monday,in the Salem Chapel, Dews- bury, the Rev. A. R. Pearson, of Longton, Staffordshire, in the chair. There were about 200 delegates from all parts of the kingdom present. The Rev. A. M'Curdy moved that the Rev. R. Le lluray, of Liverpool, be elected president for the ensuing year., The Rev. G. Packer, Halifax, seconded the resolution, whieh was supported by the Revs. H. T. Marshall, , 'W. Walshaw, and J. C. Watts, D. D., and carried unanimously.—The Rev. J. Le Eluray, in taking the chair, offered kis grateful acknowledg- ments tothe brethren who had 'introduced him .to the confbrence. He did not intend 'to refer to matters which would come before the Conference ; there was no burn- ing question except one. There were signs of union in the air. Projects of union had been on foot for a long time, and as to the ultimate results time alone could tell. It was not for him to give an expression of his own per- sonal views and feelings. He was selected to give effect to the decision of those who had elected him. He had made up his mind that on this burning question he had nothing to say. (Hear, hear.)-1 .letter was read from M. George Turver, of Dewsbury, contributing £lOO to be devoted to five different funds of the Connexion.

div.head: LABOUR CONGRESS AT LYONS.
div.p: LABOUR CONGRESS AT LYONS.

A labour „congress attended by 1,500 persons was opened on Monday at Lyons. The meeting was called under the auspices of the National Federation of Synclinal Chambers, which promoted the May-day manifestation. All the industrial centres of the south-east of France were represented. Socialist ComMittees were allowed to,be present, but on condition of not speaking after the order in which the business of the Congress wa,s to be transan- ted was settled. The subjects discussed were of a national' and an international Congress, and the places at which they could most advantageously be held. A good many delegates were for fusing them, but the original plan was adopted for holding the former at Calais, and the letter in Switzerland. There was a good deal of talk about a future European war, and how Social-Democrats shoirld act in relation to it. Delegates of the mechanical engineers said that the cry of " Vive l'Hunianite" should be substituted for that of " Vive la Petrie." M. Declaim. Deputy of the Rhone,congratulated the representatives of labour present on the unanitaity of their French brethren 1 in ceasingwork on May-day. The effect of the demon- stration on the Chambers had been very great.. 13e praised the German Socialists, and proposed that they should be thanked for having sent £4O to a French strike fund. The following resolution was voted : "That this Congress declares its approval of the plan for a general Inter- national Strike, for the purpose of obtaining The Eight -Mars-Programme,' and-recommends that the means for carrying out such a strike be discuesed at the nest International Congress."

div.head: DEATII OF THE DEAN OF MANCHESTER.
div.p: DEATII OF THE DEAN OF MANCHESTER.

The 'death of the Dean 'of Manchestw took place on. Tuesday night, at the Pafsonage, Deganwy. It has been saidlhat this marks the disappearance of the one man highAnc• in the ranks orthe Establishment who was in , tbeleast degree fitted to carry on the work and perpetn- ' atetbe traditions of Charles Kingsley and F. D. Maurice. A Radical Dean: who 'Was an uncompromising friend of working-class movements. who defended the as workers when they 'had no helper, who stood up for 'Christian Socialism, and lived the life of a great'popular leader—this was inaeed a rarity. Dean Palley was such ^a man. He was 'a Home Ruler, and be -signed the -national protest against Coercion. A 'powerful preacher, 'a trenchant andluminous writer, and a true sotil—such as he are sadly wanted in the churches, 'most of ill in the, "Establishment 'De was a brilliant organiser of men and movements. • He had no pride of any kind, and he. lived and diedin the arduous pursuit-rd high ideas.

PUSTIIN CUTTINGB MACHINERY. - X THE GILEATI.;.IC DI•i.COVBRY OF THE AGE X FvECOUGHS, COLDS, BRONCHITIS,

What inky prove a revolution in fustian cutting, one of the oldest Lancashire industries, is to all appearances imminent. Velvet cutting, though one of the most ancient of local industries, has been perhaps least the subject of successful mechanicalapplication. From tune immemorial it has been done by hand an 3 up to to-day , the same hand process has to be gone through as was applied to it hundreds of years ago. Visitors to the recent Jubilee Exhibition in Manchester will remember, that fustian cutting formed one of the attractions in the handicraft section. It is one of the most tedious occupa- tions in connection with the cotton trade, as well as one of the most exhausting. This will be apparent when it is stated that if a length of cloth, containing 100 yards has , to be cut, each two yards of the piece has to be stretched I on a frame and then the cutting operation is commenced by the cutter inserting the fine blade of a knife and guiding it delicately and carefully through each one of the rows of loops of which the web of the fabric is formed. These loops form a series downwhich the knife is readily made to travel to the end of the length of cloth stretched on the frame. In order to cut two yards of cloth, the knife has to be inserted 1,000 or more separate times and run along the line of loops, so that in order to cut a length of 100 yards it requires 50,000 insertions of the knife and the knife will have travelled over a distance of nearly 60 miles. A fus, ian cutter now on an average works 60 hours in a week, and with the exercise of diligent labour is able to cut a piece of fustian in that time for which she receives a wage of frem Bs. to 9s. The simplicity of the work would seem to lend itself ea§ily to the application ef machinery, but, though many attempts laave,been made in that direction until the pre- sent no satisfactory velvet cutting machine has been produced. It would seem however that at last an effici- ent machine is in existence, which will supersede the old hand cutting operation and prove of great service, not, only to the operative, but to the trade. By means of this invention eight or nine yards of cloth is stretched instead of two yards, and in place of the cutter having to insert the knife and force it along the race she has simply to insert it In the proper place and the machine carries the velvet towards thp knife which is held by the operator, who also controls the machinery, with a rapidity equal to six times the utmost possibility of hand cutting, and the work Is done with more regularity and certainty. Several of these machines have now been at work in an eXperimental way in Manchester for some time, and the manner in which they have behaved and the regularity and satisfaction with which the work they have done has been accomplished is in every way all that could be desired. Some of the leading velveteen firms in Manchester and in this district have taken the matter up, and it is in- tended to put down a thousand machines as quickly as possible to meet the demand for cutting which has sprung up. Its introduction will enable fustian cutting to take its place as a permanent industry in Lancashire. and it will come as a great boon to the trade because of the certainty and the regularity with which the work will be done. For sOrne years this uncertainty has been a great trouble to the trade. The machine comes there- fore at an opportune moment. A syndicate was formed some months ago in Manchester to experiment with the machine, and their labours have brought it to its present successful completion, and no time fg to be lost before it is to be utilized. The machine has already become known on the Continent and in America, and several applica- tions have been made for leave to use it there. The foreign patents will be sold, and the Company which is to be formed to work it at home will put themselves in a position to meet all the demands of the trade.

To-day' my walks take me into Penketh and Sankey, and by way of beguiling the time I try to find in these names some indication of their original meaning. The sense of humour must be strong in a people who have a Fiddler's Ferry, a very pleasant place on the margin of the river, with a boat in front, tide going out, and eddies in the ricer; nice tooling wind, and sun shining in the sky. So I have come to the conclusion that Penketh is from the British pen-y-cx, which means "the cuckoo's hill,' barbarize-a into Penketh. 1-offer it for their acceptance, though' I knowby experience how difficult it is to please some people. even when you do the very best you can for them. I have known the place off and on for the last quarter of a century, and have reason to think lam right. Not very long ago, when rambling in this direction, a crazy woman fell foil of me, which in some sort prepared me for the assault of a man in a white heat, who poured' out the vials of his wrath upon me,quite innocently, I believe.for he thought a cabinet maker, must know as ranch as a cabinet minister. Of-Sankey I think with pleasure, because I know some very excellent people there, and never come near the place without thinking of them. In Sankey I find theiCeltic seen-ee, or, literally 'the old, earth, ' or, as applied to military purposes, baen-caes —an old fort, 4 caes" being -found in names of Oaces where stones are plentiful and c 4, where the forts would be earthworks. Whether these were in that • part of the territory called Bold,' where the four moat-houses are, or in Cuerdley, where the Roman Cohorts entrenched themselves, I am not prepared to say at present. I hope, however, that the Government surveyors who are again in this district,together with the historiographers,will by- rand-by tell us a good deal on this subject more than ' we know at present. And so I leave the matter in their hands, to apply myself to the more immediate purpose of my writing, which is to tell you that I was at the Penketh Liberal Club on Friday even- ing, on the occasion of the presentation to that institution crf a portrait of the lace

The presentation was made in very feli- citous terms by Miss Broadhurst, and was supported by Mr. George Broadhurst,and received with hearty thanks by the members. While listening to one and anothei it occurred to me that I might add a few words for the benefit of those who were•not present, and to a still wider circle of acquaintance. I had known him by report for many years, but was first brought into contact with him in the early part of 1880, when a few of us went to Burtonwood to open the eyes of the people to the real position of affairs, and I cass-rccall his figure, and an out-,line of his speech, which was a vivid review of his experi- ences in politics, and of the past and prospective triumphs Of Liberal policy, together with his in- spiriting advice as to our action at that crisis. ,After the' General Election of 1880.1 wrote to him "We havethought it desirable to keepnp -some per- manent organisation iu our polling district, and the project of a club seems the most likely to succeed as affording a central point from which to work up the district and leaven the lump of political ignor- ance, against the time when another General Elec- tion comes round. We confidently expect that the club will be self-supporting after the -first start has been made, and we are sure that the knowledge that we have your approval will have its just effect upon the community here." And when the club was opened I received. the following letter, in his own characteristic handwriting,which speaks eloquently as to the course he would have pursued had he lived to this crisis in the history of the Liberal party.— 'Great Sankey, Warrington, Nov.Z.fth, 80.—Dear Sir, —I should have great pleasure in meeting you to- morrow evening, at the opening of the Earlestown Liberal Club, but fear 1 shall be unable to do so, though I vary much wish to be with you.. I think it a matter of great importance that we should in this county al least do all we can to support Liberal principles as embodied in the policy of England's greatest statesman, and that the Newton palling district. div.head: AN IRISH EDITOR'S SENTENCE REDUCED.
div.p: AN IRISH EDITOR'S SENTENCE REDUCED.

• Judge Morris heard at Strokestown County Court, Co. Roscommon, on Monday, the appeals of Mr. Jasper Tully, editor of the "Roscommon Herald," against the sentence of nine months' imprisonment with hard labour, for publishing a correspondence which, it is alleged, in- cited to intimidation. His Honour gave judgment on Tuesday, reducing the sentence to three months' without bard labour.

div.head: SCENE IN AN IRISH LAW COURT.
div.p: SCENE IN AN IRISH LAW COURT.

At a Crimes Act Court, at Waterford, on Saturday, Mr. C. P. Redmond, editor andproprietor of the " Water- ford News," was sentenced to an additional 14 days' imprisonment, and to find sureties, or undergo four months' imprisonment, for publishing intimidatory re- ports of National meetings. Dr. Counsel, barrister, who appeared for Mr. Redmond, asked for an increase of imprisonment, in order to appeal, and, on this being refused, denounced the trial as a mockery. Dr. Counsel, after a struggle and amidst great confusion, was re- moved by the.police. •

div.head: NEW BRIGHTON TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE NEW BRIGHTON TRAGEDY.

Felix Spicer, 51 years of age, was brought up on remand at the Wallasey Polize Court, on Monday, charged with the murder of his two sons, William and Henry Spicer, and the attempted murder of their mother, Mary Ann Patin, aeNew Brighton, on Sunday morning, the 25th of May. Captain Molyneux, presided. Mr. A. B. Moore, solicitors of Birkenhead, represented the prisoner.—Evidence was given by Mr. A. T. Wright, of the firm of Messrs. Wright, Beckett, and Co., solicitors, of Liverpool ; William Foulkes'Lowe, public analyst of Chester; and Joel Fitton, iron founder, living at 82,Wild- st., Derby. The prisoner was committed for trial for the wilful murder of the two children. The inquest was resumed on Wednesday, when the jury returned a ver- dict of" Wilful Murder against Felix Spicer, the father of the children.
MR. GLADSTONE ON WELSH DISESTABLISHMENT.

number of gentlemen from Camarvonshire OA an interview with Mr. Gladstone at Hawarden Castle a few days ago, and in the course of conversation Mr. Glad- stone evinced great interest in the present aspect of the controversy going on in Wales. Respecting the Rhyl resolution, he considers that the baste of one section of the party is very unwise, and counselled prudence, moderation, and unanimity. Mr. Gladstone declared that a measure to disestablish and disendow the Welsh Church would be very complicated, one much more complicated, at any rate, than Scotch Disestablishment. The Welsh Church is part of the Church of England, and the Welsh sees are all in the province of Canterbury, a fact which suggests possibilities of vast complications. Mr. Glad- stone wanted to know what he was to do if the Scotch members should decide to send an ultimatum similar to that which the Welsh Liberals had in contemplation. Disestablishment in Scotland was a far simpler matter, and is supported by greater numerical force.
