div.head: MEETING OF CONSERVATIVE MEMBERS.
div.p: MEETING OF CONSERVATIVE MEMBERS.
REVOLT AGAINST THE GOVERNMENT PROGRAMME. _ . •

The Conservative members of both Houses met on Thursday at the Carlton Club to consider the state of public business. Lord Salisbury presided, and asserted that the extremity to which obstruction had recently been carried clogged all legislative work. He suggested that the best way of coping with the difficulty would be to alter the rules of procedure so that measures after reaching the Committee stage should, if it was found impossible to pass them in one session, be carried forward and treated in the next session. The Government, he declared, were determined not to abandon their three important bills. An interesting discuSsion followed. Some members thought an autum session far preferable to the remedy suggested by the Premier, and hinted that this new mode of legislation of carrying on bills from session to session would prove a valuable weapon to the Radicals when they returned to power. After the meeting Ministers were in consultation, and it was rumoured that the Government might possibly drop the Land Purchase Bill. The Liberal Unionist leaders intend meet- ing without delay to discuss the situation. A London Correspondent, writing on Thursday even- ing, says :—Anarchy reigns in then:inks of the Conserva- tive party, and the proceedings at the Carlton Club meeting this afternoon prove incontestably that the Par- liamentary leaders are completely out of touch and out of sympathy with their followers. Lord Salisbury gave I his supporters two alterngtives to choose from, and the result showed that neither alternative was regarded with favour or approval by the most loyal and respected mem- bers of the Conservative party in the House of Commons. The first of these alternatives was decisively rejected by the great body of the Carlton Club meeting, which broke up without coming to any definite conclusion on the second. Hence it was that the First Lord of the Treasury was unable to make any statement to-night on the future course of public business, and was compelled to put off making any further announcementon the subject until another Cabinet Council had been held. Great dis- satisfaction is felt on the Conservative side of the House at the decision of the Government to give precedence to the Local Taxation Bill; and if the various tem- perance societies, and more especially the Church of England Temperance Society, do their duty in bringing pressure to bear on Conservative members, it is still quite within the bounds of probabi- lity that the compensation clauses will be defeated or withdrawn. The Conservative members, adds the I correspondent, who attended the Carlton Club meeting exercised, I hear, much freedoni of speech in criticising the conduct by Ministers of the business of the session. Mr. Balfour, Mr. Matthews, Mr. Goschen. and Mr. Ritchie I were each of them categoricallyaud explicitly denounced I for having landed the House of Commons in the present position of confusion and embarrassment. At last Lord Salisbury felt compelled to interpose, and to declare that the Cabinet as a whole were responsible for the decision that had been arrived at to give prdcedence to the Local Taxation Bill.

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE OF THE CITY OF • ‘`- ROME.
div.p: NARROW ESCAPE OF THE CITY OF • ‘`- ROME.

- The Anchor Line steamer City of Rome, from New York, with nearly 1,000 passengers, arrived at Queens- town on Sunday, and reported that at an early hour that morning, during a dense fog, she ran on the Fastnet Rock, and had a narrow escape from shipwreck. Terrible excitement prevailed amongst the passengers. The vessel, it appears, made the land going slow in a dense fog at four a.m., and although soundings were being taken continuously the Fastnet Rock was struck bow on. The vessel's forefoot got on to the rock, and but for the promptitude displayed in reversing the engines another great marine fatality would doubtless have had to be recorded. According to accounts furnished by passen- gers, the steamer trembled all over, and for a time great alarm prevailed on board. The density of the fog added to the alarming character of the situation for the pas- sengers ; but the assurance of the commander and officers that not the slightest danger existed estored quietude. The Fastnet Rock is situated about three ,miles from .laud.

div.head: MALTESE MARRIAGE LAW.
div.p: THE MALTESE MARRIAGE LAW.

On the Maltese Marriages Question "A Malta Protes- tant" thus writes to the "Daily News" :—A Battery Sergeant-Major (8.A.), a Church of England man, got engaged to a Roman Catholic girl ; they got tired of waiting for the Papal dispensation, and, each declining to be married in the Church of the other, were fffiajj, married on, so to speak, neutral ground by the Baptist minister. Now as soon as this new law poses this marriage becomes null and void, and the children illegiti- mate, for Sir Lintorn Simmons has bound the British Government to make such marriages illegal, prospec- tively and also retrospectively. This is one of many similar cases, and to say,as Lord Salisbury does, that the effect is nil as regards marriages between Catholics and non-Catholics is saying what is not the case. In fact, to gain this important point the Pope kindly says that he will legalise marriage between Protestants celebrated in Malta—a point which has never been disputed except under the Papal Canon Law, which, up to the present, has not been recognised as the civil law of Malta; and the opinion of Sir A. Dingli, the Chief Justice of Malta, is in existence (given when he was Crown Advocate), that all such marriages were perfectly legal, and could not be impugned in any part of the world.

matter say they cannot accept the judgment of Mr. justice FIELD, perhaps they will be satisfied "with the opinion of the late Mr. NASH, barrister- at-law, and counsel at one time to the Licensed Victuallers Association. He declared: "Now I
am sorry to say, having looked into this question most exhaustively,and having compared notes with IllY brethern well versed in these matters, that there cannot be the smallest doubt that in the

•strict sense no such thing as a vested interest 'exists." But why quote any opinion when the 'ease of " Sharpe versus Wakefield" was taken to test this very issue, and when Licensed Victuallers 'were beaten in court after court right up to the --Court of Queen's Bench? They know they haven't a leg to stand on, on this question of vested interest; and it is because they have no title in law—and they have certainly none in equity—that a profligate 'and a drink-ridden Government are trying to give them one, despite the persistent and incessant Protests of the people. Let them do it, if they dare. It will real their own fate ; their punishment Will be great, and it will come quickly.

THERE has been a two-nights' The Sweating System. debate in the House of Lords upon the Report of the Select Committee 11Pon the Sweating System, but neither the debate Ilor the result of the debate can be regarded as satisfactory. Lord DUNRAVEN is to be commended for introducing the subject, and for urging the need of immediate legislation; but he met with little aYlnpathy from the supporters of the Government. It is cold comfort to be told by such statesmen as lord DERBY that they must rely for a remedy for the terrible evils which the Report reveals, upon the progress of civilisation, the diffusion of educe- t,ion, and the operation of similar causes." It is like telling the starving horse that it must wait till 'the grass grows. The Archbishop of Canterbury, to his credit be it said, supported Lord DUNRAVEN. lleferring to the Report he said committee had not thought it necessary to pro- vilce a philosophical essay on causes, but had looked to the proposal of a practical remedy for evils of a !errible kind, leading to the insufficiency of pay, Pod, and air, insanitary work places, filthy dwell- -11178 and a general degradation of labour below the Point at which existence could be sastained, with dlie regard to the necessities and decencies of life. (tlear. hear.) The hideous conditions under which these poor people lived had so far been left out of 'Practical legislation, and all hat was asked was that they should have brought to bear in their favour the reniedies which had operated so beneficially through the Factory Acts. les, the conditions are indeed hideous, and the farce is hideous which ends, as the debate ended, O n Tuesday, on the motion and the amendment be- g withdrawn—that is in no resolution upon the subject being come to. Lord DE RAMSAY was the aPokesman of the Government, and the complacent twaddle which he talked—for we cannot call it anything else—was of a kind which is exceedingly irritating to those who are in earnest upon the /natter. What is it to the purpose to say that " this country had every reason to be satisfied With the results of the Berlin Conference ;" or
that "the Committee might be certain that the result of their labours would be read with great
Care by their artisans, and if by an extension of --- • •

existing legislation Parliament should see its "way to bettering their lot they might rest satisfied that they would not have long to Wait for it ?" "If anything could be done forsooth! Encouraging language truly, to men and women who are reduced to conditions

of living below those of their lordships' horses, lings, and pigs, because—to repeat the Archbishop's language—" of insufficiency of pay, food, and air, Insanitary work places, filthy dwellings, and a general degradation of labour." Can we wonder that Socialism of the most extreme type is finding

favour amongst the East-end worker-s- of London When When we see the Pecksniffs of the House of Lords dismissing the horrible evils of the Sweating System in the easy-going fashion disclosed by the debate? We are not Anarchists, but we are in- clined to think that the preaching of Anarchist doctrines up to the point of frightening the ohl Women in both Houses of Parliament would have
Wholesome effect. It is evident that nothing will be done to put down " sweating " except upon Pressure from the masses, and we should like to see that pressure speedily applied.

A woman's THE advocates of Women's Rights Triumph have every reason to be proud of the triumph which Miss FAWCETT Ilas achieved in coming out at the head of the list in the Cambridge Mathematical Tripos. If she were aCcorded what she has really earned, she would be styled Senior Wrangler ; but because she is a Woman, and man-made laws do not deal justly by Women, the honour is given to a man, although, as the result of the examination shows, she is hun- dreds of marks ahead of the man who carries off the Prize. However, there is no gainsaying the fact that Miss FAWCETT heads the list, and this will, perhaps, set the authorities think- ing that it is not creditable to them to admit Women to the examinations and deny them the fruits of their labours. Mr. GLADSTONE referred to this grave defect last week. In the course of his evidence before a Committee of the Flintshire County Council he said," I must say that I resent extremely, though lamby no means an extrava- gant innovator in the matter of women's rights, the arrangement under which girls and young women are brought to the University and absolu- tely precluded from touching one farthing of the vast wealth of the Universities and Colleges." That is a sentiment which will, it is to be hoped, be echoed throughout the land in view of Miss • ll'aweett's achievement at Cambridge. One *Wallow does not, to be sure, make a Summer; but what woman has done woman may do, and she is at least entitled to be put on a footing of equality with man. Mrs. FAWCETT, the widow nf the late Professor FAWCETT (who was at one time Postmaster-General) has long been an earnest and eloquent advocate of the higher education of 'women, and she is justly entitled to congratula- tion on the brilliant result of her daughter's train- ing. As to Miss FAWCETT, she COMBS to the front at a bound as the distinguished daughter of distinguished parents.

TEE ROBE ItiltlES AT NEWTON TOWN HALL. At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions, on Tuesday, Alfred Caldwell, 96, surveyor, of Newton-le-Willows, Pleaded guilty to having at Newton, on the Ist 131.,,a37, broken and entered the office of Richard e'erlen surveyor to the Newton Improvement °Mtaissioners, and stolen five florins, also to having entered the offices of the Commissioners with intent to steal the seal. Another charge of stealing books, Ilans, and documents belonging to the Commission- Was not proceeded with. Mr. Swift appeared on the prisoner's behalf, and, in addressing the Bench, Z'ated that until the latter part of 1888 the prisoner 4,.ad been in the employ of the Newton Commis- sioners under Mr. Brierley. He then left to be ~11,rveyor and inspector at Reddish, but for the past rune months had been out of work. This idea in Procuring the seal was to utilise it for the purpose of producing a false testimonial in order to obtain a !ituation at Flint. No doubt that was a wicked and foolish act, but he asked the Bench to remember his Previous good character and the loss and punish- Ment he had already sustained. The Bench passed • Sentence of three months' imprisonment.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Old Growler won't have it that Miss Fawcett is the first amongst women as Senior Wrangler. He says Eve has a prior claim to the distinction. She was the first to eat of the Tree of Knowledge; and the world has been full of "wrangling" ever since.

Honour to the memory of Mark Addy who has just died at Salford, aged 52. It is computed that in his time this every-day hero" saved upwards of 50 lives from drowning in the Irwell." What a splendid record! When the world has arrived at maturity, it will glorify those who save life rather than those who destroy it.

The Licensed Victuallers are of course, in favour of the Compensation Bill, and they are about to get up petitions in its support. At Warrington, the Committee, on Tuesday, "decided to engage a couple of men to obtain signatures to the peti- tion." They do well to "engage" men, for volun- teers in such a case are, we suppose, out of the question.

Mr. Coningsby Disraeli, nephew of the late Lord Beaconsfield, has been adopted as the candi- date of the Tory party for the Altrincham Division, as successor to Sir W. C. Brooks, who is retiring. The. Tories doubtless think the name of Disraeli is something to conjure with; but the Liberals have a splendid candidate in Mr. Leadam, and, with the flowing tide with them, they ought to win.

Lieutenant-Colonel Wilkinson said, at the Tory meeting on Saturday afternoon, that he hoped their candidate would follow in his uncle's foot- steps ; but in that case he should, as a young man, be a Radical Reformer—ready to tell all "and sun- dry;; that "a Conservative Governmentis an organ- ised hypocrisy." Perhaps, as the young man's name is Coningsby, he will follow the line of "Coningsby," and try to make it clear to everybody that if it weren't for the Jews the world would go to the dogs.

The Rev. G. S. Reaney preached his first sermon as a Church of England curate on Sunday; but he did not, as might have been expected, give any reason for the change that has come over him. Perhaps reason has had nothing to do with it. Dr. Parker was understood to have Mr. Reaney in his mind, the other day,when he referred to the way in which the Church took these converts to her bosom and "placed them in obscurity on their way to ob- livion."

Mr. William O'Brien was married, on Wednesday, to Madlle. Raffolovieh, who has shown herself to be in love with the Irish cause as well as with its dis- tinguished representative. Who does not wish them much happiness? But let Shelley, who had strong sympathies with Ireland, put in a word :
_ Night, with all thy stars look down, Darkness, weep thy holiest dew ! Never smiled the inconstant moon On a pair so true.

Mr. Stead in the "Review of Reviews" says of Mrs. O'Brien—" She is already as Irish as her hus- band. I look forward to her playing an important social part in the near future, when her husband, one of the ministers of the Crown, occupies a front seat on the Government benches in the Parliament in College Green."

It is to the credit of the Church that it contains a few such men as the late Dr. Oakley, Dean of Manchester. He had at heart the advancement of the masses, and he was not afraid to show it both by word and deed. How is it that the Church does not swarm with men of this kind? It is so easy for them to be good, and do goo& If the clergy stand idly by because they are afraid a movement of the people will end in Disestablish- ment, the sooner the Church is disestablishei the better.

It is time Lord Salisbury threw up the sponge as Foreign Secretary. He has quite enough to do as Prime Minister, and is getting things into a mess. We have trouble with France as to the Newfound- land fisheries; the United States are threatening to despatch armed cruisers to the Behring Sea; and Germany is pulling the strings all her own way in East Africa. All this comes of having a weak man as Foreign Secretary—a lath painted to look like iron.

But bad as is the management of Foreign Affairs the muddle in the management of the business of Parliament is even worse. . The meeting at the Carlton Club, on Thursday, showed that there is a large section of the Tory party who are in revolt at the proposal to dragoon the House of Commons into passing bills which they do not like. They are afraid that if coercion be applied now, they will suffer for it at the next election, and when the Liberals come into office. Some of the Conserva- tives present at the meeting did not hesitate to tell Lord Salisbury the truth, and point to the introduction of the Compensation Bill as evidence of want of judgment.

Salford has set a good example in holding a Town's Meeting, and unanimously passing a resolu- tion in favour of the better housing of the poor. Warrington might with advantage follow suit. There is a disposition on the part of the authorities to deal with the "Black Spots" ; but there are so many difficulties in the way—so many interested parties in high places—that all the help that can be given is needed to get anything done.

From the evidence given at the inquest, on Monday, it would seem that the young boatman who fell off his boat and was drowned in the St. Helens Canal was unable to swim. The art of swimming ought to be a portion of every school child's training, and it would .be well if ability to swim were made a condition of employment on the part of boatmen. Of course, all this implies pro- vision of places where the art can be acquired, and on this head local authorities need a great deal of stimulating.

There is an idea abroad which is fostered by "the trade " that it is quite a new thing to suggest that a license should be extinguished without compensa- tion ; and the case of Sharpe v. Wakefield is referred to as if it was the first instance of a license being thus abolished. As a matter of fact hundreds of licenses have been extinguished without anything in the shape of compensation. Speaking at Wigan, on Tuesday night, Mr. Caine stated that as many as 179 full licenses had been abolished in Liverpool without giving a farthing compensation.

Mr. Caine further pointed out that, in Liver- pool, licenses had been extinguished at the rate of about twelve per annum, whereas the Government Bill would only allow them to be reduced at the rate of one per annum. And this, too, after pay- ing compensation for the odd one! Could any- thing be more absurd, or more obstructive of pro- gress in the temperance cause! And yet the Government say their bill is in the interest of temperance The Government are like the thief who, caught with his hand in his neighbour's pocket, said he wasn't going to take anything out; he was going to put something in.

Another sample of the way in which the Union- ists have carried out their promise to give equal laws to Ireland and England: Mr. Jasper Tully, editor of the "Roscommon Herald," was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment with hard labour, for publishing a correspondence which, it is alleged, incited to intimidation. In England no editor could be proceeded against for such an offence. But the monstrous sentence has been reduced on appeal to "three months' without hard labour." It is a disgrace to us as a nation that Mr. Tully is in prison at all for a " crime " which is no crime in this country.

In the House of Commons, on Monday, Mr. John Dillon made a startling revelation of the brutal conduct of the police and magistrates at Cashel and Tipperary. He spoke from personal observa- tion; and "asked the Chief Secretary three ques- tions—first, was it legal to attack a peaceable meeting, even if it had been proclaimed, without due warning being given to allow the people to dis- perse? secondly, when no meeting was beingheld, , was it legal to charge and baton small groups of
RUNCORN POST OFFICE.
Mr. E. W. V. Evans has been appointed sorting clerk and telegraph learner at Runcorn Post Office.
WIDNES PARISH CHURCH.

The Rev. Robert Meiklejohn, formerly of Birkenhead, has, during the present week, commenced his duties as second curate to Widnes Parish Church, in succes,ion to the Rev. Parry Thomas. PROTEST AGAINST COMPENSATION FROM WIDNES.

_ On Thursday, the United Free Methodists of Widnes forwarded a protest against the Compensation Clauses of the Local Taxation Act, for presentation to Parliament by Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED on the premises at J. & W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.—Advt. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. During the month of May there was issued from Widnes Free Library 4,309 books being a decrease of 70 in the lending department and 7 in the reference depart- ment; £2 2s. 114 d. had been received for fines. The Committee have decided to purchase a number of new books at a cost of £3O.

WIDNES (377TH) STARR BOWICETT BUILDING SOCIETY. The ninth annual meeting was held on Wednesday, Mr. S. Upward presiding. The directors report stated that the balance at credit of profit and loss account now stood at £219 15s. id. an increase of £2 3s. mid. Since the society commenced there had been 43 appropriations entitling members to £ll,lOO. Of this amount £10,300 had been actually advanced, and there was £7,080 still owing to the society. The withdrawals during the year numbered 40, covering 102 shares on which subscriptions amounting to £754 Bs. 3d. had been paid. There were now 275 members. The report was adopted, and the retiring directors were re-elected. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED on the premis3s at J. & W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.—Advt. WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.. _

The 23rd annual festival of the Widnes.- Athletic Club was commenced last evening, when the various events were confined to athletes who reside in the locality. To- day the open events, for which there are 200 competitors, will be decided, and not the least interesting are the championships of the N.C.A.A., in the one milt, fiat race (scratch), and the wide jump. Amongst the most noted athletes who are expected to compete in the vari- ous contests are D. D. Bulger (Irish champion), H. Whit- tick (Cheltenham, mile champion), W. H. Morton (long distance champion). E. W. Parry, C. F. Daft, Sm. The prizes are very valuable and handsome collections from Messrs. Ellongton and Co.'s The weather being fine there was a capital attendance last night. The results were as follows :-120 yards flats race handicap: Run in five heats, and the following won their respective heats :—G. Hartland, Widnes, F.C. (5 yards) ; J. McTear, St. Helens (7 yards) ; T. E. Sudlow, St. Helens F.C. (q) ; H. 11. Evans, Warrington Harriers (7) ; R. Green, War- rington (10.) Final 1, Evans; 2, Sudlow ;3, Green. Two Miles Bicycle Race Handicap : 1, M. Bailey, St. Helens C.C. (200 yards) ; 2, E. R. Crippin, Huyton, B.C. (180 yards) ; 3, P. W. Fair, Warrington C.C. (200 yards.) Won by two yards after capital race. One mile Flat Race Handicap : 1, John Kelly, Widnes St.M. F.C. (scratch) ; 2, H. Peters, Widnes F.C. (50 yds.) ; 3, J. Whitfield, Warrington Harriers (55 yds.). Nine runners, won easily by 20 yds. Quarter mile Flat Race Handicap: (Ist prize presented by Mr. F. H. Gossage J.P). 1, J. Clark, Widnes F.C. (15) ; 2, J. Purley, Widnes F. C. (8) ; 3, P. J. Kenyon, Widnes (15) ; won by 8 yards. GARDEN TOOLi.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington Earlestown.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 14 1890
inoffensive people? and, thirdly, when a crowd was charged by the police and the people were fly- ing, no resistance being offered, was it legal to pursue and knock them down?"

Instead of answering the questions, Mr. Balfour in his usual cynical fashion, gave Mr. Dillon the lie by setting up the general statements of the police against Mr. Dillon's varticular assertions. But he was not allowed to ride off as usual, for Mr. Gladstone demanded that there should be a public inquiry, if there was a conflict of evidence. There will, however, be no inquiry; the Irish Sacre. fary has too much dread of the truth. It is signifi- cant that the Tories showed themselves very uneasy about this latest specimen of coercion; and one of their number, Captain Bethell, had the courage to say that no answer had been given to Mr. Dillon. There will be a lot of Bethells at the next election.

Dr. Talmage is not a man of Thirty-nine Articles but of Thirty-nine Pictures, for that is the number of " photos " of him recently published in America. It is stated that he has been "taken in all the atti- tudes of prayer, spiritual ecstacy, devotion, inspira- tion, exaltation, fervour, and frenzy which he ex- hibits in the pulpit." This attitudinising does not seem to have inspired reverence, for a Yankee paper exclaims :—" Ye gods and little fishes! Is the preacher's art a sham and a humbug? Is your pulpit pathos a simple matter of arching the eye- brows, and your eloquence a mere trade Can you show how you make your congregation weep by putting on the proper expression before a camera? Is it all mechanism, all acting, all hypo- crisy ?"

LOCAL NEWS.
RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes held the usual monthly sitting of this court on Tuesday but there were no cases of public interest.

A SCHOONER DAMAGED AT RUNCORN', On Saturday the schooner, Agnes Frazer, from Ply- mouth, whilst being towed into Runcorn -Docks, c.Aided with the pier head, and the stern and bulwarks were damaged. The vessel was laden with china clay. TuE CLOSING OF rEEL-ST., A special meeting of Widnes Local Board was held on Tuesday afternoon, for the purpose of considering an application of Messrs. Thomas Bolton and Sons, copper manufacturers, &c., for the closing of Peel-st. Mr. E. Carey was voted to the chair. The Board, had previously granted this permission, and the former resolution was confirmed unanimously.

WIDNES IRISH NATION&L LEAC-7E. In connection with the T. P. O'Connor's branch, a ineetin was held in St. Paul's Chambers on Sunday, under the presidency of Mr. Nolan. There should have been a debate on the question " Would it be beneficial or otherwise to the people of Widnes to hiivit the town in- corporated," but it was postponed and only ordinary business was transacted.

CORPUS CHRISTI PROCESSION AT DITTON. The annual celebration of " Corpua Christi" was held on Sunday afternoon at St. Michael's Church, Ditton. In the afternoon there was a procession of clergy, acolytes, &c., through the grounds of Ditton Hall College, headed by St. Mary's Brass Band, and Dillon Hall String Band. Afterwards high mass was celebrated before an altar erected in front of the college, and profusely decor- ated with flowers. The preacher for the day was the Rey. Father Zahm S.J.

STEALING BORROWED PLUMES AT RUNCORN. Before Mr. John Brundrit at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, a man named Luke Cavanagh, was charged with stealing a coat and vest, the property of Thomas Kirkham, landlord of the Three Crowns Inn, King-st. It appeared that the prisoner borrowed the articles for the purpose of attending a funerel but, after the sad event, instead of returning the coat, he absconded. to Warring- ton where he was apprehended by P.C. Woodrow. He was remanded until Monday. EXTRAORDINARY EXPLOSION AT WIDNES. An extraordinary accident occurred at Widnes on Saturday last. A boy, whilst playing in Moss Bank-rd., found a cartridge which Peter GrAn, a provision dealer, took from him, under the impression that it was a pencil case For some reason Griffin commenced to tile the end of the cartridge, with the r;,sult that it exploded, and severed the thumb and first linger of the left hand. His eyes were also severely injured, and it, is feared that he will lose his eyesight. He is under the care of Dr. McCambridge. UMBRELLAS BE-COVERED on the premises at J. &. W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.--Advt. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. .

The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery, on Wednesday. Mr. S. Taylor presided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastahli, Mr. W. Littler, and Mr. W. F. Salkeld (secretary). the Secretary reported that during the two months ending May 25 there were 69 interments, corresponding. period last year, 53 ; increase, 16. The fees received during the same season amounted to £65 10s. ; last year £5B 12s. 6d. ; increase, £9 17s. 6d.— The Finance Com- mittee recommended the payment of accounts amount- ing to £l7 19s. 3d. and interest falling due £3O 14s. sd. —Passed.—The Secretary was instructed to request the 'overseers to call a vestry meeting for June 26th, for the purpose of electing three members of the Board. The retiring members are Messrs. James Handley, J.P., Samuel Taylor, and Richard Moirie who are eligible for re-election.

UNLAWFULLY OBTAINING BEER AT HALTON. Robert Baker, of Loclost. and William Brown, of Halton-road, employed on the Ship Canal works, were summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday to answer a charge of having obtained a supply of beer through falsely repremating themselves to be travellers. Both defendants pleaaed guilty. About 11 o'clock on the morning of the first June the defendants called at the Castle Hotel, Halton, and representing that they had walked from Frodsham, demanded refreshments. They wrote false names and addresses in a hank kept by the landlord for the purpose of receiving signatures, of tra- vellers' and they were then eaoh served with a pint of beer. At this time P.C. Fryer came in, and knowirkg the men, informed the landlord.—Mr. Brundat said this might seem a simple thing to the defendants, but they were putting in peril the landlord of thphouse, to whom it was a very serloas matter.—A fine, of IQs. aid costs Bs, Bd, was imposed upon each defen}c.pst. IRON BeD,STE,ADS & BEDDING.—OIWI(I, 51, 13ridp-at,, Warrington.

UNJUST SCALES AT WIDNES. George Hesketh, grocer, Irwell-st., was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions o on Thursday, to answer a charge of having in his possession for trade purposes, a pair of scales which were three drachms out of balance against the purchaser.—Mr. Johnstone, inspector of weights and measures, proved the case, and the defend- ant was fined 20s. and costs. He stated that he did not know the scales were wrong until Mr. Johnstone told him. UMBRELLAS BE-COVERED on the premises at J. W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.—Advt.

TEMPERANCE LECTURES AT RUNCORN. Under the auspices of the Runcorn Circuit Wesleyan Temperance Society, Mr. Thos. Hardy, U.K.A., of Man- chester, has delivered an address on temperance topics in Devonshire-square each evening during the present week. Good audiences have assetnhled to listen to Mr. Hardy's animated and convincing speeches, and a considerable number of recruits to the cause have been obtained. On Monday, the meeting was presided over by the Rev. H. Burson ; Tuesday, Mr. B. Crosby; Wednesday, Mr. D. Bishrown, and Thursday, Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys.

THE RIVAL HERDS AT WIDNES. Money has been staked and arrangements made for a diving, swimming, and running contests between Tommy Burns, the " Hero of Runcorn Bridge" and Carlisle D. Graham, the "Hero of Niagara Falls." At high tide on Thursday neat, about noon, the rival heros will " drop " or dive into the Mersey then swim as best they can to the Widnes shore, and afterwards run a race of 10 miles on the bowling green attached to the Mersey Hotel. Great interest is manifested in the contest at Widnes, where Burns is a great favourite. Graham is in train- ing in the locality. TRAVELLIND TriuNics.—Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge- et.. Warrington.

div.head: INTI-OOMPENSATION MEETING NT FRODSII&M.
div.p: INTI-OOMPENSATION MEETING NT FRODSII&M.

A well attended public meeting wai held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Tuesday evening, for the purpose of protesting against the compensation clauses of the Local Taxation Act. Mr. W. Fairish, J.P., presided. The Rev. W. Fothergill moved "That this meeting of the people of Frodsham representing all shades of political and religious opinion cordially disapprove of the pria- ciple of the compensation clauses of the Local Taxation Bill, inasmuch as such legislation would create a vested interest in annual licenses, and render more difficult the work of temperance reformation."—The Rev. J. D. Bray seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. C. P. Fielding of the U.K.A., and carried unanimously. On the proposition of Mr. S. H. Woodward, the Chairman was requested to forward a copy of the resolution to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the President of the Board of Trade and Mr. H. Tollemache, M.P. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, on the proposition of Mr. T. A. Rigby, seconded by Mr. E. Rhodes.

div.head: LANDLORDS AND ENCRUCHMENTS IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: LANDLORDS AND ENCRUCHMENTS IN CHESHIRE.

At the meeting of the East Bucklow District Highway Board, held at the Sessions House, Knutsford,on Wednes- day, a letter was read from Mr. J. T. Brunner. M.P., written at the request of the Cheshire Liberal Federation, pointing out the necessity for constant vigilance in re- gard to landlords' encroachments on vacant land situate at the sides of public roads. Although he wrote as presi- dent of a party organisation, it was enthely a non-party nistter, and asked the assistance of the board in main- taining and enforcing the rights of the public within the limits of their jurisdiction. Mr. I3runner also called the attention of the board to the action of the Cheshire County Council in the matter.—ln reply to the Chairman, the Surveyor said there were no encroachments in their district. On the other hand, land had been given for widening roads.—A member remarked that the latest encroachment he noticed in the district was a cloud of black smoke from Mr. Brunner's works overhanging Tabley Park. (Laughter.)—lt was decided that the letter should " lie on the table." UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED on the premises at J. & W. Dutton's, Sankey-st. —Advt. DEATH OF MR. JOHN WILLIAMS, RUNCOR:4.

Another of the old inhabitants of Runcorn has passed away in the person ot Mr. John Williams, of Greenwa,y Meadows. For some time the deceased gentleman has been under the care of Dr. McDougall, but he was suffer- ing from no special disease, and the medical attendant being unable to repair the ravages of time, he peacefully expired, in the presence of his family, from the effects of old age. During his long life of 82 years Mr. Williams had seen many changes in his native place, not the least of which was its transformation from the most pictures- quo spot on the banks of the Mersey, into a dull and dirty manufactory for soap and chemicals. In his younger days, Mr. Williams was connected with the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, holding an offi- cial position at the Old Quay Docks, and whorl the concern was transferred to the Bridgewater _ . .

Navigation Campany, he still retained his sctuation, and remained with the firm for a very great number of years. Mr. Williams also carried on the business of a grocer in Church-st. About 15 years ago he went into retirement, and he had since led the quiet unosten- tatious life, which so well suited his nature. He was highly respected by a large circle of his fellow towns- men for his uprightness of character and integrity of purpose. He leaves behind a son and three daughters, the former cf whom is in Australia. The funeral will take place at Runcorn Cemetery to-day at 3 p.m.
MR. JONES AND THE RECENT GUARDIANS ELECTION AT
RUNCORN.

The following letter which has been received by Mr. D. H. Jones, draper' &c., Hight-st., Runcorn, fully explains itself :—" Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W., 7th June, 1890. Sir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to state that they have had under their consideration your appeal against the Returning Officer's return of the Guardians elected for the town- ship of Runcorn at the recent election of Guardians for the Runcorn Union. It appears that at the election re- ferred to there were nine candidates for the office of Guardian, five of whom were returned by the Returning Officer as having received the largest number of votes. You however, were unsuccessful at the election, having received ten votes less than the number recorded for the Guardian who was returned the lowest on the poll and you have called in question the Returning Officer's rcturn on the ground that many voting papers were not delivered to persons entitled to receive them, and that voting papers which were delivered, were not collected, and that if such votes had been given they would probably have altered the result of the election. The Board have been in communication with the Returning Officer respecting the 37 cases in which you state that voting papers were not delivered to persons entitled to receive them, and it is not denied that in many of the cases mentioned by you there was an omission to deliver papers. The Board direct me to point out, however, that provision has been made by Article 21 of their General Consolidated Order, dated the 14th February, 1877, relating to the election of Guardians, to meet cases in which voting papers have not been delivered, and that the persons entitled to vote might have obtained voting papers and recorded their votes under that Article. Having regard to the provision and to the large number of voters in the township, the Board do not consider that the non-delivery of voting papers to the persons named by you affords sufficient grounds for setting aside the election, although it is possible that had these persons voted the result of the election might have been different. The Board must, consequently, decide that the Returning Officer's return shall remain undis- turbed.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, S. B. Fuovis, Assistant Secretary." UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED on the premises at J. & W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.—Advt.

div.head: RUNCORN FAILURE.
div.p: A RUNCORN FAILURE.

At the Warrington County Court, on Tuesday, a receiving order was made against John Booth, of Bates's bridge farm, Runcorn, on his own petition. Mr. Percy Davies made the application on behalf of the debtor, who was adjudicated bankrupt. A FIVE-PENNY TITHE. .

It may interest- those who are dunned for tithes to know that neglect to pay a tithe of fivepence, demanded of a labourer in Cottenham, on account of a cottage he occupied, led to a distraint, and the. legal expenses amounted to ten shillings, which the landlord had to pay, as he was liable and not the labourer. Goods worth 30s. were seized on account of this five-penny tithe. An indignation meeting was held and the rector will have the satisfaction of knowing that he has helped on the cause of Dis- establishment in Cottenham. div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. E. Carey presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Wright, Brown, Mid- wood, Cook, Timmis, Neil. Hargreaves, Hayes, Taylor, Houghton, Sadler, Liddell, J.T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr (engineer), Sinclair (surveyor).

div.head: ALLEGED LAND GRABBING BY SIR R. BROOKE
div.p: ALLEGED LAND GRABBING BY SIR R. BROOKE

The following letter was read :—" Norton Hill, Run- corn, 15th May, 1890. Dear Sir,—Gorsey-lane. Allow me to call your attention to the very bad state of this road, which I believe you undertake to keep in order. With reference to the fence that your late surveyor had the discourtesy to pull down during the night, I think it would be advisable to try and come to some terms with reference to the fencing of Gorsey-lane from top to bottom and make a good road, say 40 feet wide. In order to do this Sir Richard Brooke would have to give up a portion of his land, and as the boundary between Wid- nes and Cuerdley is, according to old plans and to ,the arrangement made by your Board with the Boundary Commissioners, within the last two years, ra down the middle of Gorsey-lane, I must contend thAt your Board has no authority over land, except by arrange- ment, in the township of Cueraey. However, I am quite prepared to try to come to an amicable settlement, if you are willing to meet roe in the matter.—Yours faithfully, C. L. Evans. The Chairman Widnes Local Board."—Dr. O'Keeffe Why should we show courtesy to, a land grabber.—Mr. Heyes : There was no more discourtesy in pulling down the rails than in putting them up.—Mr. Wright denied that any arrangement had been made with the Com- missioners where the boundary should be. Let Mr. Evans tell the Board plainly what he wanted, and what he was prepared to do. He moved that the Clerk write to that effeet.—Dr. O'Keeffe: It is well-known that the ditch is the boundary, and he must not take up any more land.—The Chairman said if Mr. Evans desired to settle the dispute in an amicable way, it was better to do so without legal proceedings. —Dr. O'Keeffe said Mr. Evans would not have recourse to legal procetdings, because he knew he was in the wrong. They wanted no land grabbers, and he proposed that the letter lie on the table unti .lr. Evans wrote in a more courteous manner, and made truthful statements.—The Chairman : I don't see any- tning discourteous myself.—Dr, O'Keeffe ; He makes statements which are not correct.—Mr. Brown thought Mr. Wright's suggestion the best, and he seconded the motion.—Mr. Hayes suggested that the letter should be referred to the Highway Committee.—Dr. O'Keeffe: The Highway Committee ordered the fence to be pulled down, and they were not going to stultify themselves by yield- ing to a land-grabber.—The Chairman: No one wants any land-grabbing or any litigation. We wanf the boundary properly placed.—Dr. O'Keeffe I want to maintain the rights of the people.—Mr. Brown : We are quite as iVIRic.)IIS (42 wintain the rights of the people as you are, but I don't see any use In fighting for them if you can get them in a more amicable and less expensive way.—Mr.Wright's motion was carried, only Dr. O'Keeffe voting against. - -

div.head: . .. THE REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES ON THE C.C.
div.p: . .. THE REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES ON THE C.C.

• „ Mr. Thomas Snape, C.C., wrote as follov• s under date May 28th.—" Dear Mr. Allen. This morning's papers announce that Manchester has succeeded in the effort to include some portions of the county area within the city boundary. The result, I expect, will be to place some seats upon the County Council at its disposal. have again and again mentioned the claims of Widnes to an extra seat to Mr. F. C. Hutton, the Clerk of the Council, and shall write to him notifying my intention to claim one of the seats that will be vacated for our town. Pos- sibly we may have to wait until the proposed Warring- to and Liverpool extensions are disposed of, or even until the end of the present three years term of existence of the County Council, that is until November, 1891. But of one thing you may be assured, that I shall take the earliest possible opportunity of pressing the claim of Widnes for an extra member upon the County Council." —The Clerk was instructed to thank Mr. Snape ffir his letter, and to express a hope that lig would be able to to carry out what he wished. THE MOSS RANK CONTRACT.

_ A letter was read from Messrs. Cowburn and Sons, of Hindley, stating that they could not accept the offer of the Highway Committee with regard to their accounts, and if it were not paid at once, they should be obliged to enter an action to recover the same, together with dam- ages for breach of contract and loss through detention of money due.---On the proposition of Mr. Sadler, it was resolved that the" letter lie on the table."

div.head: GAS AND WATER.-A LARGE PROFIT..
div.p: GAS AND WATER.-A LARGE PROFIT..

The Engineer reported to the Gas and 'Water Com- mittee that on the 20th ult, the fire escape was blown over by the wind. The raising ladder was broken, and altogether the damage was estimated at £6. The mein rainfall for the month had been 1775 inches. The water in'stock was 6,669,194 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 1955. candles. It was recommended that a new saturator be provided for the sulphate plant, estimated cost £3O. That two 20f1. purifiers be constructed at a cost of about £l,OOO. That rails and entrance gates be obtained at a cost of £3O for the entrance to Pex Hill. That the tender of G. J. Sutcliffe for the painting &c. of Netherley Works for the sum of £BO be accepted. That from the first July next the charges for water be reduced as follows For water for domestic and trade purposes 5 per cent. Foij water supplied by meter fd. per 1,000 gallons, with a minimum charge of 7s. 6d. per quarter exclusive of meter rent. For water for watering streets and flushing sewers lid. per 1.000 gallons. The profit and loss accounts for the year ending March, 1890, were sub- mitted and approved, as follows :—Gas account (which includes items of extraordinary expenditure amounting to £1,796)—a loss of £176 9s. Water account—a profit of £1,600 19s. 4d. Mr. Brown, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said they hoped to be enabled to raise the gas to 20 candle power by means of the new puri- fiers. He explained that the loss on the gas works was occasioned by the erection of a new retort house, and a new coal shed. The loss would have been a great deal more if they had not had in use the Dinsmore process of making gas, as they had been enabled to use ordinary steam coal, and maintain gas at its present low price. During the year they had increased the power of the gas from 18 candle to 19i candle. The leakage had also been reduced, and this was satisfactory because there was a theory that by making gas by the Dinsmore pro- cess the condensation in the pipes would be large. The leakage, however, was only 5i per cent., which was lower than the average in ordinary gas works. A good deal of this had been due to the foresight of the late Chairman of the Committee, Mr. Gaskell.—Mr. Wright seconded ,the minutes, but he contended that water was cheap enough at present, and that £l,OOO of the profit on the Waterworks ought to be handed over to the Highway Committee for much needed improvements. He also considered that people who were outside the boundary of the township ought to have water at the same price as the ratepayers who were responsible for the hugh debt on the works.—Mr. Sadler objected to the minimum charge of 7s. 6d. for water used by meter as unfair to traders, and Mr. Brown agreed to reduce the charge to ss.—Mr. Neild supported Mr. Wright's remarks as to the disposal of the profits.—The minutes were passed, however, with the alteration mentioned.
THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
The minutes of the Health Committee contained the report of the Medical Officer of Health,which stated that

during May there were 93 births and 48 deaths, being at the rates of 38 and 18.58 per 1,000, respectively. 24 deaths occurred amongst children under one year. Zymotie diseases caused 3 deaths. 43 cases of infectious disease had been notified, including 14 of .ineasles, 3of typhoid fever, and 19 of scarlatina. Thera were 4 patients in the Accident Hospital, and 11 in the Fever Hospital.—The report was adopted.
FINANCE. The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £5,870 Os. 2d.
\ST. JOHN'S AMBUIA.NCE CLASS, RUNCORN.
INTERESTING PRESENTATIOI+S.

A public meeting was held in Bethesda Congrega- tional School, on Monday evening, for the'purpose of witnessing the presentation of the certificates obtained by the members of the Ambulance Class which had been so successfully conducted by Dr. McDougall in connection with the St. John's Ambulance Association. The Rev. Dr. Preston pre- sided, and on the platform were Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., Dr. McDougall, and Supt. Large. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman described the forma- tion of this class and its results as one of the most interesting events that had occurred during his residence in Runcorn, and he went on tc give a historical account of the grand order of the Knights of St. John of Jerusa- lem, from the time of its formation, when the Crusaders were in the Holy Land, until the present day. He men- tioned :4,,t the Rev. Mr. Burson regretted that he was unable to be pre.sent, but had told him thai if money were needed, he should be pleased to make a subscrip- tion when called upon. (Applause.) Mr. Brundrit then distributed the certificates to the 26 students who had I passed the examination out of a total of 29. The list has been published in this journal. Afterwards Mr. Brun- drit delivered an address, in which he said that associa- tion was one that ought to commend itself to all classes, high and low, rich and poor, male and female. It was useful to anyone who undertook to go through the instruction which was necessary to obtain the certificates he had distributed. The main object of the association was to give first aid to the injured, and in these days of high pressure, when everyone seemed to be rushing from one end of the !globe to the other to see who can do the journey in the quickest time, it was not surprising that in their daily papers they should see recorded numerous accidents, and it was essential that in such a community there should be an association by which aid could be given promptly and pain alleviated until the services of a doctor could be obtained. lie noticed thattwelve policemen and several railway officials had certificates in the examination, and amongst no class of men was it so necessary that they should be enabled to give relief to the injured. That this association was not trespassing upon the medical faculty was shown by the warm hearted sympathy given to these classes by medical men, and they were indebted to their fellow-townsman, Dr. McDougall, for the great interest he had taken in establishing this class. (Ap- plause.) No one but those who had attended knew the time and attention he had given in imparting knowledge which would be beneficial to all. (Hear, hear.) There were at the present time 300 centres of the Ambulance Association, and out of the hundreds of classes that had been organised in England there were 132,000 qualified members who were able to give first aid to the wounded. He thought this was very satisfactory, and he could not think that any philanthropic institu- tion was more deserving of their consideration and esteem than the one they had introduced to them that evening. It was tha intention during the coming winter to promote further classes, and he hoped that the I success of the students who had received certificates would induce others to join the ranks and that the classes would be highly successful. (Applause.)—At this point a number of the members went through the stretcher drill, and demonstrated to the audience how to bandage a broken head and a broken jaw, and fractured limbs, and how to stop the bleeding of an injured artery, &c.— Dr. McDougall then expressed his personal obligation to Mr. Brundrit for being present that night, and said the Chief Constable of Cheshire had been making an effort to have the constabulary trained up to receive first aid cer- tificates, and already 200 of the force had qualified for these certificates. This wae a step in the right direction, and when he was asked to form a class in Runcorn he had no difficulty in coming to 4, resolution to do so. The examination the members had to undergo was a very severe ordeal indeed, and he congratulated them on the hard work that had been done and on 1 the success attained. (Applause.) Be mentioned several instances where members of the class had rendered valuable aid to injured persons, and he went on to describe the classes he intended forming next winter, remarking that it would be a pleasure to devote what time he had at his disposal to the interests of the members. (Applause.) Supt. Large spoke in highly eulogistic terms of Dr. McDougall's services, and he asked Mr. Brundrit to present him with a small memento, which had been subscribed for by the mem- bers of the class.—Mr. Brundrit, amid loud applause, then handed Dr. McDougall a handsome silk umbrella, having a black ebony handle, mounted with silver, and bearing a silver band bearing this inscription :—" Pre- sented to Dr. F. McDougall by the members of the St. John's Ambulance Class, Runcorn, in recognition of his services,as lecturer, June 9th, IB9o."—Dr. McDougall, to whom the gift was evidently a surprise, said be felt proud of that umbrella, not because of its intrinsic value but because it showed t'ae relation that had existed between the members and himself, To him it had b-nii a labour of love.--Votes ç. thanks to th'6 Chairman and Mr, Brundrit concludett the proceedings, the latter gentleman announcing thaw he would subscribe a guinea to the class in future.

MEETING OF RAILWAY MEN AT WIDNES. A meeting of railway men was held at the Rail- way Hotel, on Sunday, in support of the hours pro- gramme of the Railway Servants Union. There was a large attendance. Mr. Joseph Peters, of Edge Hill, presided. He explained the history of the hours movement and stated that it had increased the membership of the society by 14,090 men and had especially benefltted the North Western men by increase of wages, shortening of hours to some, and the payment for Sunday labour to others, who had not hitherto had that privilege. He argued their union , was the first step to the success of the movement and pointed out the solid unity of the capitalists as an ex- ample to copy, allowing no sectional differences to inter- fere with the end in view. Railway men had broken through the barriers of tyranny years ago, and now possessed the right of free combination and should wield that power for their political and social advancement. Now was the most opportune time that railway men had ever presented to them for a forward movement, ' and he trusted that whilst they would be fair andreason- able in their demands they would maintain their right to just and courteous treatment by the Railway Com- pany. Mr. Peters then read the hours programme, and forably commmented upon the long hours and low I rate of pay that is the evil characteristic of the I railway service, a,nd pointed out in detail how the pro- gramme had been devised to meet the case of every grade. Overwork especially came in for strong condom- nation,and, he contended, ought to be restrained alike in the interests of public safety, the interests of health, and the overcrowded state of the labour market. He wound up with a vigorous appeal to the non-unionists to dismiss I their idle fears and join in the movement to abolish the evils which afflicted the railway sarvice.—Mr. Martin Lyons, of Manchester, moved a resolution, embodying the hours programme, and it was seconded by Mr. A. Meer, travelling secretary, who appealed to the non- unionists either to do their honest duty by the pro- gramme, or substitute a better plan, and in an animated manner he pointed out how they acted as a retarding force in every struggle yet attempted by the society, and thus proved enemies to a cause he knew they were at heart friendly to. He implored them to consider what waste of life there was on railways, what homes left cheerless, and children fatherless, the pain and suffering of the maimed, the grinding tyranny of official- ism, and ask themselves whether they could conscienti- ously remain apathetic while the battle raged under the flag of a Society he hoped they would take that oppor- tunity of joining. Other speeches were made, and the resolution was carried unanimously. Afterwards a considerable addition was made to the strength of the society.

div.head: INTERESTING ROAD QUESTION AT _NORTON,
div.p: INTERESTING ROAD QUESTION AT _NORTON,

At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Henry Reynolds, Charles Jones, of Norton, was summoned for having on the 29th May at Norton, allowed his dog to be at large unmuzzled.—Mr. Humphreys defended.—P.C. Jackson deposed that the iog was at large in Pepper-st., and Mr. Humphreys con- tended that the public had no legal right on the road.— P.C. Jackson said he had known the road for four years and he had never known it closed against the public. It was included in his beat.—lnspector Bowyer, P. S. Woolley, and P.S. Costello also gave evidence that Pepper-st. was a public place.—Mr. Humphreys for the defence stated that the dog was not in Pepper-st., but was actually in a meadow close to the read leading to the Ship Canal Works. The officer was nowhere about at the time, but a few minutes afterwards he came up the road, followed by the dog, from the direction of the Ship Canal IV orks. The case had arisen through spleen on the part of the officer who had threatened that he would make it hot for the defendant because he had prevented him from join- ing a club.—Fred Jones deposed that the dog was not in Pepper's-st., and that Pepper-st. was not a public road.— Mary Jones and Walter Jones gave similar evidence.— Frederick Weir said Pepper-st. belonged to Sir Richard Brooke, and the road came in his holding. He was liable to repair the road. It was not in any sense a public road, and he had stopped people and carts from going along many a time.—By Superintendent Large: The public used the road but only by courtesy.—Mr. Reynolds: They use it and you don't stop them.—Witness I can stop them from going through my yard. I cannot say whether I can stop them from going up the road.—Supt. Large : I suppose a dog can bite anyone on that road as well as anywhere else? (Laughter.)—Witness : I sup- pose so.—John Frodsham said he was in Norton Estate office for 12 years. The road was included in the farm and the public had no right to useit except on sufferance. —By Mr. Brundrit : It was seventeen years since he had been in Norton Estate office.—Mr. Brundrit said 12 years public access to a road would give the right to use it. He failed to see that it had been proved that this was not a public road which was the material point. A fine of 6d. and costs £1 was imposed.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.

The Committee of the Runcorn Musical Society are taking time by the forelock, and are already making arrangements for next season. They have decided to give an orchestral concert on November 4th, with two vocalists; the Messiah on December 16th; and the Elijah in Lent. The Secretary (Mr. R. W. Pierpoint) is in communication with first- class artistes with a view to engagements. Alto- gether concert-goers may anticipate a season of good things. The present order for the muzzling of dogs is quite as offensive to the owners as it is harrassing to the four-footed friend of man, which has to don the "cage," and any place where they could have a free run would be deemed a perfect elysium by the intel- ligent animals. Mr. Charles Jones, of Norton, appeared before the Runcorn magistrates, on Monday,and through his advocate, Mr. Humphreys, contended there was such a desirable spot in that picturesque township. Constable Jackson alleged that he found Mr. Jones' dog without the regulation muzzle,in what, for want of a better name I suppose, is called Pepper-St., and the defence was that this street was not a public thoroughfare, and that, therefore, the dog was at perfect liberty to roam un- restrained. It could not be denied, however, that the public had access to the street, and as Superin- tendent Large pertinently suggested, the dog could bite there as well as anywhere else. The magi', trates'came to the conclusion that the dog ought to have been muzzled, and Mr. Jones, for his disobedi- ence to the law, had to pay the sum of .£1 Os. 6d. Underlying the "doggy "part of the business,there is a more important question. Evidence was given showing that this street, or lane, had been used by thepublic,without let or hindrance,for a period of at least 25 years. Although at one time there might have been" a gate at the lower part," and the people had originally been allowed to pass along on "suffe- rance," by the lapse of years a public right to use the road has been acquired. Mr. Brundrit, the res- pected chairman of the Bench, informed the Court that twelve years' public access would give the right of use, and there is no doubt that in this case the "right of use" has been amply acquired. It is said that, as a retort upon the adverse decision of tho magistrates as to the dog, the public will be prevented from using the lane in future, but it is to be hoped that the people most concerned will have the courage to resist any such attempt, and the evi- dence as adduced at the Police Court would success- fully uphold such resistance. The mention of Norton brings to mind that at the last meeting of Widnes Local Beard Dr. O'Keeffe applied the term "land grabber" to the agent of Norton Estate. A few int,nths ago, Mr. Evans caused to be placed in the neighbourhood of Gorsly- lane, Crouton, a line of fencing which the Local Board decided was an encroachment upon the public rights, and they promptly authorised the Surveyor to root the fence up, and throw it into a gutter which they contended was the boundary of Sir Richard Brooke's estate. Mr. Evans has now re- opened the question, and the Local Board, with a desire to avoid litigation, whilst by no means in tear of it, have invited him to lay his views and pro- posals before them in extenso and they will consider them. There has been sadlx too much filching of public land by landowners in the past, and it is pleasing to see a public body so ready to repel what they consider an invasion. Those associated commercial concerns of the Widnes Lepel Board, the Gas and Water Works, continue in a most flourishing condition, and, on Tuesday, Mr. Brown.as chairman of the Committee, had the satisfaction of announcing a profit on the Water Works of .£1,609 although the precious fluid is sold at a cheaper rate than at any other town in the neighbourhood. On the gas works a loss of .£176 98. was announced, but it must be remembered that during the year a new retort house was built and other improvements effected at a cost of £1,796. So that had the usual practice of debiting the cost of such permanent structures to capital charge been carried out, a handsome profit would have been shown in the gas undertaking. However taking the gas and water together, there is a surplus balance of over £1,400. and this is to be used for still further cheapening the price of water. Mr. Wright and Mr. Neil contended that water was already cheap enough, and that at least a thousand pounds of the profits ought to be appro- priated for reducing the General District Rate or for carrying out public improvements under the super- vision of the Highway Committee, Of course the ratepayers get the benefit of the money in either case, and the Board agreed that it should go towards a teduction in the price of water,as that com,moc) ity is indispendlN to all people.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICES—On Sunday sermons were preached in the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Frodsham, by the Rev. J. W. Butcher, of Liverpool, the morning sub- ject being "The Bible and Humanity," and the evening, "A Purpose in Life." In the afternoon the Rev, gentle- man conducted a special service for scholars, teachers, parents, and friends, the subject being "Lessons from the flowers." The children and their friends brought flowers, which were distributed afterwards. rho scholars, with the assistance of the choir, rendered the hymns and the anthems "Give thanks to God" (William Youens), and "The Lord is mystrength " (Caleb Simper under the conductorship of Mr. T. Sant, in a creditable manner. Mr. W. H. Pickering presided at the organ. The collections amounted to £23.

div.head: CHEMICAL WORKERS' UNION.
div.p: THE CHEMICAL WORKERS' UNION.

A well-attended meeting of the St. Helens mem- bers of the Chemical Workers Association, was held in the coach-house, Cotham-st., on Friday. Mr. P. J. King addressed the meeting at some length and said a few weeks ago he told them that they were organiing a campaign against the cowards, black- legs and knobsticks. The union in St. Helens was now strong enough to assert itself, and he hoped that during the election of the various yard com- mittees anyone who was afraid to assert himself and was ashamed of his connection with the union and frightened to speak to the managers or tore- men, would be relegated into private life, and that they would elect men who would fearlessly dis- charge their duty. They did not want irrational or imprudent or hot-headed men or fiery enthusi- asts connected with the committee. They wanted reasonable, rational men who would look at every thing put before them from a business standpoint and deal with it accordingly. He referred to the dispute in a Widnes chemical works, where he said the men came out on strike on their own responsibility. As he considered their case a. just and reasonable one he asked them to stand firmly by those men, no matter bow long they were out, so that they could show them that, although the matter was not Connected with the union, they could help their brethren hi their trouble. (Hear hear.) Those men demanded nothing unreasonable In the adjoining yards, and in St. Helens they were getting 3s. and he did not see why they should not get it there. (Hear, hear.) He instructed them as to several of the rules and then said he wanted to give a finishing touch to the organisation that month, and if they would help him he would undertake that in the next month there would not be a man connected with the chemical works in St. Helens who would be outside the union. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: BEFORE TEE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE TEE MAGISTRATES.

Timm BY LAD. At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday morning, a lad named James Derkin, (13), was charged with steal- ing a silver breastpin, the property of William Henry Palmer, from Mr. Edward Connors stables. The lad, who admitted the offence, was ordered to pay the costs. The prosecutor did not press the case, and it was stated that the, parents of the boy were very respectable, though Poor.

div.head: MUZZLING. ORDER.
div.p: THE MUZZLING. ORDER.

John Wainwright, butcher, Buttermarket-st., was summoned to the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, on a charge of having allowed a dog to be at large and unmuzzled on the 4th June.. P.C. Davies said that the dog, although it had a strap on, bit a• boy on the arm.. Evidence to the same effect was given by the lad.---' Alderman Sutton remarked that nine out of every ten dogs in Warrington that were supposed to be muzzled were insufficiently muzzled.. A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted.

NEGLECT OF, FAMILY. A case of desertion of family was heard by the Warring- ton magistrates on Monday, when a wire worker named Charles Fairbrother was charged with having, on the 19th March, deserted his three children' who had become chargeable to the Union. Mr. Basil Shearer, inquiry officer, said that the prisoner's children—aged twelve, seven, and five years—were admitted to the Workhouse on the 19th March,and had cost the Guardians about M. Prisoner had left the town, and on returning on Saturday was apprehended by P.C. Frank Jones. The Bench committed Fairbrother to prison for three months, with hard labour. THE MAINTENANCE OF A " CLIO," BOY. , Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, James Amies was summoned to show cause why he should not be o,rdered to contribute the maintenance of his son on the ship" Clio." Mr. Forshaw (Messrs. P. Davies and Forshaw) appeared on behalf of the defendant, and said that an application was being made for the dis- charge of the boy from the "do," and he asked that the magistrates would allow the summons to stand over until the result of the applicatiot was known. The magistrates' clerk said that the boy was being maintained at the present time, and that the maintenance should be paid for. The Bench refused the application, and made an order on defendant to pay 2s. 6d. a week. , A CASUAL WHO WOULD NOT WORK FOR HIS •On Thursday morning, a man named John Mason (23), a labourer, last from Manchester, was charged in cus- tody at the Warrington, Police Court, with having refused to perform the customary task of work when a Casual inmate of the Warrington Workhouse. He was also charged with having wilfully damaged a door. The •case having been proved, Major Litton ,said that the prisoner ought to do something for what he received at the Workhouse.—Prisoner What, for a. piece of dry "chuck !"—Porter Curry stated that the casuals got bread and water for supper and breakfast, and bread and cheese, or what was called " scouse," for dinner.— Mason was committed to prison for a month. Flkl.t.K.N YEARS OF MISERY AND STARVATION. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Saturday, John Edwards, Dial-court, was charged with having been drunk and having used threats towards his wife.—Mrs. Edwards, in the course of her evidence, stated that she and the prisoner had been married 17 years, 15 of which had been to her years of misery and starvation. He was constantly abusing her. On Tuesday he came home drunk and began to break the crockery. She remonstrated with him, and he threatened to "knock her neck out." P.C. Frank Jones proved seeing the prisoner drunk and hearing him threaten -his wife in default a 'finding sureties to keep the peace, the prisoner was committed for a month; and on the charge cf drunkenness he was ordered to undergo a further term of 14- days' hard labour.

- - ALLEGED THEFT OF,A HALF-SOVEREION. At the Warrington _Police Court, on Monday. Jane Cowley, wife of a stone-mason, employed on the Ship Canal, was charged with having stolen half-a-sovereign from Catherine Daley. Prosecutor keeps a lodging-house in Scotland-road, and the prisoner ^ had been lodging there a few days. On Saturday she had-as. 4d. to pay for her lodgings, and.handed Mrs. Daley a two shilling piece. For change Ml:s. Daley gave her, it was alleged, a half-sovereign and twopence, intending it for a six- pence and twopence. As soon as the mistake was dis- covered the police were informed and the prisoner taken into custody. A purse containing Is. 7d. was found on her. The Bench regarded the case as one of strong suspicion, but thought the evidence insufficient to convict, and accordingly discharged the accused. _

div.head: FAMILY DESERTION.
div.p: FAMILY DESERTION.

At the Borough Police Court, at Warrington, Richard Kean was brought up on a charge of having neglected his three children. Mr. Harbourne, relieving officer, said that on Tuesday morning he visited the prisoner's house in Cartwright-st., and found that there was neither food nor fire there. He gave an order for the three child- ren to be admitted to the Workhouse. Mrs. Kean told him that her husband had only given her 15s. out of 235. he had earned last week, and that he was drunk every day. Mr. Shearer said that prisoner had had good work ih connection with the election of Gnardians, but he got drunk and other people had to finish the work. Mr. J. White said that prisoner had been twice charged with assaulting his wife, and once with neglecting to maintain her. He was now sent to prison for a month.

div.head: AN UNREGISTERED DAIRY.
div.p: AN UNREGISTERED DAIRY.

Joseph Woodward, Longford-st., was fined .10s. and costs by the Warrington magistrates on Monday, for having, on the 4th inst.,carried on business as a dairy and cow-keeper without being registered. Inspector Norman said that nine or ten weeks ago the defendant applied to have his premises registered, but witness de- clined to register them on the ground that they were in an unsanitary condition. The defects were remedied, and the defendant instructed to again apply for registra- tion of the premises. In consequence of his neglect to do so, he had been summoned. The Inspector added that it was very necessary tot have the Daries, Cowsheds, and Milkshops Order, 1879, stringently enforced. An out- break of plPuro-pueumonia had taken place in the borough, and would cost hundreds of pounds. THE CONSEQUENCF.9 OF A BYBEE. . . .

On Monday, at tke Warrington Police Court, a man named James Kelly was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Dallam-lane on Saturday afternoon, and with having assaulted John Brown at the same time and place. A disturbance took place between Kelly, Brown, and other men in the Three Pigeons vaults. They were rejected, and on getting into the streets Kelly, it was alleged, knocked Brown down and kicked him several times. The Bench ordered Kelly to pay a fine of ss. and costs.—Arising out of this case was A charge of theft against Mary Kelly and Jane Tickle. During the truggle between the men a sovereign and a shilling fell out of Brown's pocket. .The money, it was alleged, was picked up by Kelly, and given to Tickle, who went away with it. When taken into custody 13s. 4kl. was found In the possession of Tickle. These prisoners were fined 20s. and costs.

div.head: COUPLE OF COWARDLY RUFFIANS.
div.p: A COUPLE OF COWARDLY RUFFIANS.

Two powerfully built men, named Stephen Collins and Thomas Mitchell, were charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with having stolen from the person of John Kelly, on Sunday night, at Arpley, a pipe and a silk pocket handkerchief. The complainant stated that wheenear Monk's rope walk at Arpley; Collins came up to him, and struck him a violent blow in the face, demanding witness's pipe. Complainant closed with him. Whilst fighting with Collins, Mitchell came up and struck complainant a blow in the face. Witness, seem" that the odds were against him, managet' to es- cape, but Collins overtook him under the iron 'ridge and knocked him down. Collins held him and knelt on the back of his neck, took the handkerchief and pipe from him, and endeavoured to steal his money, but assistance came. P.C. Condliffe proved arresting the prisoners. The complainant appeared, he said, to have been very severely handled, his face being covered with blood. Each of the prisoners was committed to prison for a month in default of paying a fine of 10s. and costs.
UNPROVOKED ASSAULT ON A WARRINGTON SCHOOL- MISTRESS. On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court,. a . '

married womah named Jane Johnson, living in Hay- dock-st., was brought up on a warrant charged with, having assaulted Mary Josephine Bellian, mistress of the Orford-lane School. Complainant was on her way home from school on Monday afternoon, when the prisoner came up to her in Tanner's-lane, and without any pro- vocation attacked her. She caught hold of the complain- ant by her hair, and struck her several times in the face. Bystanders interfered, and the prisoner was induced to leave complainant alone. Prisoner denied the assault, and complained that Miss Bellian had refused to admit a child to the school. Complainant said that the boy had not attended the school since the early part of February. When apprehended by P.S. Rowbotham prisoner admitted the assault, and said she thought she would get two months for it. The Bench committed her to prison for one month, with hard labour. At the close of the case a witness Complained that the prisoner had said, "I'll stab you when I come out," and the Chief Constable told her to inform the police if the woman molested her. A DRUNKEN MILITIAMAN ROBBED OF HIS COAT. A disgraceful case was investigated by the Warrington magistrates on Tuesday, when a Ship Canal labourer named John Coslin was brought up in custody on a charge of having stolen from the person of James Tully, a jacket and muffler, of_ the value of 10s. ed., and 7s. 2-id. in silver and copper. The prosecutor is a labourer, and also a militiaman, and should have pro- ceeded on Monday with his regiment to Altcar for train- ing. He left home in the morning between nine and ten o'clock with 12s. or 13s. in his pocket. He visited several public-houses, and later in the day met with the prisoner. The prosecutor, while in a state of intoxica- tion, and the prisoner and a man not yet in custody, during the afternoon went to some waste land off Battersby-lane, where prosecutor fell asleep. Prisoner and the other man were seen by several young ladies liv- ing in the neighbourhood to put grass in the prosecutor's mouth and to slap his face. They then robbed him of his coat and muffler, the first named being pawned at the shop of Mrs. Tunstall by the prisoner, who gave a
