div.p: false name and address. When charged, prisoner ad- mitted stealing the coat, but not the money. In answet tb the Bench, he explained that he was a labourer on the Ship Canal. He had been ill, and had been allowed 10s. from the club.—The Chairman (to the prosecutor) : We have no sympathy with a man who deliberately spends his money in drinking the whole day. You have brought this trouble upon yourself, and you deserve it. You take a certain course, and. you get a certain result.—Prisoner was committed to gaol fora month, with hard labour.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair), and Mr. Robert Garnett. DRUNICENNESS.—Lawrence Mack, for having been drunk and disorderly in Sankey-st., on Friday evening, was fined ss. including costs.—Catherine Brqwn, an old offender, was sent to prison for a month on a similar

charge. A LOCAL AHAZON.—Catherine Bowdon, Tanne,s-lane, was charged With having been drunk and disorderly, on Friday, in Wilderspool-rd., also wit& having assaulted Mary Ainsworth, at the same time and place.—The Chief. Constable said that the prisoner deserved to be severely dealt with. She was a terror to all she came across, whether by night or day. She could fight like a man, and often did so, and • was 'proud of it.—Prisoner was committed far a month, With hard labour. MoNn&v.—:-Before Aldermen Holmes and Sutton. DRUNKENNESS.—A navvy named John Brown, for be- ing drunk and refusing to quit the Norton Arms Hotel, and also for assaulting Millington, the barman.was com- mitted to gaol for 14. days, in default of paying a fine of 10s. and costs.—The following persons were summoned for drunkenness, and dealt with as follows :—William Gaghan, Market Gate, on Saturday night, fined ss. and costs, or seven days ; John Macdonald. Town Hill; Satur- day night, fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days; John Mc- Nichols, for attempting to rescue the latter from the police, was fined a like amount ; John Dunn, Saturday night, Buttermarket-st. fined ss. and costs ; William Farrell, Bank-st., fined lbs. and costs. Taarr.—A youth named Frederick Leigh. 24, Golden- st., wal committed to gaol for three months, for steal- ing a coat, value 305., the property of Felix Maginn, on the sth June. CHIMNEY& ON FIRE.—For having allowed the chimneys of their dwelling-houses to be on fire, Gebrge Smith and Kate Kent were ordered to pay &shilling each. STONE THRowtrzo.—Thomas Baguley was fined ss. and costs for stone throwing in Winwick-st., on the 2nd inst. • A &mar/ DltivEn.—Thcimas Wariey, carter, Knutsford- road, Was summoned for having been asleep whilst in charge of a. horse and cart in Cockhedge-lane, on the 3rd June.—A fine of 7s. 6d., including costs, was imposed. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—John Carr was charged on a war- rant with having 'assaulted Thomas Hynes on the 7th September, 1889 ; and.with having wilfully broken three panes of glass at Hynes' residence. It was alleged that the parties met in Buttermarket-st. when, without the least provocation, Carr struck the complainant in the face with his fist. He afterwards followed the complain- ant home, and threw some bottles at the windows, smashing three panes. Prisoner admitted that he had struck the complainant, but said it was with his open hand. He denied having broken the windows. He had been away from the town ever since the occurrence, working at Rochdale. The Chief Constable said that the prisoner had been 43 times before the Court. If be had stayed away the police would not have fetched him.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed. TIIESDAY.—Before_Mr. R. Garnett and Mr. W. Owen. . . .

DRIINKENNESS.—Thomas Smith, charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on the afternoon previous, was fined 55., including costs.— Martin Higgins was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., on the previous afternoon. It was his ninth appearance. A fine of ss. and costs was

- imposed. - SCHOOL CASES.—Several persons were summoned for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, the usual fines being inflicted. Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, proved the cases. AN ABSENTEE.—MichaeI Hogan, who admitted being an absentee from last year's training of the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Militia, was fined 405., including costs, the alternative being seven days' imprisonment. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes and Mr. John - Fairclough. DRUNKENNESS .—For this offence Patrick Clynes was fined 10s. and costs, Isabella Parry ss, and costs, Frances Riley ss. and costs, and Frank Smith 10s. and costs. THIIRSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Major Pickmere.

DRUNICENNESS.—Joseph Smith and Ellen McCormick were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Academy-st., on the night previous. Smith was fined ss. and costs, and McCormick, who was said to be an old offender, was sent to prison for a fortnight.—Samuel Wilson, a coloured man of middle age, who gains his living as a travelling musician,' was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Mersey-st., on the previous evening, and was ordered to pay the lock-up fee. SLEEPING °u.—For this offence a man named Hart was sent to prison for seven days, with hard labour. FkmAr.—Before Mr. John White and Alderman Harrison.

DRUNKENNESS.--Bridget Dolley was charged with ba- ying been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st. on the previous night. She was dismissed with a caution. LADS IN TROUBL4—John Griffin, John Bellian, and Joseph Leonardy, lads, were brought up in custody on a charge of having been on enclosed premises in Bold-st., the same morning, with intent.to commit a felony. The two first-named lads received a very bad character from the police. Griffin was sent to prison fer three months, Bellian for a month, and Leonardy was discharged with a caution. ' WINDOW SMASHINO.—Mary Ann Tarney was sum- moned for having, on the 25th May, done damage to the amount of 10s.' by breaking windows on the property of Thomas Smith Holland. She was fined 20s. and costs, including the damage, or 14 days' imprisonment in I default.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MoNnex,---Before Mr. James Tinsley. DIIIINKENNESS.—George Corrighan was charged with being drunk at Rixton, on the previous Saturday, and was tined 2s. 6d. and costs. John Evans, charged with a similar offence on Sunday evening last, at Rixton, was also fined 2s 6d. and costs. Thefts, and costs were paid in each case.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. 'MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. H. Reynolds. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.—John Barclay was fined 6d. and costs, Bs. 6d., for allowing the chimney of his dwelling to be on fire. .....

STRAY Doos.—William Peck, of Runcorn, and George Leach, of Halton, Edward Mills and George Hughes, of Weston, were each fined 6d. and costs, Bs. 6d., for per- mitting their dogs to stray at lar,6 unmuzzled. Dnurrx AND DlSORDERLY.—Christopher Hagan, Sarah Ann Hughes, and William John Scott, were each fined ss. and coats for being drunk. A DEPRAYBD DOMESTIC SERVANT.—Annie Fernehough, 17 years of age, was charged with having, on Whit- Tuesday, stolen a shilling, belonging to Joseph McQuinn, boot dealer, High-st., and also with stealing four brooches, twelve yards of lace, and a shilling, belonging to May Boole, a machinist in the prosecutor's employ. It appeared that on the day in question Mr. and Mrs. McQuinn went to Llandudno, leaving the prisoner in charge of the hou* and the children. When they returned at night, the prisoner had gone and left the children, and it was found that the cash box and Hoole's clothes box had been broken open. Subsequently the prisoner was apprehended at Warrington by P.C. Woodrow.— Superintendent Large said the prisoner was wanted at Salford on a similar charge.—She was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

MAINTENANCE OF A WlFE.—Jonathan Fairhurst, of Hatton, was summoned to show cause why he should not comply with an order of the magistrates to contri- bute 7s per week towards the support of his wife,who is an inmate of Chester asylum.—Mr. Linaker, who ap- peared for the Board of Guardians, said , defendant was £lO 15s. in arrears, but he had that morning paid £5, and he asked for an order for the payment of the re- mainder in a month.

DAMAGE AT WESTON QUARRY.—F. Allman, and Wm. Cobb, boys, were charged with having on the 24th May, at Weston, unlawfully committed damage to the property of the Runcorn and Helsby Red Sandstone Co., Limited. —Arthur G. Guest, manager of the CO., said the Co. had suffered considerably from damage done by boys and youths, and this case was brought as a warning. The defendants had deliberately broken a long plank which they had been using for the purpose of climbing to birds nests. The defendants pleaded guilty, and were ordered to pay the ditnage, and costs Bs. 6d. each.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. H. Gaskell sear. and Mr. H. GaskeD junr.

EDUCATION ACT.—A number of persons were fined ss. for not sending their children regularly to school.--John Waithead, Church-st. ; James Dean, Pear-st. ; Robert Bond, Thorpe-st. ; and Edward Weir were each sam- mooed te show cause why they should not contribute towards the support of their respective children who are inmates of the Hightown Truant School. Westhead was ordered to pay 2s. ed. per week; Weir, Is. 6d.; Bond, ,• and Dean, 9d. DRUNEENNE.4.9.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Rose Ann Carney, Moon-st. ; Thomas Radley, Church-st. ; Jaines Mason Pear-st. ; John W. Williams, Pitt-st., and Rose Kelly, e.ee-st. - BREACH oi THE PEACE. —For this offence Mary McDer- mott of Beamont-street, was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months. Duo AT LARGE.—Michael McConville, of Grenfell-st., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs forallowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled. TM& LODGERS. —Pierce Wall, of • Caroline-street, was summoned for assaulting Lydia Ball on the 7th inst. There was some feeling between the parties with refer- ence to a lodger, and it was alleged that the defendant pulled a quantity of hair off the complainant's head. A line of Ds, and costs was imposed.

, WARRINGTON V. CHEETHAM HILL. The first or tnesei fixtures was played at Warrington on Saturday, and re-- suited in a win for the home team. Messrs. Crosfield and C. G. Lawton faced the deliveries of H. A. Swallow and J. Lawton. Mr. C. G. Lawton 'playing ao'ainst his brother, got.him away for 10 (three '2s and a 4) in his second over. Both batsmen afterwards played very steadily, and with 34 runs placed to the home team, W. H. Pennington succeeded Lawton at the railway end. The separation, however, came from the other end, Mr. C. G. Lawton retiring (1 for 37). Four runs later Mr. Crosfield played on to his wicket. Mr. Clarke was bowled at 42, and at 50 Mr. Smith retired. WARRINGTON V. CHEgTHAM ELUL (2ND ELEVENS)•— This match was played at Cheetham Hill, on Saturday, and resulted in a splendid victory for the visitors. The home team batted first, making a bad start, three wickets being down for six runs. The captain and Lang took the score to 38, by good cricket, and Southern hit freely for his 26, five wickets being down for 71. Collier and Kershaw made a determined stand for the eighth wicket, causing several bowling changes, and were not parted until they had put on 34 runs. The total eventually reached.ll9. The flelding of the visitors was not so good as usual, and the bowling, with the exception of Bell. who took six wickets for 35 runs, was expensive. Howard at the wicket received favourable mention by the spectators. Adarnson and Jefferson commenced for the visitors, and put on 28 for the first wicket. Brown

hit freely, and with Jefferson, took the score to 65. The captain and Muir by careful play gradually took the score to 100, and then, when victory seemed secure, hit very freely. When the match was , won the fielding of the home team became very loose, hnd the pair taking every advantage, put 172 on the board, at which num- ber the captain was caught at the wicket, having played beautiful cricket for pc,. his cutting aad defence play being much admired. 'Muir soon followed, his 43 having been well put together. Bell and Dunbobbin hit away during the remaining 20 minutes left for play, and just succeeded in reaching the 200. The home team were very strong, and the Warrington team deserve all praise for their performance. They should give Sefton a very good game on Saturday at the Arpley ground. MURDERS IN LONDON.

About six o'clock on Sunday evening a shocking tragedy was discovered to have taken place in Grove- road, Holloway, .London. Mr. oak 3, aged about 60. years, it appears is it chemist, but has been out of employment for many months, during which time he has occupied a first-floor flat at 27, Grove-road. Shortly after six o'clock cries of murder were heard, and when the other lodgers entered the room it was found that Mr. and Mrs. Oaks and their boy, about eight years old, were under the influence of poison presumably prussic acid. The lad died almost immeditely but,in the case of the parents, the father, finding at te poidon was ineffec- tualto complete his purpose, ha , it is alleged, cut his wire's throat and his own t Whey* were removed to the Great Northern Hosproff, where they are de- tained."4oppo are entertained of their recovery. An exciting scene was witnessed in Bolsover-st., Great Portland-st., London, on Saturday. Shortly before six o'clock a Frenchman was standing in Great ritchfield-st. watching a Punch and Judy show, and presently he croSsed the road, and, knocking at the door of No. 123, asked for Francois De Grove. Almost at the same moment De Grove came home, and the two men had an altercation on the doorstep. They then walked away, and while they were in Bolsover-st., De Grove's com- panion drew a revolver, and, levelling it at him, fired. The bullet entered De Grove's left breast just below the heart. The stranger made off, but there were a number of people in the street who witnessed the occurrence, and they gave chase. When one of them attempted to stop him he fired again, but missed, and was secured. lathe meantime the injured man was taken to the Middlesex Hospital, in Goodge-st., where he died on Sunday after- noon. His assailant's name was subsequently ascertained to be Francis Manton.

He was not in favour of a man being deprived of his property simply because he happened to be a publican. A licensed vic- tualler had a claim to justice preciselythe same as a man engaged in any other trade. He agreed in the main that publicans have a title to compenaation, and he would be glad if the deputation could suggest some scheme which would meet their views and be acceptable to the public, under which the compensation desired by the trade might be allotted. Mr. H. Mitchell (Birmingham Breviers' Association) intimated that they were not prepared to suggest a scheme, but would support any moderate scheme of temperance legislation.

GREAT DEMONSTRATION IN LONDON. A demonstration of metropolitan temperance and poli- tical associations against the "compensation" clauses in the Local Taxation Bill was held on Saturday afternoon in Hyde Park. The march to the park was made in five separate divisions—viz., the east, west, north, and north- east, and south-west. The western division marched to- the park direct, entering mainly at the Marble Arch. The other sections were massed on the Embankment,and went by way or Bridge-street, Birdcage Walk, Buck- ingham Palace-road, Grosvenor Place, and Hyde Park Corner. There was a great display of banners, in all about 400, and over a hundred bands of music. Among _

the uniforms those of the Salvation Army, the Gooa Templars, and the Catholic contingent were the most prominent. The temperance' societies and the political organisations brought their own flags bearing their distinctive mottoes and devices but many had been improvised and on these the demonstrators . .

had very forcibly expressed their sentiments towards the Government Bill in such words as " Compensation for Bung? Decidedly not." On a Scotch plaid banner carried by the London Scots Temperance contingent . , „ . .
were the-words " We'll no' grease the fat coo AnOther

had the effigy of a gibbeteep' üblican, and the scroll con- tained the lines,' " Ritchie's pills will not digest; Law- son's and Caine's are the best. There were sixteen plat- forms, and from each of these the following resolutions were moved;

"1, That this meeting indignantly protests against the Government proposal to provide money from the public funds for the purchase of ' interest' in premises licensed for the sale of intoxicating liquors, Parliament- ary enactment's and the highest legal decisions having uniformly limited the privilege conferred by a license to .the yearly term for which it is granted.- And the nicet- ing reprobates the attempt made by her Majesty's Ministers, unsanctioned by . the electors and in defiance of public opinion to create a vested interest in licences, involving hundreds of mil- lions of money, and thus to endow a class already dangerously rich and powerful at the cost of un- told poverty and wretchedness of Feat masses of our fellow-countrymen. And this meeting hereby adopts the following petition to Parliament, and requests the Chair- man to sign it on behalf of the meeting :—"Co'lhe Honourable the Commons of Great Fritain and Ireland in Parliament assembled : The humble petition of inhabi- tants of London assembled sI one of the meetings con- stituting the aggregate demonstration in Hyde Park, June 7, 1890, showeth,--that your petitioners view with intense disapprobation the compensation clauses of the Local Taxation Bill, Your petitioners- therefore pray your honourable House to exclude such Clauses. from the Bill, and to enact a measure by which the inhabitants of localities would be enabled freely and,_directiv to vetothe issue or reissue of licences within 'the* respective dis- tricts. And your petitioners will evil. pray. , , Z • "2. • That this meeting strongly cdtideinne the actlim of the Right Hon. Henry Matthews, her Majesty's Secre7 e tary of State for the Home Department, in having i t ;tructed the Metropolitan Police authorities to prey . he various processions to this demonstratioi:Otriveisin ' he ordinary thoroughfares of the metropillis, thus attempting to obstruct a peaceable deecepstration of public opinion and causing needless irritation to great masses of law-abiding citizens." One of' the last platforms to be occupied by speakers was No. 4, which was allotted more partic- ularly to the temperance party. The Chairman did not arrive till nearly half-past six, whilst the vari- ous teetotal lodges, with their bands and banners, failed to put in an appearance' till seven o'clock, although they left the Embankment at half-past font.. Owing to the late arrival of the organised temperance contingents, they were not present at the first part of the proceedings.—Mr. Caine, M.P., presided,. and amongst those present were Mr. Conybeare, ! M.P., Dr. F. R. Lees, Mr., Joseph Malins, Mr. John Sutherland, &c.— A very large and enthusiastic audience gathered at pier form No. 7,that of the London Municipal Reform League. Here Professor Stuart, M.P., presided, and in his open- ing speech said the Bill had been introduced in the House of Commons in the most surreptitious manner, and it should be opposed by every.possiblo means.—The ' other speakers at the platform included Mr. Picton,M.P., Mr. Atherley Jones, M.P., Mr. John Burns., Mr. W. Saunders and Mr. R. S. Jackson, Mr. CoStelloe presided at platform No. 13, ,where Sir Thomas Ferrer and Mr. Causton had been announced to speak. The former, however, sent a letter apologizing for his absence on the ground yf indisposition, whilst the Chairman explained that Mr. Causton, whom he had seen on the way, had evidently been prevented from reaching the platform on account of the density of the crowd He read Sir Thomas Farrer's letter, in which he said: "Whatever may be the truth with respect to the diminu- tion of public-houses, it i,s certain .that the diminution which can be effected with the money by this Bill can hal. eno practical effect in diminishing drinking. It will, on the otherhand, increase the custom and the value of ' the rethaining public-houses. Whatever may be the truth about compensation, no reasonable 'person wishes to give license holders a stronger vested interest or a larger claim to compensation than they now 'possess. But this must be the inevitable result' of the Government Bill."--Mr. B. T. L. Thompson proposed the first resolu- tion; which was supported by Mrs. Costeiloe, and carried amid great enthusiasm.—Mr. Arthur Pollen proposed,. and Miss Jane Cobden seconded, She resolution condemn- ing the conduct of the police . authorities, and it was carried amidst enthusiasm. Miss Jane Cobden presided at the Women's Liberal Ass:3.666mi platform, at -which the chief speakers were Dr. Kate Mitchell, Miss F. Balgarnie, the Countess Shack, Mrs. Costelloe, and Mrs. Jacob Bright. . -

div.head: COMPENSATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

CARDINAL MANNING ON LICENSES, &c. ' Cardinal Manning has an article in the "Contempor- ary Review "on the question which has been raised by the Local Taxation Bill. His Eminence recalls the failure of the licensing clauses in the Local Government Bill two years ago, and says that Mr. Goschen's• pro- posals are tenfold worse than Mr. Ritchie's. He asks :
-- • Is the drink trade a condition of life to the party now in.government ? Is it not possible to maintain the con-

stitutional and conservative traditions of the Empire without buying or bribing the goodwill of the drink trade? The worst enemy of Lord Salisbury's Govern- ment could hardly impute a lower motive or harbour a
more dishonouring suspicion. And yet here we are once more face to face with the same covert scheme to estab- lish and to endow the drink trade, and that for the first

time with the money of the people of England, in viola- tion of the facts of history, the decisions of the law, and the welfare of the people at large. We complain_ of this all the more intensely, because the condition and the future of the drink trade ought to be discussed and decided on its own merits only, and as a question of prime and vital importance to the United Kingdom. Instead of this we have now for the second time a covert and indirect introduction of the whole question, treated not as a matter of history, and law, and policy, but as a scheme of -linance. It is upon this ground, and, not on the plea that moneys raised upon granting of licenses can be better applied, that we earnestly appeal to the public opinion and public conscience of the country, including the Government itself, to obtain the excision of this portion of Mr. Goschen's Budget as the same opposition two years ago cut out the licensing clauses from Mr. Ritchie's bill. • His Eminence once again restates the reasons and laws which govern the drink trade : " 1. Encouraged by brewers, distillers, and publicans, and by all interested in it, both in private life and bir Chancellors of the Exchequer for the sake of revenue, nevertheless the drink trade has at all times of our his- tory been subjected to rigorous limitations to repress its -evil effects by the Acts df the Legislature. The' drink trade has never had need of legislative promotion, but has always needed legislative repression. It stands alone in the history of free trade. ' 2. A „license to sell intoxicating dribit is a legal lirnitac. tion and precaution taken against the trade. So &nig it frojn eersonal property negotiable, or giving claim to continuance or renewal, it is a dimple permission to .sell Intoxicating drink under two stringent limitations, the one in point of time, that is, for one year only, ./ and the other in point of conduct, that is, on the part ' of the holder of the license and on the conduct of the business.

3. A license, therefore, is a permission to the holder and a prohibition under penalty to all other men to sell intoxicating drink. The whole licensing system is in- tended to restrict and 'minimise the extent of the trade. It was to put away tippling-houses and to limit the num- ber of places, where intoxicating drink was sold, that the first license was granted in the time of Edward VI. They were grantql.only to personscommended by local autho- rity as fit to lhold the responsible duty of checking the ,hea of intemperance.

By what torture of reasoning (he asks) can it be con- tended that an annual license is a personal iroper a negotiable value, attaching either to the,infide the house? So much for the history of It lir itself. Again and again for many' yeArtOniblican'a, and licensed victuallers have attempted, to set ‘. claim of a vested interest. Both Parliament and a judges have made short work of this vested interest. 1. The Act 35 and 36 Victoria, Chapter 27, section 6, defines the tenure of a license. "It shall be in force for one year from the date of its being granted." The Act 9 George IV., chapter 1, section 13, says for one year. "and no longer.' 2. Justice Stephen, in the Court of QUeen's Bench, November, 1882, said : " By the renewal of a license we mean a new license granted to a man wha had otie before." 3. Mr. Patterson, in his book on the Licensing Acts, says of the Act of 1873. " There is nothing in this or other Acts to make it compulsory OR the justices to renew the license any more than in or- dinary cases." 4. In— the' " Justice of the Peace," in 1883, it was laid down f "The discretion of the licensing justices to grant or refuse or transfer a victualler's license is absolute, and they are not obliged to state any reason for their refusal." 5. Lord Chief , Justice Cock- burn in the Court of Queen's Bench, May 18th, 1878, 'said "According to the Act of 1828 the justices have the same discretion to refuse a renewal as they had Ito refuse granting a new license. 6. Viscount Cross, when Home Secretary, declared that magistrates had just the same power to refuse renewals as they had, to refuse new licenses. 7. Sir William Harcourt,' when Home Secretary in 1883, said the law is that every license is annual, and may be refused ; the magistrates have power to prohibit any sale. 8. Mr. Justice (now Lord) Field, in the Court of Queen's Bench, November, 1882, said" In every case, in every year, there is a new license granted. You may call it renewal if you like, hut that does not make it an old one. The Legislature does not call it a renewal. The Legislature is not capable of calling a new thing an old one. The Legislature recognises no vested'right at all in any holder of alicense. It does not treat the interest as a vested one in any way." 9. Baron Pollock, also in the Court of Queen's Bench, January 31,1884, said "The notion that there is a pro- perty of the landlord in a license cannot be considered as sound law." 10. Mr. Justine (now Lord) Field and Mr. destine Wills, April 30, 1888, united in the same judg- ment. Justice Wills said, in 1874, that a new license is defined as a license granted at a general annual licensing meeting in respect of premises in respect of which a similar license has not been granted before, which was a littfe modified f rem the definition of the Act of 1872, but 'only to correct a mistake from the use of the words " licensed premises," inasmuch as premises were never licensed, the license being in all cases a persgnal one. 11. What wonder, then, that the late Mr. Nash, barrister-at- law, and counsel to the Licensed Victuallers' Association, said : " Now, I am sorry to say, having looked into the question most exhaustively, and having compared notes with my brethren well versed in these matters, that there cannot be the smallest doubt that in the strict sense no such thing as a vested interest exists. . . . The mere mention of the term vested _interest should be avoided, as it infuriates every Quilt from the Queen's Bench downwards." Nevertheless, Mr. Geschen assumes that publicans have a vested interest to be compensated, overturning without a word the decisions of judges and the definitions of the Legislature.. In defiance of all these Acts and authorities, Mr. Goschen's Budget would create for the first time a vested 'interest in the holding of a license, and the effect of creating this vested interest would render it impossible to deal with publigans without compensation. Never- theless, our history shows that from 'he time Of Edward 111. to this day Parliament has dealt with the drink trade, , reducing and prohibiting its sale in England, Scotland, , and Ireland,often by extensive and peremptory measures, without a particle of compensation. But now it may be said that surely to put a man out of a lawful trade, on which he has lawfiffly entered, without compensation is obviously unjust, and to which I answer (says the compensation, I. ;if he has entered upon it with,a full know- ledge that his tenure of it is for a year only. 2. No ; if upon the tenure of a year he has,inade imprudent outlay. 'There is no compensation for imprudence. Imprudence must bear its own neriaity. 3. No; if he has more than compensated himself already during his year's tenure out of the large profits, which were obviously the reason and the motive for seeking the license. The profits of a public-bouse are notoriously so large that a year's trade is a disproportioned remuneration • both on money spent and on toil involved. In this sense license is of the nature of a monopoly, and gives to a publican an exclusive right in the midst of his neigh- bours to make for a year a peat profit in the sale of in- toxicating drink. He has no right to compensation be- cause he cannot obtain the profit and the monopoly of another. year. ' MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S VIEWS.

div.head: IHE MIDLAND BAPTISTS.
div.p: IHE MIDLAND BAPTISTS.

A conference of pastors and delegates of Midland Baptist Churches at VVorierhampton, on Wednesday, passed a resolution expressing strong disapproval of the compensation clauses of the Local Taxation Bill. ' THE GOVERNMENT'S INTENTIONS.

Lord Newark, M.P., who recently forwarded a memorial to Mr. Smith from the brewers and inaltsters of Nowark in favour of the Government licensing proposals, has received the following acknowledgment from the right hon. gentleman , 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, June 9. Dear Lord Newark,—Pray assure your constituents that the Government are fully sensible of the importance in the public interest of passing the Local Taxation Bill this session. They intend to use every effort and all the powers they possess tai do so.—Believe me, yours very faithfully, W. H. SMITH. MR. CAINE SUPPORTED BY HIS CONSTITUENTS. A crowded public meeting on the " compensation " clauses of the Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Bill was held at, Barrow, on Wednesday night, presided over by Mr. Caine, member for the borough. The proceedings throughout were orderly. A resolution supporting Mr. Caine's action against the clauses was enthusiastically and almost unanimously adopted. Mr. Caine strongly urged that the Government werepressing this bill to their own absolute ruin, and said they richly deserved it. He maintained that the Government could not defy the Christian and moral sentiment of the country. A COUNTY COUNCIL CONDEMNS THE PROPOSALS, The Anglesey County Council, on Thursday, discussed the Government Licensing Bill, and adopted a resolu- tion condemning the proposal to compensate publicans.

div.head: -TON- DRAINS.
div.p: -TON- DRAINS.

Sir,—The stench we have complained of for years past from the street drains is now past bearing. Our child- ren are constant sufferers from sewer-gas sore throat, and have to be sent away at intervals to recover. We have had diptheria in the street, and I find the Medical Officer of health has repeatedly called the attention of the authorities to the dangerous and disgraceful state of the drains. It would appear,however, that our Medical Officer of Health is a dummy, paid for giving advice which is not followed, and simply a useless and expen- sive ornament without any power. The wisdom of Town Councillors is a standing subject for " Punch," but when they neglect things as they are doing at present, to the injury of the community, it is quite time they made way for others more capable and with a better knowledge of their duties. I myself have been like others unable to move anyone in the matter, and unless something is done we shall have to leave our house and the town, and go to where the drains are kept in decent condition and where the Medical Officer of Health, if there is one, has some power to prevent the wilful spreading of diseases caused by sewer gas.—Yours truly, THOMAS FLETCHER. [We shall be glad if other inhabitants will speak out as plainly as Mr. Fletcher. They must "keep pegging away" if they would get anything done.—En. Ex.]

div.head: PUBLICANS' COMPENSATION BILL.
div.p: THE PUBLICANS' COMPENSATION BILL.

is a truism to say, that if there is one com- munity more than another in this country that would reap enormous benefits—socially and financially—from a large reduction of licenses, it is Warrington. Flanked by two gigantic breweries, with three smaller ones in our midst, and an army of retailers sufficient to supply the wants of a town six times its size, there need be no wondering at the results. This very competition itself, being confined to a limited demand, is sufficient to ac- count for one half the attendant evils of the drink traffic. It drives a large minority of publicans to a vicious abuse of their privileges ; in order to obtain a living out of their licenses they are forced to encourage drunkenness, gambling, betting, drinking in prohibited hours ;in fact, if they can only succeed in hoodwinking the police, they will resort to almost anything in order to push the sale of drink. There are scores of men in the town who can testify to the truth of this ;men who have embarked their hard earned savings and lost all, because they were too honest to resort to such illegal practices. It is such licenses as these that ought not to be renewed nor trans- ferred. They may be easily distinguished by their frequency of transfer, and this reason alone should be sufficient to enable magistrates to exercise their discre- tionary powers of refusal. It is possible, just, and legal to do this, if only the authorities would hav3 backbone enough to cast off the trade influence which overshadows them. Yes; trade influence ; that is the lever, and to break it is the key to the whole problem. To talk of custom, equity, and vested interests, may serve to cover the thraldom of the mighty Bung, but it is the duty of this generation to prevent the ignorant and short-sighted policy of the past from reaching its final triumph in the House of Commons. Now or never is the time for both parties. The matter has become urgent and vital to the common weal of our country. Brewers, publicans, and everybody connected with the trade, know perfectly well that if they lose this chance of forcing a crutch Government to give them compensation, it will be good- bye to their hopes from a sound one. Hence it is they are so idUant over the persistent effortS a their friQud* to oblige them, Let us hope that public opinion will once more be too strong far them, as it was two years ago; if not, then we all be committed to as gigantic a piece of folly as ever disgraced the Statute Book, which will create another National Debt, while we shall have the gloriaus satisfac- tion of knowing that it will be squandered among the already over-gorged brewers—Yours truly, DONO VAN. 11th June.

div.head: RACK-RENTED TRADERS AND TOILERS.
div.p: RACK-RENTED TRADERS AND TOILERS.

Sir,—By the unbounded generosity of the Press, the growth of our two important National Unions (the "Tenant Tradesmen's Union " and the "Working Man's Home Union ") has been far in excess of my most san- guine expectations. Tradesmen have overcome their wonted apathy, and aroused themselves to the tact that by combination alone can the future aggression of modern landlordism be restrained, and the rapacity of the past be adequately diminished. Working-men did not lack courage from the onset. They needed only someone to lead, and around him have they rallied heartily and eagerly. The objects of both Unions are closely allied. Traders and toilers have one common enemy—the rapacious landlord and his agent—who cripple the enterprise of the one, and limit the purchas- ing rower of the hardly earned wages of the other. The objects aimed at by both Unions may be classfied as : (I). Those which can be attained only by the slow pro- cess of legislative enactment. (2). Those which can be more speedily attained by loyal and complete union among the landlord's victims themselves. Traders and shopkeepers justly claim the full benefit of the goodwill of the business which they alone have created, and of the permanent improvements which they have paid for, as well as undisturbed tenancy so long as agreed coven- ants are duly performed. Working-men demand that the rent of their homes shall not be raised to a higher rate of interest on the value of the property than is charged to the middle classes of the community, and that good repair and sanitation shall be guaranteed. Both traders and toilers have common cause in the more just distribution of rating, and its continuous attachment to all classes of property, to ground rents and to building land kept back to " grow in value." They each recognise that trade and labour should be fully represented in Parliament, and in all local bodies. Landlord Parliaments are opposed to trade and labour interests, and vestries composed of house farmers hold out no hope to the over-rented and over-crowded working-classes. Every club and association (political or social), every Trade Union and Friendly Society in London and throughout England should immediately form local branches of each of these Unions. As there is not any fee whatever for membership, so there is no just reason for any tradesman or working-man standing aloof from these important " self help "movements. I will gladly forward post free any number of membership forms that may be required. Applications should be addressed to me at the International College, Finchley-rd., London. —Your obedient servant, JAMES HAYSMAN (President of the Unions.) 10th June 1890.

div.head: GOVERNMENTS POLICY.
div.p: THE GOVERNMENTS POLICY.

Sir,—The Government are rushing on to their latter end with an utter disregard to the national voice and the national will. They seem infatuated with a determin- ation to encumber the statute book with some of the worst measures that could enter the minds of men to conceive. Their Irish policy is a national disgrace, a disgrace to any country having the least pretentions to liberty. They use Ireland as a manufactory for crime, having Mr. Balfour as manager, the removables as fore- men ; with the police and emergency men as the work- men, their tools the baton, the carbine, the revolver, and for heavy work the battering-ram. Mr. Balfour talks o; " boycotting " with a mighty shew of indignation and pious horror, hut it is not so despicably mean as "shadowing." The man who leaves his fellow man severely alone is not so mean and contemptible as the one who dogs his footsteps, listens to his words, and thrusts and intrudes himself on his privacy in the zealous endeavour to manufacture a criminal that he may gratify his bloodthirsty spirit by thrusting him into prison where he can slowly torture him to death. This is Irish policy and "firm Government." The Government's Irish policy, their endeavour to .gild the drink traffic in order to acquire a little elec- tioneering strength by making fast friends of the drink makers and sellers, their Irish Land Bill, by which they try to endow the Irish landowner at the expense of the English taxpayer, their tithes bill by which they will if they can perpetually and forcibly endow the parson at

the expense of the parish, these three—the parson, the I publican and the Irish landlord—are their fast friends, and before leaving office they will if possible endow them all, and it is all done they say in the interests of justice religion and temperance. What a farce ; if it were not so wicked it would be ridiculous. These measures, so odious to the great majority of the nation, they push on with a recklessness that is astonishing. They may succeed with their mechanical majority in disgracing the statute book but it cannot be for long. Surely common sense must prevail to prevent such men as Lord Harlington and his followers from blindly following Goschen, Balfour and Co. into the same lobby to vote for the endowment of shaky publicans and drink mongers at the avowed expense of their victims for, say they, we take this endowment from the drink and give to the drink back again in buying up nonpaying drink property. Can absurdity further go? Unsophisticated people would suppose that when a thin.,, is no longer of use it should be put quietly on one side. If hurtful destroy it, if a nuisance suppress it, but don't talk of buying it and giving a fancy price for it. Common sense says away with it, and the world will be that much the better when it is gone. If working men studied their own interests there would be lots of this property for sale but no buyers; there would be race courses to let and grand-stands deserted. The best tip a workingman can get is to tip his money into his own pocket and not to let the drink- seller tip it into his till. He must know that he has no more money than he wants, none for drink or the )urchase of rotten licenses.—l am, sir, yours respect- 'ully, Sankey Bridges, June 10th, 1890.
CYMRO.

div.head: SUSPICIOUS AFFAIR AT
div.p: SUSPICIOUS AFFAIR AT
WARRINGTON.

A PUDDLER CHARGED WITH CAUSING THE DEATH OF HIS PARAMOUR. On Wednesday a woman named Emily Bailey, 37 years of age, who lodged in Dial-st., died under cir- cumstances of such suspicion that an investigation was made by the police, with the result that a man with whom she had been cohabiting was detained on suspicion of having caused her death. This man, Peter Morris, an underhand puddler, was on Thurs- day morning brought before Majors Pickmere and Litton, at the Borough Police Court, and formally charged, on suspicion, with having caused the death of Emily Bailey, or Morris, some time during Satur- day night or Sunday morning, when at a lodging- house in Dial-st., kept by a Mrs. Kimblin. From a statement by the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt), it appears that Morris is employed at Dallam Forge. Ile is a native of Park Gate, near Rotherham, and for several years past has been in the habit of com- ing to Warrington, working at one or other of the forges in the town. He has been in Warrington for about nine months past, and has lodged at different places. He was accompanied by the deceased, Emily Bailey, who was generally supposed to be his wife. Prisoner said, Mr. Hunt remarked, that he , had lived with her for eight years, but had never been married to her. The deceased., with whom the prisoner had lodged eight years, was the daughter of Jas. , Bailey, of Netherfield-lane, Park Gate, near Rotherham. ' The deceased and the prisoner lodged for some time at McKennell's in Winwick-rd., but on Saturday, May 24, they left. On that day prisoner assaulted the woman. He struck her and gave her a black eye. The same night they went to lodge at Kimblin's in Dial-st., and they had remained there ever since. Nothing remark- able occurred until Saturday last, when it appeared that , shortly after six o'clock the prisoner and the deceased returned to their lodgings. The latter carried some eat- ables, and appeared to have been marketing. She was perfectly sober; but the prisoner was slightly under the influence of liquor, and it was noticed that he was not in a very good temper. Kate Kimblin, a girl 17 years of age, daughter of the landlord, heard some angry words used by the prisoner and .the deceased while they were in the back kitchen. She also saw the prisoner deliber- ately kick the deceased in her side. Ile was wearing a clog at that time. Shortly afterwards the prisoner went upstairs apparettly to bed, but at eight o'clock he and the deceased were seen sitting in front of the fire. The accused got up suddenly, seized the woman by her ears, and lifted her from the chair on which she was sitting. He shook her and held her by the oars, and the deceased exclaimed" Oh, Peter, don't." Of these circumstances (he the Chief Constable) had two witnesses to speak. At about ten o'clock the accused went to bed, followed at eleven o'clock by the deceased. Nothing more was heard of them till about a quarter-past twelve, when Mary Kimblin heard a noise in the bedroom of the deceased. She noticed that there was a light in the room. Listening at the door, she heard some one snoring heavily. She pushed the door open, and found the deceased lying on her back on the bedroom floor. She was fully dressed. The prisoner was then in bed, but awake, and Mary Kimblin said to him, "Come and help me to lift her up. The prisoner replied. "No ; she is drunk. I gave her a drink of water a while ago." He refused to assist to lift her into bed. The witness was prepared to say that the Woman Was perfectly sober when she went to bed. Mary Kimblin got the assistance of two lodgers from another room. and the deceased was lifted on to the bed. She did not appear to regain Consciousness, and remained ill der'' int: the eight and the next morning. About noon on Sunday the accused went to Mr. T. J. Garnett, relieving officer, and obtained an order for Dr. Peacocke to attend the deceased. The doctor, however, was from home,and Dr. Geary tcok charge of the case, and attended the woman from tjiree o'clock on Sunday afternoon till her death. Dr. Peacocke also saw her. She never appeared to regain consciousness, and died on Wednesday morning lat half-past six. Information was subsequently given to the police. Strange to say, although it was known that the woman was dying on Tuesday night, the prisoner went to bed as usual, and next morning went to work as unconcerned as possible. He said nothing about the matter in any shape or form. The doctors refused to give a certificate as to the cause of death, and Mr. Hunt directed Inspector Spinks and Sergeant Rowbottom to make inquiries and to bring the prisoner to the Police Station, so that he might hear the statements of the witnesses to be called to give evidence on a future occasion. The body of the woman was examined, and a raw wound, apparently caused by a kick, was found on her side. There were slight bruises on other parts of the body. He (Mr. Iluat), had written to the Coroner, and reported the facts of the case, and had also conferred with the magistrate's legal adviser (Mr. White.) Under all circumstances he thought it his duty to detain the prisoner. It was then decided to take formal evidence sufficient to justify a remand. Kate Kimblin said: The prisoner ' lodged at our house, and the deceased lived with him. We thought she was his wife. On Saturday night, between six and half-past, I was in the back kitchen with Morris and the deceased came in, and the two had a few words about some meat. He wanted the deceased: to buy some meat for Sunday., but she said "Let us get our dinner before we do so." He replied "No, get it now," and as the deceased was going away he kicked her on her side.—Major Pickmere : When he gave her a kick did she fall P—Witness : No. He kicked her between the back and the side.—The Chief Constable : And she went away as soon as she could 7—Witness : Yes, into the middle kitchen. Mary Kimblin said: On Saturday night, about a quarter-past eleven, I had occasion to pass prisoner's door. I saw a light. I listened, and heard someone snoring heavily. I opened the door and went into the room, and found the deceased lying on her back on the floor. I asked prisoner what was the matter, and he replied "She is drunk." I said "No, she is bad; help me to lift her." lie refused to do so, and I aroused two men, who lifted her from the floor and put her on the bed. The prisoner refused to give any assistance. The two men were about a quarter of an hour trying to restore her to consciousness. The prisoner was sober, and spoke quite sensibly. The woman died at our house , about half-past six on Wednesday morning.—The Chief 1 Constable: Did anyone complain to you about his abuse! —Witness: Yes, she told me on Saturday morning that he was a brute to her, and that no one but God above knew what she had Ciad to put up with from him.— The Prisoner: Had she complained during the week that she was ill ?—Witness : No.—Prisoner: You say that when you came into the room you found the woman lying on the floor. Where was I 2—Witness: In bed.— Prisoner: Did you not meet me at the bottom of the stairs with a quart jug of water in my hand P—Witness : No you were in bed.—ln answer to :the Chief Constable, witness said she had examined the body of the deceased, and found bruises on it as well as a raw wound. Mary Leicester said she saw the prisoner lift the de- ceased off her chair while she was in the kitchen. He lifted her up by her ears, and she said "Oh, Peter, don't."—The Chief Constable: What had passed between them ?—Witness: Nothing, except that they nad a few words.—The Chief Constable: Did he get up suddenly and assault her P—Witness : Yes.—Major Pickmere : What did he do when he got hold of her ?—Witness : He raised her from the chair by her ears.—The Chief Con- stable: Did he shake her ?—Witness : Yes. Major Litton asked if a post-mortem examination had been made of the body of the deceased? The Chief Constable replied that it would be made in time for the inquest. The Clerk asked the prisoner if he had anything to say why he should not be remanded. The Prisoner : I say lam not guilty of the charge that has been made against me. It is a false one. Prisoner was then remanded till Monday next, pend- ing the post-mortem examination and the holding of the inquest.

THE INQUEST. An inquiry into the circumstances of the death of Emily Bailey was held yesterday afternoon at the Bride- well Parade-room, before Mr. Samuel Brighouse, the Coroner for South-West Lancashire. The Coroner having briefly referred to the facts of the case, evidence was called.

Bridget Kimblin,—wi-dOw, 17 Dial-st., keeper of a lodging-house, said that the deceased and the prisoner Morris had lodged at her house as man and wife for about three weeks. When she came to the house at first she had a black eye. Witness did not see much of the

couple. On Saturday evening deceased was sober, and was apparently in good health. On Sunday morning witness again saw deceased, at about ten o'clock in bed. She was unconscious. Witness remonstrated with him because he had given no regard to his wife lying uncon- scious, and he said, "I got up and stretched her arms r and legs, and then went to bed." Witness said " With- out giving any alarm to anyone?" and he replied "Yes." Some time afterwards he said he was frightened he had hurt her neck, and witness told ihim to go for a doctor, which he did. Deceased died on the morning of Wed- nesday. Morris did not seem much affected by the ill- ness of his supposed wife. Witness did not see Morris strike the deceased. Witness understood Morris to ex- plain that she fell on the floor in a fit. Deceased appeared to be a sober woman, and a quiet one. She was sober at six o'clock on Saturday evening—fly prisoner Morris 1 At first she believed the deceased had died in a fit, until she heard afterwards of his treatment of her. Deceased, when at first she ,came to the house, said that she had

had a stroke about nine years ago. Catherine Kimblin, daughter of the last witness, gave evidence similar to her statement made before the magis- trates on the previous day, to the effect that on Saturday she saw prisoner kick deceased in the side. He gave the kick with his full force, and deceased ran out of the room. Witness did not see her again until Sunday morn- ing, when she went upstairs in consequence of what her sister had said. It was then about eleven o'clock, and , deceased was unconscious. Prisoner was downstairs, and never menticned to witness that the woman was ill. , Deceased was a saber woman but she seemed a little childish. Mary Ann Lester, a lodger at Kimblin's, also repeated evidence given before the magistrates on Thursday. At about seven o'clock on Saturday evening, she deposed, she was in the kitchen, when she saw prisoner take the deceased by the ears, and lift her off the chair. Pri- soner appeared to be sober. On Sunday morning, at about nine o'clock, prisoner came downstairs and said to witness " Pollie, I wish ybu'd go upstairs and look at my missus, I have had a very bad night with her." Wit- ness went upstairs and found the deceased in bed uncon- scious. Catherine Wade, another lodger at Kitnblin's, deposed that deceased was a quiet and sober woman. On Satur- day evening witness saw prisoner'and deceased together. He kept looking at her, and looking at her, and then sprang up, took her by the ears, lifted her up, and shook her. He never spoke when doing so, but she said—" oh, Peter, don't." Witness had never seen deceased have a fit but she heard that she had had a stroke. Mary Kimblin said that at about midnight on Saturday she heard a noise in the bedroom occupied by prisoner and the deceased. In the saine room a second couple were sleeping. Witness went to the room and saw the deceased lying on the floor. Witness awakened the the woman in the other bed, and asked "How long has she been like this," and the woman replied that she was that way when she came up. Witness asked Morris to give assistance, but he said "No she's drunk. She'll soon come round." Witness fetched two men from another room, who tried to restore consciousness. Prisoner was again appealed to to help, but he refused, The two men and witness lifted deceased up, and bad ' to lift her over Morris to put her into the bed, as he I refused to move out of the way. Deceased did not regain consciousness. The noise witness heard was that of snoring, and not that of a fall. Dr. Peacocke deposed that he saw the deceased alive , on Saturday night. She was then in a comatose condi- tion. There was a slight mark behind the right ear. He was told that she had gone into that state quite natu- rally. On Thursday he and Dr. Bowden made a post- mortem examination. He found a bruise behind the right ear, and an extensive bruise on the left buttock. It was as large as the palm of his hand. Opening the skull they found a large clot of blood. The brain itself appeared healthy, and the organs of the body were also healthy. The cause of death was compression of the brain, caused by this clot of blood. The bruise on the buttock had nothing to do with the, cause of death. The clot of blood was found on the same side as the wound behind the ear, but a man could scarcely have caused that by taking hold of the ear. It would want violence of some sort. It would require a blow, or a fall on a knob.—By the Chief Constable: Witness had had pointed out to him the spot where the deceased was found on the bedroom floor, but he could see nothing which could have caused that clot of blood to accumulate. Police Sergeant Rowbotham deposed to arresting the prisoner on suspicion of having caused the death of the deceased. Prisoner, replying to the charge, said " I know nothing about it," He seemed surprised at hear- ing that the woman was dead. Prisoner then made a lengthy statement as to the movements of himself and the deceased on the Saturday. When in the house he just got hold of her ears in a lark, and without any intention of hurting her. The idea, he said, of lifting a woman twelve stone weight by the ears. He thought that it was beyond all reason. When they were upstairs deceased was going round the foot of the bed when she dropped on the floor. He had seen her in fits before. He laid her on her back, and then fetched some water, with which he sprinkled her forehead. He then told the jury how, during the night, he did,what he could for her. The Corouar said that the evidence showed that death was due to compression of the brain, caused by a clot vf blood, and in the doctor's opinion that clot had been caused by violence of some sort or another, received either accidentally or at the hands of some other person, either accidentally tit criminally. The question was whether the jury thought there was sufficient evidence to juntify them in saying that the prisoner had caused the death. On the Saturday he kicked her on the but- tock, but the doctor said that had nothing to do with the death. Later on, the evidence said, he shook hor by the ears. It was very easy to exaggerate the actions of a man, especially if you had some feeling against him, and he had no doubt that the witnesses, although speaking the truth, felt that the man behaved to the woman in a very callous way. To his mind the violence, if any, had been received when she went upstairs, and there was no evidence to show that Morris actually did it. After considering in private the jury came to the con- clusion that there was no evidence to connect prisoner with the death, and returned an open verdict. At the same time they were of opinion that there had been an amount of brutality used to hedeceased that was revolt- ing to the feelings of them all. The Coroner, addressing Morris, said that as far as the Court was concerned the jury had returned an open verdict. It was quite right on the part of the police to bring him before the Court, because of the callous in- difference that he had shown to the deceased. He had only himself to blame for the position he had got him- self into. Innocent or guilty lie had brought that upon himself by his callous indifference to the woman's suffer- ings.

THE SHIP CAN AL TRAGEDY.
VAUGHAN COMMITTED FOR MANSLAUGHTER.

At a special sessions held at the Warrington Bridewell yesterday, before Captain T. E. With ing- ton (in the chair), and Mr. J. Tinsley, Edward Wm. Vaughan, 22 years of age, a labourer, on the Ship Canal, was charged on remand with having, on the 27th April last, at Rizton, wilfully murdered Thomas Elliman by shooting him with a pistol. Superintendent Weir conducted the prosecution and Mr. A. Browne appeared for the prisoner. On the suggestion of Mr. Browne the witnesses were asked to leave the court until they were called to give evidence.

THE DISCOVERY Of THE BODY. The first witness was Thomas William Traverse, sur- veyor, 'Leigh, who produced a plan of the Ship Canal cuttiug at Rixton.--Joieph Arstall, a boot and shoe maker at Rixton, deposed that the deceased man was about 88 years of age, and was an engine driveror tenter, and worked at what was known as the "Rocker" pump. On the morning of Sunday, 27th April, deceased, who lodged at his house, left to go to his work, and witness arranged to take his dinner. He did so, and arrived at the "Rocker" pump about ten minutes to two in the afternoon, but could not see the deceased. He looked into the canal cutting and saw deceased lying on his back at the bottom. He went towards him and found that he was dead. Witness saw a young man standing on the opposite embankment, and in response to his calls the young man went to the canal yard, and brought Mr. Westall. Information was afterwards given to the police. On the night previous the deceased had shown to him a new revolver and a box of cartridges which he said he had bought. The revolver and cartridges produced were the same. Witness did not notice any marks of a struggle and there were no out- ward appearances to show how deceased :came by his death. On the body being removed to his house and stripped witness saw a small hole in his breast. In reply to Mr. Browne witness said the deceased was a much taller man than the prisoner.—Frank Harris, described as a " slasher " over the engines, and living at the huts, Rixton, said on the Sunday forenoon in question he saw the deceased in the sheds at the canal works and he saw the prisoner near the pumping engine. He did not see either of them again until ihe discovery of the body of the deceased. Witness saw the prisoner there about 5 minutes after the lsody was found and witness heard Mr. Westall ask the prisoner if he had had any drink that day and the prisoner made no reply. A man came up and said he had heard a shot fired and it seemed to be a heavy shock to the prisoner, who during the day seemed to be frightened and worried. The prisoner assisted witness in carrying a door to the place where the body was lying. Witness left the spot to bring a trolley and when he returned the prisoner had gone. By Mr. Brown: Witness knew both the prisoner and the deceased and they were both very quiet men. They seemed to be on good terms with everyoneand he did not know that they had ever quarrelled. ---------

THE WOUND NOT SELF-INFLICTED. Dr. Jago, of Cadishead, deposed that he had made a post-mortem examination of the body and was assisted by Dr. Caudwell. lie described the nature of a liullet wound which he found on the right breast, and said he saw no marks of powder. The direction of the wound was from above downwards, and the bullet produced was found by witness on the left side ef the deceased's chest, and in his opinion the bullet caused the death. He found bullet holes in the deceased's clothing corresponding to the wound. He should say that the weapon from which the bullet was discharged would be held in front of the deceased and to his right, and the pistol must have been held above the wound in order to give it a downward direction. The weapon must have been held at least 18 inches from the body, and in his opinion the wound was not self-inflicted.—ln answer to Mr. Browne witness said that at the inquest on - the first occasion he gave it as his opinion that the shot was fired at a distance not exceeding three or four feet. —Dr. Caudwell, of Cadishead, gave similar testimony and said he agreed with the evidence of Dr. Jago as to the cause of death. He did not think the wound was self- inflicted.

THE PRISONER AND HIS REVOLVER. Henry Westall, "walking ganger "on the Rixton sec- tion of the Ship Canal, gave evidence that the prisoner came to his house on the Sunday afternoon, and reported that the man at the " Rocker" pump was dead in the cutting. He went there, and found Ellaman lying dead. He asked the prisoner "Have you 'blokes' been having any • booze' here, to-day 2" and the prisoner made no re- ply. He then sent for the police, and gave orders for the body to be removed. He asked the prisoner what he had been doing as he had not seen "Tom" that morning, and the prisoner said, "I saw him after he had washed out the boilers. I have been pumping two hours and could not make any impression on the water, and I walked up the incline to see what was the matter when that young man called out to me to say that he was dead.' The prisonq ought to have returned to his work at the pump, but on going to look for him, he found that he had gone, and he did not again see him until tht inquest at Hollins Green, on the 2nd inst. The prisener seemed in an excited state.— ' Cliarhei Bryant, an engine driver, gave evidence that on the Sunday morning deceased showed him the revolver and cartridges produced and said he had bought them on the previous night. On the Monday witness found the revolver and cartridges in a musical box in the deceased's engine house.—ln reply to Mr. Browne witness said that when the deceased was show- ing him the revolver he did not appear to know how to handle it—James Barlow, a boatman, living at Rixton, stated that about noon on the Sunday he along with two other men named Ditchfield and Clarke were walking in the neighbourhood of the canal cutting and sae; men standing in the bottom of the cutting. Shortly after they had passed they heard a shot fired, but they were then unable to see the two men. He did not then know either of the two men in the cutting —William Clarke, farmer, and James Ditchfield, fustian-cutter, gave corro- borative evidence.—George Chesworth, a pumpdriver, stated that on the Sunday morning in question the prisoner showed him a revolver which he took from his coat pocket. The prisoner replaced his revolver in his pocket without making any remark or saying anything. The prisoner's revolver was a smaller one than that produced. In reply to Mr. Browne witness denied that he had taken the prisoner to his (witness's) house on the Sunday morning, or that he and the prisoner had been shooting starlings or rats that morning.—Edward Latham, (16), a labourer, said that on the Sunday morning in question he saw the prisoner with a revolver in his hand near the Boathouse Inn at Rollina Green. Prisoner had the pistol in his liand and said he would bet a sovereign he could knock a flower out of his hat, which he then had in. Witness asked" Do you think lam a dummy" (laughter), and the prisoner replied" I won't hurt you.' Prisoner was not then sober. TRH PRISONER LEAVES ram DISTRICT. George Knight (15), a waggon greaser, gave similar evidence and added that in the afternoon when the body of Elliman was being carried away he saw Vaughan going away over the fields. He heard Vaughan ask a woman how far it was to Manchester and on being told it was about 12 miles away, the prisoner walked quickly in that direction.—Fanny Hudson, wife of George Hudson, a labourer, Rixton, said on the Sunday after noon in question she saw the prisoner coming from under a hedge near her home. Ile got into the highway and asked if that was the road to Maechester. She said it was, and he then went along in the direction of Man- chester.

THE POLICE INVESTIGATIONS. Police Constable Schofield, of Rixton, gave evidence as to receiving information of the discovery of the body and visiting the canal cutting. He searched for Vaughan in the vicinity but was not successful in finding him.— P.C. Fleming, of Poulton, deposed to acting according to instructions cia the 29th ult., when he visited the canal huts at Latchford, and received the tin clothes-box pro- duced. Among other articles it contained were some ball cartridges, some letters, clothes and 211 in gold. The prisoner had claimed the box as his property.— Sergeant Barnes, stationed at Padgate, gave formal evidence as to searching the district for Vaughan. He also received the bullet produced from Dr. Jago. and it was similar to the bullets found in the cartridges of the prisoner's box.—Thomas Dainteth, gunsmith, Warring- ton, stated that the bullet found in deceased's body could not possibly be fired from the revolver (deceased's) pro- duced. The bullet corresponded with those found in the prisoner's box. In reply to ,Mr. Browne, witness said he thought from the appearence of the descased's coat that the revolver had been fired about six or eight inches away as there were marks of the powder near the bullet hole.

THE PRISONNR'S ACCOUNT. Superintendent Weir deposed that in consequence of the search for the prisoner, who was then known as " Fred Rent," being unsuccessful, he had him gazetted and photographs circulated throughout the United Kingdom. On the 23rd May he received the prisoner into custody from the Ross (Herefordshire) police' and was informed by them that the prisoner had given him- self up. The prisoner said "I am come to give myself up for the shooting at Rixton." He (Superintendent Weir) afterwards charged the prisoner with the offence. The prisoner replied " Wilful—no; it was'not wilful, it was an accident. I did not shoot him, he shot himself. I will tell you how it was. Neither of us were doing anything. I had cleaned out ,my boilers and was wait- ing for Elliman to get the water away before I started. It was no use me pumping :any water until he had got what I had pumped away. I was standing near my boilers and saw Ellitnan standing at the top of the slope near his pumping engine. Be called out to me and said "tiring that thing up with you." I knew he meant my pistol. I took my pistol out of this coat pocket" (point- ing to one he then had on "and put it into the pocket of my blue one I then had on. I walked up the bottom of the cutting and he came down the slope and met me where his body was afterwards found. I showed him the pistol and thought the barrels were all discharged. I had been shooting rats that morning and thought I had dischargelail the barrels,but it seems there was one left. While he was examining the pistol I turned round to do something and I heard him call out "Oh, Fred, I've shot myself." I turned towards him and caught him as he was falling. I held him up as long as I could and then let

him down. Ile died with his head on my arm. I was frightened and did not know what to do. I waited about and saw his landlord come with his dinner and saw him find Elliman in the cutting where I left him. He called and I went to him. He told me to go and fetch someone and I went and brought the walking ganger. Iwas afraid and did not know what to do and I then went away." ' In reply to Mr. Browne witness said the police author- ities at Ross gave the prisoner and his relatives a very excellent character. Lie was present at the coroner's inquiry and u a result of the verdict arrived at the Coroner did not commit prisoner for trial.

_ TEM DEFENCE AND THE RESULT. Prisoner was then formally charged with the offence. and, on the advice of his solicitor, he pleaded not guilty. —Mr. Browne, speaking for the defence, said that the magistrates had now to consider whether there was a prima-facie case made out, that would warrant them in committing prisoner either for murder or manslaughter. Before they could commit on a charge 04 wilful murder, it must be shown that there was some motive. There must be malice. In this case was there a single motive shewn—a single quarrel indicated. Was not there, on the other hand, specific evidence that the prisoner was one of the most civil men on the canal; and never known to have a quarrel with anyone. It the most it was either manslaughter or a case of accident. He submitted that the occurrence was acci- dental. A Coroner's jury, after a long hearing, could not find that it was wilful murder, and could not find that Vaughan was guilty of an intention to do any harm. Seeing that the Coroner had not committed him fer trial, they would be quite justified in finding that the occurrence was accidental, and that they would net be justified in sending him for trial.--Captain Withing- ton said that they had considered the case, and had consulted with the Clerk. They were quite satisfied that there was no case of wilful murder, but it was their duty to send prisoner for trial on the charge of manslaughter.—Mr. Browne said that he had no witnesses to call at the present time, but he wished to renew an application for bail.—Superintendent Weir did not offer any objection, and the Bench intimated that if sureties were forthcoming by to-day (Saturday) they would accept bail, prisoner in £3.00, and two sureties in £5O each. The Assizes at Liverpool, to which the prisoner is com- mitted, open on the 26th of next month.

div.head: LATCHFORD BRIDGES.
div.p: THE LATCHFORD BRIDGES.

Since the public meeting which was held in the Parish Room, Latchford, on the question of abandon- ing Grappenhall-road swing bridge and Ackers-lane swing bridge, with a view to obtaining a high-level vehicular bridge, three petitions have been pre- pared on the subject. The first petition is in favour of the course which the Manchester Ship Canal Company propose to take, and the second and third are against it. The first one is addressed to the Daresbury High- way Board, in favour of the high-level bridge on the chip Canal at Latchford. It is as follows:—"We, the undersigned residents or property owners in Latchford. Grappenhall, and the vicinity, believing. it to be of the utmost importance to the district generally that there should be a permanent high- level vehicular bridge over the -hip Canal in Latch- ford,' desire to express our cordial approval of the plans submitted by the Ship Canal Company, to the Daresbury Hignway Board on May Bth." The second petition, which is addressed to the Committee of the House of Loads, has been signed by 350 of the residents of the neighbourhoods affected. It is as follows That your petitioners have observed, and disap- prove of, notice on the part of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, of an addition to, and alteration of, their above-named Bill, which is now before your right honourable House. The Manchester Ship Canal Act, of 1885, provides for three swing bridges across the proposed Ship Canal in the district in which your petitioners reside, namely, one at Knutsford Road, one at Grappenhall Road, and a third at Ackers' Lane. This was accepted as satisfactory to the inhabitants, but the Manchester Ship Canal Company urged that it would be incon- venient to work Grappenhall Road bridge and Knutsford Road bridge through their being so near each other, and it was 'proposed, as shewn by the said Bill, that the Grappenhall-road bridge should be abandoned, and that in lieu there- of, a high-level footbridge should be provided to carry people across the Ship Canal, at a point be- tween Grappenhall Road and Wash Lane, where the new railway station for Latchford is to be placed. Three meetings of residents of Latchford were held, at which this proposal for the footbridge was ac- cepted, although it was urged that a high-level vehicular bridge might be obtained in place of the footbridge, if Acker's Lane swing bridge were also abandoned. The Daresbury Highway Board took the same view, in accordance with the recommenda- tions of their Special Sub-Committee, and at a meet- ing of the Board, held on April 30th, it was unani- mously resolved "That the Board can only agree to a high-level vehicular bridge on condition that the i Acker's Lane swing bridge s retained." Bight days afterwards—that is, on the Bth May—the Daresbury Highway Board, without consulting the inhabitants, and to the surprise of the inhabitants, reversed its unanimous decision, and decided to, approve of a high-level vehicular bridge at the sacrifice of Acker's Lane bridge. ,On this sudden reversion of policy becoming knoWn, a public meeting of the residents of Grappenhall, Latchford, and vicinity, was held on May 15th, in the Parish Room, Latch- ford. It was well attended by all sections of the inhabitants, and after considerable discussion, the following resolution was adopted: "That this meet- ing of the inhabitants of Latchford, Grappenhall, and vicinity is strongly of opinion that two swing bridges, one at Grappenhall Road, and one at Acker's Lane, ought not to be abandoned in order to obtain , a high-level vehicular bridge near Latchford Sta- tion, and it can only agree to a high-level vehicular bridge on condition that Acker's Lane swing bridge is retained." Your petitioners are,very desirous that the wishes of the inhabitants in this respect, should be respected, and that your honourable House will re- fuse to consent to abandon two swing bridges in order to obtain a high-level vehicular bridge. They would point out that such a high-level vehicular bridge, situated on no main road, will be a great hardship and inconvenience to pedestrians, es- pecially those journeying between Latchford, Ackers Lane, Lumb Brook, Appleton, and Stockton Heath. The people, for instance, from these dis- tricts, who attend the Baptist Chapel, in Wash-lane, or Christ's Church, in Wash lane, will be compelled not only to go much further round, but will have to go over a bridge which will be at least 50 feet above the ordinary level. They submit that this will be a great hardship, especially in winter and at other times when the weather is inclement, and they do not see why they should be deprived of the toe of the proposed swing bridge at Acker's Lane, in accor- dance with the plans originally agreed upon and assented to by the inhabitants and the Daresbury Highway Board. They would point out, too, that a high-level- vehicular bridge, to be of real value, ought to be placed on a main road, such as the Knutsford Road or the Northwich Road. It will be seen from the new plans, that one object of the high-level bridge will be to attract traffic to the high-level goods,station which is to be constructed at Latchford. The gradients for the bridge, and to this high-level goods station, will be 1 in 25, and your petitioners submit that a road of 1 in 25 from the high-level goods station to Grappenhall- road, or from the high-level goods station to Wash- lane, terminating in each case at railway bridges under the railway embankment, will be exceedingly dangerous, in frosty weather, to vehicular traffic. But the main objection of your petitioners is to the hardship and inconvenience that will be caused to the great mass of the community by abandoning two swing bridges, on two important roads, in order to obtain this high-level vehicular bridge. They would, therefore, respectfully urge that your honourable House, whether or not assenting to the high-level vehicular bridge, should refuse to con- sent to the abandonment of Acker's Lane swing bridge across the Canal. Your petitioners object to any alterations or amendments being made in the Bill, whereby powers may be granted to the said Ship Canal Com- pany to the prejudice of your petitioners, as afore- . _

_ said. Your petitioners,therefore, humbly pray your right honourable House that the Bill may not pass into law in the manner proposed to he amended by the said Ship Canal Company, or that any alteration of the preamble clauses and provisions of•the Bill may be made prejudicial to the property, rights, and in- terests of your petitioners, and that such other re- lief may be given 10 your petitioners in the pre- mises as to your right honourable House in their , wisdom shall deem meet. And your petitioners will ever pray, &c. The third petition has been prepared on behalf of the Warrington Corporation, and objects to the present proposals of the Company on various grounds.
