YACHT REGATTA.
The chief even; at the "Southern Yacht Club Regatta yesterday afternoon was won by the Thistle, the Valkyrie being second. The Forty Tonner match was won by Creole with Deerhound second.

LY.IIII. POLICE CHANGES.—Negotiations have for some time been pending respecting changes in the Lymm police force. On Tuesday afternoon Acting-Sergeant Cook was transferred to Northwich, where he will be promoted to the rank of sergeant. P.C. Ennion, of Warburton, will fill the vacancy at Broom Edge. THE VOLUNTEERS.—The Lymm Volunteers marched to Oughtrington on Sunday morning, for Divine service at St. Peter's Church. There was a good attendance, the band playing en route. The sermon was preached by the Rector (the Rev. W. G. Knocker). Captain Jones and Dr. Williamson-were in command. The men went by way of Rush Green, and returned down Higher- lane. • SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT.—On Saturday morning a serious accident occurred to a bricksetter named Peter Moores, who resides in Henry-st., Lymm. Whilst assisting in erecting some buildings in Rush Green, the scaffolding suddenly gave way, and Moores was precipitated to the ground, his injuries being of a very series nature. The injured man was picked up and taken to Dr.Williamson's' house, where he received every attention. PETITION AGAINST THE PUBLICAN COMPENSATION CLAUSES. —The officers of Zion Chapel, Cherry-lane (In- dependent Methodist), on behalf of the members of the church, have signed a petition against the Government proposal to compensate the publicans at the expense of the ratepayers. The petition was forwarded to Mr. Brunner for presentation on Tuesday evening. It would have been sent to the member for the division, but it wasfeared he might not be in his place to present it. KICKED IN THE Fenn BY • Honsa.—A groom named Edwin Mairs, residing at Lymm, met with serious accident on Friday night. About ten o'clock he went to the Spread Eagle Hotel, Lymm, and was asked his opinion about a pony which was in a stable at the rear of the premises. Directly he went towards the animal it kicked him in the jaw with its hind feet, and rendered him unconscious. He was at once taken to Dr. William- son's surgery, where it was found that the upper jaw had been badly shattered and several of the teeth had been knocked out. CONFIRMATION.—On Monday afternoon the Bishop of Chester (Dr. Jayne), held a confirmation at St. Mary's Church. The clergy present were the Rector, the Rev. G. W. Guest, the Rev. R. Coward (curate), Rev. W. G. Knocker (rector of St. Peter's, Oughtrington), Rev. J. W. Challenor (curate of St. George's, Altrincham), Rev. G. Egerton Warburton (rector of Warburton), and the Rev. H. A. D. Surridge (vicar, of High Legh.) There was a good congregation, the candidates hailing from Lymm (28), Oughtrington (2), Warburton (14) High Legh (2), Liscard (1.) THE NEW GAB MANAGER.—Ak special meeting of the Lymm Local Board was held on Monday afternoon, at the Board-room, to appoint a manager for the Lymm Gas Works, in the place of Mr. Graham ,resigned. There was a large attendance, Mr. H. Cameron (the chairman of the Board) presiding. The five candidates selected by the Board on Thursday attended, and were indivi- dually examined as to their capabilities. Messrs. Wil- liam Severs (of Cross Gates, Leeds) and Dale (Altrin- cham), were the two final selections. Mr. Rogers pro- posed, and Mr. Swallow seconded, that Mr. Severs be appointed. Mr. Brazendale moved that Mr. Dale be accepted. Mr. Forstet seconded, but on the vote being taken Mr. Severs obtained a majority. The original resolution was then put to the meeting as a substantive motion and carried unanimously. Mr. Severs was accordingly declared elected. Loog AFTER THE CHANGE.—On Monday, at the Altrin- cham Petty/Sessions, a young man named Israel Leigh was charged with stealing 9d., the money of J. Rawles, at Lymn.—Mrs. Rowles, who lives at Top-lane, Lymm, said that on Saturday night, she went to the shop of Mrs. Rowlinson for some potatoes. She put a shilling down, and Mrs. Rowlinson put 9d. change on the count- er. She, however, omitted to take up the money.—Miss Rowlinson said that about ten minutes after Mrs. Rowles had left the prisoner came into the shop and purchased two penny packets of cigarettes. lie handed her ed., and she returned him 4d. in copper. She saw him pick up 9d. from the t punter, and she asked him if that was his money, and he said it was. - In a few min - utes Mrs. Rowles came in, and said that she had forgotten her change, when Mrs. Rowlinson at once suspected that the 9d. picked up by the prisoner was the money, and gave information to P.C. Griffiths, who arrested the prisoner the same night.—The prisoner stated that he handed Miss Rowlinson a shilling, and alleged that she put the 9d. into his hand.—This statement was, how- ever, denied, and the prisoner was ordered to pay a fine of ss. and 7s. costs.

div.head: EXTENSIVE THEFT OF BOOKS.
div.p: EXTENSIVE THEFT OF BOOKS.

At Stockton-on-Tees, yesterday, John Keine was com- mitted for trial, charged with stealing £2OO worth of books belonging to William Frankland, bookseller. He rented a room over a warehouse, and by cutting a hole through the floor, abstracted the books.

div.head: TERRIBLE FATALITY IN I WELSH QUARRY:
div.p: TERRIBLE FATALITY IN I WELSH QUARRY:

Yesterday morning, Griffith Jones, an aged settmaker, was accidentally kilted at the Welsh Granite Company's Quarry, Llanaelhaiarn. The deceased was working upon a ledge when a mass of rock, weighing four tons, des- cended from an upper gallery, falling upon Jones and crushing him to death, the remains being terribly dis- ...figured. He was 60 years of age.

SALVATION ARMY RIOT. A Berlin telegram gays :—The entry of the Salvation Army into Barmen ended in a great riot. The people stoned the Salvationists, whose leader, Captain Gibson, had to be protected by the police.

div.head: LIVERPOOL TAILORESSES' STRIKE..
div.p: THE LIVERPOOL TAILORESSES' STRIKE..

. Yesterday morning the tailoresses who are on strike in Liverpool, were still as a rule determined to accept no- thing short of their full demands for a reduction of two hours work per day. Theirexpectations of victory have been much intensified by the fact that a large number of the middlemen have shown a disposition to signin favour of the demands of the girls' associations. Some seven- teen of these employers have now granted the terms, and others are giving in.

div.head: LONDON. POLICE COMMISSIONER.
div.p: THE LONDON. POLICE COMMISSIONER.

A rumour reached municipal circles in Liverpool yesterday afternoon that Captain Nott-Bower, the head constable of Liverpool, had been appointed by the Government as successor to Mr. Munroe in the office of Chief Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police. This is believed to be exceedingly probable. When Sir Charles Warren resigned this position some twelve months ago Captain Nott-Bower was a candidate for the office. It was then said that he would have had the appointment but for the fact that the Home Secretary, Mr. Matthews, considered it right that Mr. Munro, who was the assist- ant commissioner, should be appointed to the chiefship. The Central News states that yesterday afternoon the Home Secretary appointed Mr. Howard Senior, chief ,constable of the Metropolitan police, to be Assistant Com- missioner in room of the late Colonel Pearson.

YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—FRIDAY. MISCELLANEOUS. Several provisional orders were advanced a stage. On the motion of Lord Rolston, the Working Classes Dwellings Bill was read a second time and referred to the Committee on law. The House then adjourned HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FRIDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. A NxwWnir.—On the motion of Mr. Richard Power, a new writ for North Donegal was ordered, James Edward Murphy having resigned. MR. MUNRO'S RESIGNATION.—Mr. MATHEWS read Mr. Munro's letter resigning the commissionership of police. The resignation was accepted on the , ground of differ- ences with the Home Secretary respecting the, adequacy of the police superannuation proposals. MORE BATONING IN IRELAND. Mr. DILLON asked whether it was true that a group of people, assembled last Wednesday at New Tipperary to express pleasure at Mr. Wm. O'Brien's marriage, were charged and batoned by the police, who carried away a flag. , (Loud Opposi- tion cheers.) Mr. 13m.,Foua said he had telegraphed to Dublin for particulars. Mr. Dit,LoN said he would re- peat the question on Monday. (Cheers.) BURIALS AT ASHTON-IN-MAEERFIELD.—The HOME SEC- RETARY' in reply to Mr. Caleb Wright, said he was in- formed by the vicar that there was only room for a dozen private graves in the cemetery yard of Ashton-in-Maker- field, and that, pending certain arrangements, he had given notice that no new graves should allotted to in- dividuals other than members of the congregation, or those who could claim privilege. This was not a matter in which the Home Office had any jurisdiction, and if any person felt aggrieved he had his legal remedy. THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.—The debate OR the Local Taxation Bill was resumed. Mr. CAINE con- demned the Bill as one for the extinction of public-houses that were already breaking the law. It was a measure to buy out blackguards at the expense of respectable traders. and he could not consent to buying out those who were an evil to the community, a danger to society, and who ought long since to have been got rid of by the magistrates themselves. Mr. LLOYD GEORGE believed that the Bill would delay temperance reform. Mr. T. W. RUSSELL said if he had believed the Bill created a a newvested interest he would oppose it to the utter- most, but he did not believe anything of the kind. He thought that would do something for temperance and for —that reason he would vote for it.—Mr. GLADSTONE took exception to the arguments of the last speaker and defended the designation of that Bill as a Public House Endowment Bill, and said he knew of no terms that would more adequately describe it. That the Bill would operate as an endowment was clear, for the moment it became the law of the land every interest in every public-house would be greatly increased in price in the ' market, and could not be acquired except at an increased price. He expressed his intention to give the bill the utmost opposition, and he urged the Government to - withdraw the compensation clauses before it was too , late.—The CHANCELLOR or THE EXCHEQUER defended the provisions of the bill. [LEFT SITTING.]

r FIIENCH STRIKERS SET AT LIEERTY.—At a Cabinet Council held on Saturday morning, President Carnot, on the proposal of M. Fallieres, Minister of Justice, signed a decree granting a partial or full pardon to 72 persons undergoing sentence for offences committed in connec- tion with strikes. The sentences on 24 individuals only, most of them foreigners, who are gravely compromised, are maintained. GENERAL SIR HAVELOCK-ALLAN ROUGHLY USED.—At the .anti-compensation demonstration in London, on Saturday, as the crowd was leaving the Park, Sir H. Havelock-Allan, M.P., who was on horseback, was mis- taken for the Commissioner of Police, and was set upon by a gang of roughs, who pelted him with stones and earth, and tried to pull him off his horse. Leaving the Park by Stanhope-gate, the General rode slowly along Park-lane, and on a further attempt to lynch him, the police drew their staves, and dispersed the mob.
